title: 2.6 Million Fewer Americans Have ACA Coverage After Enhanced Subsidies Expire; HHS Blames "Phantom" Enrollment
institution: ACA Health Insurance Marketplace (HHS/CMS)
status: Ongoing -- enhanced subsidies lapsed at the end of 2025 and were not renewed by Congress; enrollment data through February 2026 shows the decline continuing
date_of_action: 2025-12 (enhanced ACA subsidies expire) through 2026-02 (enrollment data showing the decline)
what_changed: Enhanced ACA marketplace subsidies -- expanded tax credits that had made coverage more affordable for millions -- expired at the end of 2025 after Congress did not act to extend them. In February 2026, Trump officials proposed new ACA plan options featuring lower monthly premiums but deductibles exceeding $15,000 for individuals and $31,000 for families -- a structural shift officials framed as expanding choice, which critics say would leave enrollees exposed to catastrophic out-of-pocket costs before coverage meaningfully applies. A KFF poll reported in March 2026 found roughly 8 in 10 Americans with ACA marketplace plans were already paying higher health care costs following the subsidy expiration, with many enrollees cutting back on essentials like food and gas to afford coverage, while others reported reducing medication use or dropping coverage entirely as premiums and out-of-pocket costs rose. By April 2026, the coverage loss was also straining hospitals directly, not just enrollees: a healthcare-finance analysis found U.S. hospitals face an estimated $68.6 billion in lost revenue across 2026-2027 from rising uninsurance tied to the subsidy expiration and Medicaid changes combined. Florida -- one of ten states that never expanded Medicaid, leaving its hospitals with no expanded state safety net to absorb the loss -- was hit hardest: Bloomberg reported the state lost more than 440,000 marketplace enrollees in 2026, with between 750,000 and 1 million Floridians at risk of losing coverage overall given the state's above-average reliance on the enhanced subsidies; Florida, Georgia, and Texas together accounted for over 43% of national marketplace enrollment for the 2026 plan year. Individual Florida-serving hospital systems quantified their own exposure: HCA Healthcare projected a $1-1.2 billion 2026 hit from the lost subsidies, and AdventHealth projected roughly $1.5 billion in lost annual gross patient revenue from combined Medicaid and marketplace cuts. Federal data released in mid-2026 then showed the fuller national scope: roughly 2.6 million fewer Americans had ACA marketplace coverage in February 2026 than a year earlier, with Ohio and Oklahoma each losing nearly a third of their enrollees -- steeper drops than any other state -- and average costs for enrollees who wanted to keep their existing plans had risen 114% following the subsidy expiration. HHS, under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., attributed a significant share of the enrollment decline to a federal crackdown on 'phantom' or fraudulent enrollments -- citing an estimated 2.6 million improper or phantom enrollments nationally, including more than 1 million without a valid Social Security number, and suggesting nearly half of ACA enrollment growth from 2021-2024 may have been improper. Independent analysts and state officials disputed that framing, saying the enrollment collapse was more directly attributable to the subsidy expiration itself, sharply higher post-expiration premiums, and separately tightened eligibility rules restricting which immigrants can access subsidized coverage. CNBC reported the premium increases affected roughly 22 million Americans -- over 90% of ACA marketplace enrollees nationwide -- with premiums more than doubling for many after the subsidy expiration.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: HHS under Kennedy publicly attributed the enrollment decline primarily to a fraud/'phantom enrollment' crackdown rather than to the enhanced-subsidy expiration or premium increases that independent analysts identified as the more direct cause.

estimated_impact.summary: Roughly 2.6 million Americans lost ACA marketplace coverage in the year after enhanced subsidies expired, with the steepest state-level losses (nearly a third of enrollees) in Ohio and Oklahoma; HHS's public framing of the decline as primarily fraud-driven is disputed by independent analysts, who point instead to the subsidy expiration and resulting 114% average premium increase as the more direct cause.

Independent analysts and state officials attribute the bulk of the decline to subsidy expiration and premium increases, not fraud; HHS's own estimate of historical improper-enrollment growth (2021-2024) is itself a contested figure disputed by ACA-marketplace advocates, though a detailed rebuttal was not reviewed for this entry. Separately, insurance-market analysts warned in May 2026 reporting that the enrollment drop -- disproportionately among healthier, price-sensitive enrollees who leave first when subsidies shrink -- will leave insurers pricing 2027 plans against a smaller, sicker risk pool, projecting a further round of rate increases; this is a forward-looking analyst projection, not yet an observed 2027 rate figure, and should be framed as such.

Officials also proposed new low-premium/high-deductible ($15K individual/$31K family) ACA plan options.

title: Arizona SNAP Enrollment Cut in Half as State Adds Paperwork, Cuts Caseworkers to Avoid Federal Penalties Under Trump's Benefits Law
institution: Arizona Department of Economic Security (implementing federal SNAP rules under HR1/OBBBA)
status: Ongoing -- enrollment decline continuing as of May 2026, steeper federal error-rate penalties phase in starting October 2027
date_of_action: 2025-07 (HR1/OBBBA enacted) through 2026-05 (enrollment data)
what_changed: Following passage of Trump's HR1 ('One Big Beautiful Bill') tax and spending law, which imposes steep financial penalties on states with high SNAP payment error rates (Arizona's 2025 error rate was 10.8%, putting the state at risk of up to $300 million in penalties by fiscal year 2028 if the rate continues) and shifts more administrative costs onto states, Arizona increased the paperwork required of SNAP applicants while simultaneously cutting the caseworker staff available to process it. The number of Department of Economic Security staff reviewing SNAP eligibility fell from 1,370 in July 2024 to 880 by mid-2026. As a direct result, Arizona's SNAP enrollment collapsed from approximately 910,000 people in June 2025 to about 452,000 by May 2026 -- roughly a 50% decline in under a year. Applicants have described being unable to reach a caseworker despite placing up to 100 phone calls to the program. Food bank visits in the state now exceed SNAP enrollment for the first time, as many people who remain legally eligible for benefits are unable to navigate the increased paperwork burden with reduced staff support to process it. Update 2026-07-28: HR1 cuts SNAP by an estimated $187 billion nationally over the next decade, per NBC News reporting -- Arizona's enrollment collapse documented in this entry (roughly 200,000 children among those losing benefits) is one state-level instance of that broader national reduction, with food banks nationally reporting record demand as a result.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Signed HR1 into law, establishing the SNAP error-rate penalty structure that states including Arizona say has driven them to add paperwork requirements and cut caseworker capacity to avoid steep federal financial penalties.

estimated_impact.summary: Arizona's SNAP enrollment fell by roughly half in under a year as the state responded to federal penalty incentives by adding paperwork burdens and cutting caseworker staff rather than absorbing the administrative cost -- resulting in eligible families losing access to food assistance not because they no longer qualify, but because they cannot navigate the process with reduced state support, with food bank demand now exceeding SNAP enrollment for the first time.

title: Army cancels training courses, cuts pilot flight hours amid $4-6 billion budget shortfall tied to Iran war and border deployments
institution: U.S. Army
status: Ongoing -- shortfall and resulting cuts were still in effect as of May 2026 reporting
date_of_action: 2026-05 (reporting of internal Army budget documents)
what_changed: Internal Army documents showed the service facing a $4-6 billion budget shortfall, driving cancellation of training courses, cuts to pilot flight hours, and warnings of reduced overall readiness. The Army's premier combat-engineering school, the Sapper Course, was canceled, as was an artillery course set to begin at Fort Campbell, Kentucky. Aviation readiness was hit particularly hard, with pilots limited to minimum required flight hours. III Armored Corps, the Texas-based headquarters overseeing roughly 70,000 troops and hundreds of tanks, saw its training budget cut by nearly $292 million in late April 2026. Officials linked the shortfall to costs from the Iran war, an expanded southern-border military mission, rising personnel and fuel costs, and an ongoing National Guard deployment to Washington, D.C. projected to cost roughly $1.1 billion for the year -- money originally budgeted for training and readiness effectively redirected to cover these other mission costs. Update 2026-08-02: Surging fuel prices tied to the Iran war are a specifically quantified driver of the shortfall -- the average price the Pentagon paid per barrel of fuel climbed from $154.14 in October 2025 to $195.72 in April 2026, a nearly 27% increase in six months, adding more than $1 billion in unplanned costs to power jets, tanks, and other equipment. The Air Force alone is burning through roughly 10% more fuel than it had projected amid the ongoing Iran war.

title: Trump Fired the BLS Commissioner for 'Rigged' Data — His Own First-Term BLS Commissioner Called the Firing 'Totally Groundless'
institution: Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Department of Labor
status: Complete (commissioner fired and replaced; broader data-integrity concerns escalated, not resolved -- Labor Dept. Inspector General opened a formal audit; BLS has since lost 12 of 35 senior leaders)
what_changed: On August 1, 2025, hours after BLS reported that job growth had slowed to just 73,000 for July -- below expectations -- and revised the two prior months' job gains down sharply by a combined 258,000 (the biggest two-month downward revision since April 2020, at the start of the COVID crisis), Trump fired BLS Commissioner Erika McEntarfer via a Truth Social post, writing: 'I have directed my Team to fire this Biden Political Appointee, IMMEDIATELY... She will be replaced with someone much more competent and qualified.' Trump provided no evidence that McEntarfer, a Biden appointee confirmed to a fixed term in 2024, had manipulated the data, and Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer publicly supported the firing the same day, naming Deputy Commissioner William Wiatrowski as acting director. This was the first time in the Bureau's history a commissioner had been fired, rather than completing or being reappointed past their term. Separately, Trump's own budget proposal for the year had already called for an 8% staff reduction at BLS, and the Urban Institute separately documented a broader pattern across federal statistical agencies of data being removed from government websites or having fields altered in connection with executive orders targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion programming. Since the firing, BLS has lost 12 of its 35 senior leadership positions, per Brookings. The Labor Department's Office of Inspector General opened a formal audit of BLS's data-collection challenges for its inflation and labor-market reports. Separately, BLS's routine annual benchmark revision (released 2026, covering the year through March) found the economy added 911,000 fewer jobs than initially reported -- a large revision, but one BLS and outside economists (EPI) describe as a normal, transparent statistical process using more complete data, not a correction of an error or evidence of the manipulation Trump alleged in firing McEntarfer. The FY2026 budget also cut BLS's jobs-report and inflation-data budgets by about 8% each, alongside a similar workforce cut, consistent with the broader resource-constraint pattern this entry already documents.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Directly ordered the firing via social media, framing the weak jobs numbers themselves as evidence of manipulation. Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer publicly endorsed the move, stating she supported ensuring 'the American People can trust the important and influential data coming from BLS.' Notably, William Beach -- who served as BLS Commissioner during Trump's own first term -- publicly and specifically rejected the firing on the record: 'The totally groundless firing of Dr. Erika McEntarfer, my successor as Commissioner of Labor Statistics at BLS, sets a dangerous precedent and undermines the statistical mission of the Bureau... This escalates the President's unprecedented attacks on the independence and integrity of the federal statistical system. The President seeks to blame someone for unwelcome economic news.'

estimated_impact.summary: Beach, in a subsequent PBS interview, gave a specific technical rebuttal to the manipulation claim rather than a general political objection: he explained the commissioner has no direct access to alter the underlying data collected by career civil servants, and that the July revisions reflected genuinely new information (from state and local education-sector reporting) rather than any political interference -- 'no one disputed that we shouldn't use more information then to correct the initial estimates,' he noted, adding that comparably large revisions occurred during his own tenure as commissioner amid COVID, for unrelated reasons. The Urban Institute warned the firing 'undermines the integrity of the federal statistical agency data ecosystem' broadly, since BLS data (alongside the Census Bureau, Bureau of Economic Analysis, and other statistical agencies) underpins decisions made by governments, businesses, and individuals worth far more than any single jobs report.

estimated_impact.caveat: This entry concerns the firing and the specific, technical dispute over whether commissioner-level political interference in BLS data is even mechanically possible (Beach's rebuttal directly addresses this) -- it is a narrower and more specifically evidenced claim than the broader 'data integrity across federal statistical agencies' concern the Urban Institute raises, which draws on separate incidents (website data removal, DEI-related field changes) not specific to the BLS commissioner firing itself. These are related but distinct concerns and should not be conflated when citing this entry.

Core facts (the jobs numbers, the firing, the public statements) are corroborated across CNBC, PBS News, and the Urban Institute with no factual dispute about what happened, only about whether it was justified. Re-verified 2026-07-20: no reversal or vindication of the firing has occurred; if anything, the data-integrity concern has broadened institutionally (IG audit, senior-leadership attrition) beyond the single-commissioner dispute this entry originally documented. The 911,000-job benchmark revision should be presented carefully -- it is a much larger number than the original 258,000 two-month revision that preceded the firing, but EPI and BLS's own methodology describe annual benchmark revisions as routine, not as further evidence of manipulation either way; don't conflate the two figures or imply the larger number is itself scandalous without that context.

title: Federal Prisons Losing Corrections Officers to ICE en Masse After BOP Wage Cuts and a Canceled Union Contract
institution: Federal Bureau of Prisons
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition -- House Judiciary Democrats sent a formal letter to BOP Director William Marshall III in February 2026 demanding an immediate response; no confirmed remediation identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025 (ongoing through Feb. 2026 reporting)
what_changed: A ProPublica investigation found BOP has lost more than 1,400 staff members as corrections officers left federal lockups nationwide -- from Florida to California -- for ICE, which more than doubled its officer and agent headcount during a monthslong recruiting blitz offering $50,000 signing bonuses and substantially higher pay. Compounding the exodus, BOP itself cut wages by as much as 25% for frontline officers, instituted a hiring freeze, and canceled its collective bargaining agreement covering more than 30,000 federal correctional employees. ProPublica's reporting described federal prisons running low on basic supplies including food and toilet paper amid the staffing collapse. One BOP official told ProPublica: 'We're broken and we're being poached by ICE.' In response, four House Judiciary Democrats sent BOP Director William Marshall III a six-page letter in February 2026 demanding he explain how he plans to address the 'persistent, unsafe conditions' and 'pervasive shortage of critical staff.'

title: Commerce Department ban on Census Bureau statistical-noise privacy protections
institution: U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Economic Analysis (Department of Commerce)
status: Ongoing (order in effect as of June 2026; could be revoked by a future administration before the 2030 census)
date_of_action: 2026-06 (order issued; effects unfolding through 2030 census preparation)
what_changed: The Commerce Department, which oversees the Census Bureau, issued an order banning 'noise infusion' - one of the bureau's core techniques for anonymizing survey and administrative-record data before public release, mandated by federal law (13 U.S.C. §8) to protect respondents' confidentiality. Noise infusion has been used for decades, and more recently through a differential-privacy system built under former chief scientist John Abowd, to make it mathematically much harder to re-identify individuals in small-area statistics. The order leaves the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis only one remaining privacy option: 'coarsening' data (releasing broader, less-detailed categories) or not publishing some statistics at all. Data experts warn this could make data for many rural counties and small communities unpublishable, and that 2030 census redistricting data preparation - already underway - will need to be redesigned from scratch. The order followed, and is intertwined with, a separate 2025 lawsuit by America First Legal (co-founded by White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller) challenging the bureau's differential-privacy system, and came after a broader thinning of the bureau's statistical expertise amid Trump administration workforce cuts. It was issued with no public technical rationale, no advance opportunity for outside statisticians to review or comment, and no response from Commerce to a reporter's request for specific examples of the harm it claims to be fixing. Separately, the America First Legal lawsuit referenced above was dismissed in February 2026 by a three-judge federal panel as time-barred (plaintiffs waited too long to sue), which also rejected Rep. Byron Donalds's standing theory. When plaintiffs refiled, they dropped the differential-privacy challenge entirely and now focus solely on a different technique, statistical imputation (used to fill in missing population data) -- meaning the June 2026 noise-infusion ban was not compelled by any court ruling; it was a standalone Commerce Department policy action, issued independent of and after the litigation's core privacy claim had already been abandoned by its own plaintiffs. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- no new court filings or Commerce Department statements identified since the prior update.

primary_proponent.role: U.S. Secretary of Commerce, whose department issued the order and oversees the Census Bureau and BEA
primary_proponent.note: Commerce, under Lutnick, published the order banning noise infusion; Commerce spokesperson Kristen Eichamer defended it publicly as necessary to 'maintain public confidence' in the data, while declining to provide examples of noise infusion having undermined data integrity when asked directly by NPR.

estimated_impact.summary: Removing the bureau's primary legally-mandated privacy technique, with no substitute of comparable quality, is expected to shrink or eliminate published statistics for small counties, rural areas, and minority communities, and to force a redesign of 2030 census redistricting-data preparation already underway.

estimated_impact.caveat: Commerce's stated rationale is that 'indiscriminate use of noise infusion...ultimately undermined confidence in the department's products and cast doubt on their integrity,' and that coarsening better 'upholds our duty to safeguard the privacy of those who provide information' - i.e., the administration frames this as a pro-privacy, pro-integrity move, not a cut. Independent data-user advocates (Beth Jarosz, Association of Public Data Users; John Abowd, former Census chief scientist) and an anonymous current bureau employee dispute this, calling the change 'cataclysmic' for data production and noting it removed the normal scientific/public review process. Long-running controversy over the differential-privacy system predates this administration - Alabama Republican officials sued to block it in 2021 - so this is a continuation of a genuine, multi-year methodological dispute, not a one-sided fabrication.

confidence_note: High confidence on the existence, timing, and content of the order and the range of expert reaction, based on NPR's direct interviews with the Commerce Department spokesperson, a former Census Bureau chief scientist, and outside data-user advocates, corroborated by a September 2025 Commerce Inspector General audit and a CBPP policy report documenting broader statistical-agency budget and staffing pressure. The ultimate real-world impact on specific datasets is still unfolding and not yet independently audited. Re-verified 2026-07-20: worth noting clearly that the June 2026 noise-infusion ban and the America First Legal lawsuit are related but now legally separate tracks -- the lawsuit that originally challenged differential privacy no longer does, and the ban wasn't a court-ordered outcome. Don't cite the litigation as the ban's legal cause. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change to report.

title: Commerce Department bans Census Bureau's main privacy technique, forcing coarser or withheld data
institution: Census Bureau and Bureau of Economic Analysis (U.S. Department of Commerce)
status: Finalized -- Department Administrative Order 216-26 in effect
date_of_action: 2026-06 (order reported)
what_changed: The Commerce Department issued Department Administrative Order 216-26, banning the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis from using 'noise infusion' -- a widely-used disclosure-avoidance technique that adds small random statistical variation to published data so individuals can't be re-identified while still allowing detailed, granular statistics to be released. The order designates 'coarsening' (releasing less granular, more aggregated statistics, or withholding some datasets outright) as the preferred disclosure-avoidance method instead, and bars noise infusion for any statistical product going forward. Data scientists and demographers warned the change would force the bureau to either publish blurrier, less-detailed data or withhold some datasets entirely, since coarsening and noise infusion aren't interchangeable substitutes for the same privacy goal.

primary_proponent.name: Howard Lutnick
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Commerce
primary_proponent.note: Department Administrative Order 216-26 was issued under his department's authority; reporting attributes the order to the Commerce Department generally rather than quoting Lutnick personally on this specific decision, so this entry follows the schema's standard for using the highest-ranking accountable official when no more specific individual is on record.

estimated_impact.summary: Detailed Census Bureau and BEA statistics used for redistricting, disaster response, housing policy, and economic planning are expected to become less granular or unavailable, since agencies now have to choose between coarser aggregation and withholding data rather than using the noise-based method that let them publish detailed figures while still protecting privacy.
estimated_impact.caveat: No dollar or headcount figure has been reported for this policy -- the harm is a data-quality/availability degradation rather than a budget or staffing cut, so this entry has no quantified 'figures' the way most GSR entries do. Impact is described by data experts and demographers (Census Bureau's own disclosure-avoidance researchers, academics cited by NPR/Science) rather than an independent audit.

confidence_note: Well-corroborated by numerous independent outlets (NPR, Science, Wyoming Public Media, South Carolina Public Radio, FlowingData) and the Commerce Department's own order text/framing as reported. No formal GAO or Inspector General finding on this specific policy has been identified.

title: CFPB Ordered to Stop All Work, Nearly Defunded — Federal Judge Called It 'Hanging by a Thread'
institution: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
status: Ongoing litigation (Senate Banking Committee held a confirmation hearing for permanent-director nominee Brian Johnson on July 23, 2026; committee vote expected before the August recess, full Senate vote anticipated September 2026); Vought's acting-director authority under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act expires August 1, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-02-10 (stop-work order issued) through 2025-12-30 (federal judge's 'hanging by a thread' ruling)
what_changed: On February 10, 2025, newly installed Acting Director Russell Vought (who simultaneously serves as OMB Director) ordered all CFPB staff and contractors to stop working entirely and not return to agency offices. DOGE personnel were given access to CFPB's HR, payroll, and enforcement-records systems around the same time; Elon Musk posted 'CFPB RIP' on social media. A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order on February 14, 2025 blocking further firings, data destruction, or funding cuts, but by then CFPB's website had already been taken down and staff locked out of buildings and systems. Vought separately moved to cut off the agency's Federal Reserve funding entirely and canceled roughly $100 million in CFPB contracts. Court filings from CFPB leadership itself, filed in March 2025, proposed shrinking authorized staff from 1,174 to 556, sparing only the legal division (which defends the agency in the litigation over its own dismantling) from cuts. In April 2025, despite the court order, about 1,400 employees who had chosen to remain received layoff notices -- a reduction that would have left only about 200 of the agency's original ~1,700 staff. By December 2025, more than 30% of CFPB's authorized staff had departed. On December 30, 2025, the same federal judge overseeing the case rejected the administration's argument that Vought could lawfully withhold the agency's funding, ordering him to request continued Federal Reserve funding, which he did -- keeping CFPB funded through at least March 2026. A February 2026 report from Sen. Elizabeth Warren's office estimated that changes imposed after Vought took control of CFPB had cost Americans at least $19 billion in lost financial relief -- $15 billion from two rescinded rules (an overdraft-fee cap projected to save $5 billion/year, and a credit-card late-fee cap projected to save roughly $10 billion) plus nearly $4 billion from dropped enforcement actions and unfulfilled consent orders. In May 2026, CFPB removed roughly 1,700 web pages of consumer advisories, press releases, and testimony predating February 2025 from its public website (The Guardian's later, more precise count -- comparing the current site against Internet Archive Wayback Machine snapshots and a mirror site maintained by a former CFPB employee -- found at least 2,200 pages deleted as of early June 2026; the two figures describe the same underlying deletion campaign rather than separate events, with the most common deleted-page topics being enforcement, mortgages, banking, and rulemaking; CFPB also deleted its blog entirely and removed all press releases predating February 2025). Also in May 2026, acting CFPB Director Russell Vought ordered all remaining CFPB staff -- including roughly 450 workers previously based out-of-state -- to relocate to a new, smaller Washington, D.C. headquarters, ending remote work entirely; the bureau terminated leases on all four of its regional offices (San Francisco, Atlanta, Chicago, and New York). The new headquarters space, at 445 12th Street SW, has capacity for only about 550 workers -- roughly half the bureau's remaining headcount of approximately 1,100 -- a mismatch reporting characterized as designed to drive further attrition beyond the office's stated capacity limit alone. Relocation began June 1, 2026 with a hard compliance deadline of August 31 or termination. In June 2026, Trump nominated Brian Johnson -- a former CFPB deputy director under Kathy Kraninger and current Capital One executive -- to be permanent CFPB Director. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, said: 'Starting in August, Russ Vought can no longer legally serve as Donald Trump's hatchet man at the CFPB. So here comes the next hatchet man to try to finish the job.' Also in June 2026, CFPB removed all prior public reports describing its own supervisory activity. On June 22, 2026, Senate Banking Committee Democrats sent a formal letter to Acting Director Vought demanding an accounting of the deleted content and its legal basis. Senior leadership reported to the new headquarters starting July 6, 2026, with full D.C.-area staff required back five days a week by July 13. The Senate Banking Committee held Brian Johnson's confirmation hearing on July 23, 2026; Johnson declined to endorse eliminating the CFPB and said he keeps an 'open mind' about staffing levels, while deflecting questions about the agency reportedly dropping 42 enforcement cases against presidential donors. Separately, the D.C. Circuit remanded NTEU v. CFPB (the litigation over the Bureau's proposed 2026 reduction-in-force) back to the district court and held the appeal in abeyance, after CFPB and NTEU jointly asked for a stay pending Johnson's confirmation so he could decide whether to proceed with, modify, or abandon the RIF plan. Committee advancement is expected before the August recess, with a full Senate vote anticipated in September 2026 -- meaning Johnson is very unlikely to be confirmed before Vought's August 1 FVRA deadline, raising the practical likelihood that Acting Deputy Director Mark Paoletta becomes acting director in the interim (if Johnson is not confirmed by August 1, 2026, Paoletta would become acting director in Vought's place). Ahead of a Vought oversight hearing, a July 2026 follow-up report from Sen. Warren's office found an additional $7.5 billion in costs in the first half of 2026 -- ~$15 billion cumulative from abandoning the credit-card late-fee cap, ~$7.5 billion from repealing the overdraft-fee cap, and ~$4 billion from dropped enforcement actions and abandoned settlements/consent orders (including the 42 dropped enforcement cases against presidential donors) -- bringing the cumulative total Warren's office attributes to the CFPB rollbacks to up to $26.5 billion.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: Acting Director of CFPB (concurrently Director of the Office of Management and Budget)
primary_proponent.note: Vought was one of the architects of Project 2025, which explicitly called for Congress to abolish the CFPB (p. 837 of the document). He has publicly criticized CFPB staff in interviews, telling The Charlie Kirk Show that 'all they want to do is weaponize the tools of financial law against basically small mom-and-pop lenders and other small financial institutions.' This is the same official whose separate impoundment-related actions (NIH funding, broader OMB spending disputes) are covered in other entries across this project's Government Services Redirected and Cabinet-Level Legal Exposure trackers.

estimated_impact.summary: The presiding federal judge's own characterization is unusually direct for a legal ruling: she wrote that the administration was 'actively and unabashedly trying to shut the agency down' through funding cuts after being blocked from doing so through layoffs, and that CFPB 'is hanging by a thread.' The agency's own reporting states it had returned $19.7 billion to consumers since its 2010 creation as of January 2025 -- the scale of consumer-facing enforcement work now substantially curtailed. Former 13-year CFPB attorney Lisa Rosenthal, who resigned after the stop-work order, described the halted work (protecting victims of predatory payday loans, supervising student loan and auto-financing practices) in terms of what it no longer was: 'This work that I had carried out for these decades and that I cared so deeply about -- this was no longer that work.'

title: CIA Offers Buyouts Agency-Wide and Freezes Hiring to Realign Workforce with New Priorities
institution: Central Intelligence Agency
status: Implemented -- buyout offer and hiring freeze took effect February 2025; broader multi-year workforce reduction plan reported as ongoing
date_of_action: 2025-02-04 (buyout offer announced, February 6 deadline) through at least 2025-05 (multi-year reduction plan reported)
what_changed: On February 4, 2025, the CIA under newly confirmed Director John Ratcliffe offered buyouts to its entire workforce, giving employees until February 6, 2025 to accept -- a two-day window -- in exchange for eight months of pay plus benefits if they chose to resign. The agency simultaneously imposed a hiring freeze and began reviewing already-extended conditional job offers to new recruits, indicating offers not aligned with the agency's new focus were likely to be rescinded. Ratcliffe framed the changes as realigning the CIA toward new priorities, including a greater focus on the Western Hemisphere (targeting drug cartels and other threats not traditionally treated as top-tier adversaries) and covert operations, rather than legacy Cold War-era regional priorities. Beginning around March 7, 2025, the CIA also began terminating some probationary employees (generally those with fewer than two years on the job) citing a review of personnel suitability, following a federal judge's ruling allowing Director Ratcliffe to dismiss employees at his discretion -- a distinct, involuntary action layered on top of the earlier voluntary buyout program. National-security reporting at the time warned that the cuts came as U.S. intelligence had confirmed Russia and China were actively attempting to recruit recently fired or at-risk federal employees with security clearances, using LinkedIn, TikTok, and job postings, raising concern that thinning the intelligence workforce during a period of active foreign recruitment efforts compounded the risk. Reporting in May 2025 indicated this was part of a broader, multi-year plan across U.S. intelligence agencies to reduce the CIA's workforce by approximately 1,200 positions, with several hundred employees already having taken early retirement or the buyout by that point.

title: CISA Lost Roughly One-Third of Its Workforce, Including Election Security and Threat-Sharing Capacity
institution: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing (Kristi Noem was replaced as DHS Secretary by Markwayne Mullin, confirmed March 24, 2026; Mullin says the president has met with a likely CISA director nominee; DHS plans roughly 600 new CISA hires once a director is confirmed, with an initial 329-role 'mission-critical' hiring plan already underway -- about 180 tentative offers were out by the end of June 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-01 through 2026-06 (rolling cuts across multiple rounds: buyouts, layoffs, forced reassignments)
what_changed: Since January 2025, CISA -- the nation's primary civilian cyber-defense agency, created in 2018 specifically to coordinate federal response to critical infrastructure attacks -- lost roughly 1,000 employees, about one-third of its workforce, through a combination of buyout offers, early retirements, formal layoffs (reduction-in-force notices), and Management Directed Reassignments transferring CISA staff to ICE, CBP, FEMA, and the Federal Protective Service (refusing a reassignment could be grounds for termination). DHS Secretary Kristi Noem personally halted federal funding for the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) in March 2025, eliminating roughly $8.3 million of its remaining 2025 budget -- MS-ISAC provided threat-sharing services to state and local governments. The cuts disproportionately hit CISA's election security and disinformation-monitoring functions, which had drawn Republican criticism as politically biased 'censorship' under the prior administration. The agency has operated without a permanent, Senate-confirmed director since January 2025. The early 2025 cuts had specific, named costs: by March 4, 2025, NOTUS reported over 100 CISA cybersecurity experts had been laid off, including agents specifically assigned to track Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon, the Chinese state-sponsored hacking campaigns that had already infiltrated U.S. telecom networks and critical infrastructure; by March 8, 2025, CBS News reported the toll had grown to 130+, including top recruits working on CyberSentry, a program built specifically to detect cyberattacks against the U.S. power grid, pipelines, and water systems. On March 5, 2025, former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce testified to Congress that the mass federal firings -- more than 100,000 workers government-wide by that point, including 130+ from CISA -- would set back U.S. cyber defenses against China. Joyce continued sounding this warning publicly: at the Black Hat security conference in August 2025, CISA spokesperson Marci McCarthy defended the staffing purges as a return to the agency's 'core mission,' while Joyce countered that the U.S. had 'backslid' and lost critical national-defense capability, with nearly a third of CISA's workforce gone by that point. Congress's own October 2025 government shutdown compounded the damage months before the separate February 2026 DHS funding lapse described below: the Washington Post reported only about 35% of CISA staff remained active during the October shutdown even as ransomware and Chinese cyberattacks intensified, and Politico reported the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act -- the law providing legal liability protection for companies that voluntarily share cyber-threat data with the government -- lapsed during the same shutdown, prompting some companies to halt that cooperation entirely. Later that month, House Democrats formally accused DHS, under Secretary Noem, of unlawfully reassigning CISA cybersecurity staff to ICE, CBP, and the Federal Protective Service during the shutdown -- the same Management Directed Reassignment mechanism described above -- alleging the diversions violated the Antideficiency Act; a separate New York Times report the same week noted the cuts had also reached the State Department's cyber-diplomacy function. During the shutdown, on November 10, 2025, WIRED reported the Congressional Budget Office itself was hacked by a suspected foreign actor, an incident experts tied directly to the shutdown-driven halt in routine federal patching, monitoring, and device management. In December 2025, Bloomberg reported the administration eliminated CISA's retention-incentive pay program -- a tool used to keep cyber defenders from leaving for better-paying private-sector jobs -- despite the agency already having lost over a third of its staff; the change exposed many remaining employees to pay cuts of up to 25%, a further attrition risk on top of the losses already documented here. The February 2026 DHS funding lapse compounded this attrition: The New York Times reported CISA furloughed more than half of its remaining workforce during the shutdown, leaving fewer than 1,000 employees on duty at the nation's primary civilian cyber-defense agency during the funding gap; ABC News separately reported that with DHS unfunded for 45 days during that same shutdown, CISA furloughed roughly 60% of its remaining workforce, disrupting vulnerability assessments and further weakening federal cyber defenses at a time when officials were warning of rising Iran-linked cyber threats to critical infrastructure, including power, water, and federal civilian networks. Also in February 2026, acting CISA Director Madhu Gottumukkala moved to reassign two senior career officials -- CIO Bob Costello (CISA's CIO for over four years) and acting Chief Human Capital Officer Kevin Diana -- giving them seven days to accept new roles elsewhere in DHS or resign, following an earlier unsuccessful attempt to oust Costello over a contracting-decision dispute that other political appointees had previously intervened to stop. Kristi Noem was replaced as DHS Secretary by Markwayne Mullin, confirmed by the Senate 54-45 on March 24, 2026. In April 2026, Sean Plankey, Trump's first nominee to lead CISA, withdrew his own nomination, writing 'After thirteen months since my initial nomination, it has become clear the Senate will not confirm me' -- the nomination had been held up by a mix of Democratic senators (Ron Wyden, over a withheld telecom-security report) and Republican senators (Rick Scott, over an unrelated Coast Guard shipbuilding dispute), plus broader holds affecting all DHS nominees. CISA is now led by acting director Nick Andersen. Mullin has since said the president has met with a likely CISA director nominee (not yet named or formally nominated as of this update) and that DHS believes CISA needs roughly 600 new hires, though a full rebuild can't proceed in earnest until a director is confirmed. CISA has begun an initial hiring plan for 329 'mission-critical' roles, with about 180 tentative job offers extended by the end of June 2026 -- the first concrete numbers behind CISA's previously-announced, more general 2026 hiring push, which agency officials had cited the workforce reductions as having hampered preparedness for potential conflict with China. By June 2026, of CISA's authorized 3,292 positions, only 2,324 were actually filled -- a nearly 1,000-position gap. Five of the agency's ten regional directors were serving only in acting capacity, disrupting the primary points of contact state and local governments rely on for federal cybersecurity assistance. Update 2026-07-27: state election officials from both parties told USA Today that, ahead of the 2026 midterms, they no longer expect federal agencies to reliably share election-threat intelligence with them -- a direct downstream consequence of the CISA staffing cuts and reduced regional-director capacity already described above. States say they're increasingly relying on private technology companies and nonprofits to fill the gap in federal threat-sharing coordination.

title: Congress Rescinded $1.1B From Public Broadcasting; CPB Dissolved After 58 Years
institution: Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB)
status: Complete (CPB formally dissolved January 5, 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-04 (board members fired) through 2026-01-05 (CPB board votes to dissolve)
what_changed: In April 2025, Trump fired three members of CPB's board of directors; the fired directors argued in subsequent legal action that the dismissal was governmental overreach targeting an entity whose congressional charter specifically guarantees its independence from political control. In July 2025, Congress passed a $9 billion rescissions package (canceling previously appropriated funds) requested by the White House, including $1.1 billion earmarked for CPB through fiscal year 2027 -- the first time in nearly 60 years Congress had voted to not fund CPB. The House vote was 216-213, with all but two Republicans in favor; in the Senate, only Susan Collins (R-ME) and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) broke with their party to vote against the package, alongside two House Republicans (Brian Fitzpatrick, Mike Turner). Trump signed the bill and wrote on Truth Social: 'REPUBLICANS HAVE TRIED DOING THIS FOR 40 YEARS, AND FAILED....BUT NO MORE.' CPB announced August 1, 2025 that it would begin winding down, eliminating most staff positions by the September 30 fiscal year-end and retaining a small transition team through January 2026 to handle compliance and music-rights obligations. When the Senate Appropriations Committee subsequently declined to restore any funding for the following budget year, CPB's board voted to formally dissolve the organization entirely on January 5, 2026, rather than continue to exist in a defunded, vulnerable state -- CPB President and CEO Patricia Harrison described this as protecting 'the integrity of the public media system' by closing on the organization's own terms.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Personally pushed the rescission package and has repeatedly called CPB a 'monstrosity,' arguing public broadcasting -- particularly NPR -- displays 'extreme liberal bias.' OMB Director Russell Vought, who requested the rescissions package on the administration's behalf, told reporters afterward the administration would 'likely' send additional rescissions packages, saying 'there is still a great enthusiasm for these rescissions bills, because Congress wants to be a part of voting for these cuts and making them permanent.'

estimated_impact.summary: CPB funded more than 1,500 local radio and television stations nationwide; roughly 70% of its money went directly to 330 PBS and 246 NPR member stations. NPR President and CEO Katherine Maher estimated approximately 96% of all classical music broadcast in the United States airs on public radio stations specifically. The impact fell most heavily on rural and small-market stations with fewer alternative funding sources: specific documented effects include KCTS in Seattle abandoning long-form journalism ambitions, WFAE in Charlotte closing its community engagement facility, and WPSU in State College, Pennsylvania considering shutting down its radio station entirely. Sen. Susan Collins, despite voting to preserve funding, articulated the underlying tension directly: 'I share the frustration with the biased reporting by NPR, and I would support defunding it. Nevertheless, local TV and radio stations continue to provide important coverage' -- citing Maine-specific examples like the emergency alert network and local high school sports coverage.

title: CPSC's Three Democratic Commissioners Fired, Battery-Safety Standard Withdrawn, Agency Left in Republican-Only Rump
institution: Consumer Product Safety Commission
status: Complete (firings litigated and now final following the June 29, 2026 Trump v. Slaughter ruling)
date_of_action: 2025-05-08 (firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court finalization)
what_changed: On May 8, 2025, President Trump fired three of the CPSC's five commissioners -- Alexander Hoehn-Saric, Mary Boyle, and Richard Trumka Jr., all Biden appointees -- citing 'neglect of duty or malfeasance in office' without further detail, hours after the three had voted to block DOGE representatives from entering CPSC headquarters to fire staff employees. The CPSC's founding statute allows removal only for 'neglect of duty or malfeasance in office' and requires no more than three of five commissioners share a political party, structural protections designed to preserve a bipartisan agency that regulates the safety of thousands of consumer products. The fired commissioners sued; a federal judge in Maryland ruled the firings unlawful and ordered reinstatement, and the Fourth Circuit declined to stay that order, but the Supreme Court granted an emergency stay on July 23, 2025, allowing the firings to proceed while the appeal continued. During the roughly five weeks the three commissioners were absent, the two remaining Republican-aligned commissioners -- Acting Chairman Peter Feldman and Douglas Dziak -- withdrew a previously approved (3-2 vote) e-bike and lithium-ion battery safety testing standard from public comment; lithium-ion battery fires from e-bikes and similar devices have been a rising home-fire and fatality concern nationally. The same two commissioners released a CPSC FY2026 budget request proposing to cut the agency's funding and staffing and to transfer CPSC's functions to the Department of Health and Human Services, led by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court's ruling in Trump v. Slaughter -- which held FTC commissioners' for-cause removal protections unconstitutional -- prompted CPSC Acting Chairman Feldman to state publicly that the fired commissioners' 'claims should now fail as a matter of law,' effectively finalizing the terminations. As of this writing the CPSC operates with only two commissioners, both Republican-aligned.

title: Federal Disease Surveillance Cuts Coincide With Emergence of Flesh-Eating Bacteria, Screwworm, and Malaria-Reintroduction Risk
institution: HHS/CDC and USDA disease-surveillance programs
status: Ongoing -- most surveillance reductions remain in place as of mid-2026; the ocean-monitoring-instrument removal was reversed after congressional opposition
date_of_action: 2025 (surveillance program cuts begin) through 2026-07 (reporting on emerging health threats)
what_changed: The Trump administration reduced or eliminated multiple federal disease-surveillance programs beginning in 2025. As of July 1, 2025, CDC's FoodNet (the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network, a CDC/USDA/FDA/state partnership covering 10 sites) stopped requiring reporting on six of the eight pathogens it was built to track -- Campylobacter, Cyclospora, Listeria, Shigella, Vibrio, and Yersinia all became optional, leaving only Salmonella and STEC (E. coli) mandatory; Cyclospora surveillance had been mandatory since 1997. The administration also began removing hundreds of deep-sea ocean-monitoring instruments used to track ocean conditions that help predict pathogen proliferation, including Vibrio; this removal was later reversed following congressional opposition. USDA lost 18% of its workforce (more than 20,000 employees) in the first half of 2025. USAID, dismantled entirely in 2025, had provided global disease-surveillance and response funding, including stripping more than $300 million from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization and targeting roughly 80% of global malaria grants for termination, ending a U.S. malaria-prevention investment that had exceeded $9 billion since 2005. These reductions coincided with the emergence or resurgence of multiple disease threats in 2026: a 2026 Cyclospora outbreak that food-safety commentators say the weakened surveillance system was slower to detect and characterize (though some analyses argue the surveillance changes did not directly cause the outbreak itself -- see caveat); Vibrio vulnificus ('flesh-eating bacteria') cases in Florida and detections in New York coastal waters (CDC estimates roughly 80,000 Vibrio infections annually, with about 1 in 5 Vibrio vulnificus wound infections fatal, sometimes within days); the first confirmed U.S. case of New World Screwworm in June 2026, with over a dozen animals infected, threatening the cattle industry; and a CDC warning in May 2026 that 'the country remains susceptible to malaria reintroduction' despite the disease's 1951 eradication in the U.S.

estimated_impact.summary: Public health experts, including former CDC director Tom Frieden and infectious-disease specialists, warn the surveillance reductions have left the country less able to detect emerging disease threats before they spread widely -- a concern illustrated concretely by the near-simultaneous emergence of flesh-eating bacteria in new coastal areas, the first U.S. screwworm case in decades, and a CDC-flagged malaria-reintroduction risk.

title: DOE's nuclear waste cleanup office loses nearly half its workforce, GAO finds
institution: Department of Energy, Office of Environmental Management
status: Ongoing -- 45% vacancy rate at end of FY2025 per GAO, with site-level rates as high as 100%; DOE plans to hire 174 workers in FY2026
date_of_action: 2025-03-04 (first Carlsbad Field Office lease-termination attempt) through 2026-05 (GAO report)
what_changed: The Carlsbad Field Office's eventual collapse to 100% vacancy had an earlier warning sign than the GAO report alone shows: on March 4, 2025, DOGE included the Carlsbad Field Office's 90,000-square-foot Skeen-Whitlock Building lease on a spreadsheet of more than 7,000 federal leases marked for termination, citing roughly $810,000 in annual savings. The office, staffed by about 200 workers, directly manages the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP) -- the only U.S. site licensed to permanently dispose of transuranic nuclear waste, including plutonium-contaminated material, stored in a deep salt formation -- and includes an emergency response center for handling nuclear-material accidents. Following bipartisan New Mexico congressional pushback (Rep. Gabe Vasquez among others) over the national-security and public-safety risk of disrupting the only facility of its kind, GSA reinstated the lease within days, confirming by March 6, 2025 the office was no longer slated for termination. That reversal, however, did not stop the underlying workforce attrition documented below: a Government Accountability Office report found the Department of Energy's Office of Environmental Management -- responsible for cleaning up nuclear contamination from World War II- and Cold War-era weapons programs at sites across the country -- ended FY2025 with a 45% vacancy rate, roughly half its needed workforce. Of 409 staff who left in 2025, 76% (312) departed through the White House's deferred resignation program; nearly half of those departures (180) were in positions GAO classified as mission-critical, spanning engineering, contracting, physical sciences, and IT management. Vacancy rates varied sharply by site: 62% at Los Alamos National Laboratory, and 100% -- every position empty -- at the Carlsbad Field Office, the same office whose building lease had been targeted, then spared, a year earlier. GAO further warned that 35% of DOE-EM's remaining 856 employees will be eligible to retire by the end of 2030, meaning attrition is likely to continue independent of any further resignation programs. DOE has said it plans to hire 174 workers in FY2026, which GAO's analysis indicates would still leave significant workforce gaps.

title: DOE Dismantles Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, Cancels $3.7B+ in Awarded Projects
institution: Department of Energy (Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations)
status: Complete (office wound down; zero FY2026 funding provided by Congress)
date_of_action: 2025-05-30 (first project terminations announced) through 2026 appropriations (OCED zeroed out)
what_changed: The Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (OCED) was created in 2021 to manage roughly $27 billion in funding for large-scale clean energy demonstration projects -- hydrogen hubs, direct air capture hubs, long-duration energy storage, and industrial decarbonization -- and had committed over $18 billion to about 100 projects by November 2025. Congress's FY2026 appropriations bill, passed in early 2026, formalized the outcome by providing zero new funding to OCED and directing DOE to report quarterly on the redistribution of the office's remaining obligated and unobligated funds.

title: NLRB Deleted DOGE System-Access Records Before GAO Investigators Could Examine Them

title: DOJ Civil Rights Division Lost 70% of Its Attorneys — Voting Section Down From 30 to 3
institution: Civil Rights Division, U.S. Department of Justice
status: Ongoing (departure rate now over 75%; Voting Section led in acting capacity by a former Public Interest Legal Foundation attorney; White House reportedly considering defunding a related election-observer program)
date_of_action: 2025-01 (initial departures begin) through 2025-10 (Justice Connection's most recent departure count)
what_changed: Since President Trump's January 2025 inauguration, an estimated 250-260 attorneys -- roughly 70% of the division's approximately 365-person attorney roster -- have resigned, accepted the administration's deferred-resignation offer, or been reassigned elsewhere within DOJ. By October 2025, Justice Connection (a support network founded by former division attorneys) estimated the departure count had grown to nearly 400 people, about 75% of attorneys. The Voting Section specifically -- responsible for enforcing the Voting Rights Act -- fell from an estimated 30 attorneys in January to just 3 by May 2025. The section devoted to ensuring nondiscrimination by recipients of federal funds was left with no attorneys whatsoever, per the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights. Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon, confirmed in April 2025, sent new mission statements to each of the division's 11 sections shortly after taking office, redirecting the Voting Section's focus from protecting against discrimination toward pursuing voter fraud, and telling the Educational Opportunities Section that its work required 'the full dedication of this section's resources, attention and energy to the priorities of the president.' Career section-chief managers -- in some cases with decades of institutional tenure spanning multiple administrations of both parties -- were removed from leadership roles and reassigned to processing public records requests or complaint intake, which several described as a deliberate push to induce their resignation. By August 2025, DOJ was actively soliciting permanent internal transfers from other CRT sections to refill the most depleted offices (Voting, Employment Litigation, Educational Opportunities), some of which were themselves already down more than 75% of their attorneys. The Voting Section is now led in an acting capacity by Maureen Riordan, previously an attorney at the Public Interest Legal Foundation, a conservative legal group whose stated mission is to 'fight against lawlessness in American elections' -- a notable leadership choice for a section this entry documents was redirected toward pursuing voter fraud rather than voting-rights enforcement. As of March 2026, the White House was reportedly considering ending funding for a separate, longstanding DOJ election-observer program aimed at protecting minority voting rights, according to CBS News sources. Departures across the division have continued to be counted at roughly 75%, consistent with Justice Connection's October 2025 estimate already in this entry, rather than climbing further as of this update. Update 2026-07-26: a DOJ spokesperson has since gone on the record denying the reported consideration of ending the election-observer program's funding, stating the Department 'has no plans to end its monitorship program which is integral to assessing compliance with federal voting rights laws across the country.' This resolves the 'reportedly considering' item from the prior update with an explicit denial, though it does not address or retract the underlying reporting that such defunding had been discussed internally. Reuters reporting (Feb. 2026) found the division's unit prosecuting police and federal-agent misconduct lost roughly two-thirds of its attorneys, from about 40 down to as few as 13, with charges under the civil rights statute most commonly used in federal excessive-force cases falling about 36% to 54 total in 2025 -- the lowest since 2020. Section supervisors reportedly instructed staff early in the administration that law-enforcement-misconduct investigations would proceed only in egregious circumstances (e.g. a death in custody or sexual assault), with state and local authorities expected to lead most other cases. Former DOJ lawyers cited in the reporting expressed doubt the diminished section could conduct thorough investigations of recent incidents, including the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis -- the same shootings this tracker's prosecution/cabinet-level/bondi-doj-renee-good-widow-investigation-2026.json entry documents DOJ leadership blocking a standard investigation of and instead pressuring an investigation of Good's widow.

They need to pursue them elsewhere. That's not going to be happening at the DOJ.'

Joseph Rich, who led the Voting Section from 1999-2005 under both a Democratic and Republican administration, raised a specific operational concern about the reduced Voting Section potentially bringing voter-fraud suits 'right in the middle of an election.'

title: USAID/CDC Staff Removals Slowed Response to an Unidentified Deadly Illness Cluster in DRC's Equateur Province -- Cause Never Definitively Confirmed
institution: USAID (in dismantlement) / CDC global health security programs

date_of_action: 2025-01 (USAID/CDC staff removed from DRC posts, CDC ordered to halt WHO collaboration) through 2025-03 (illness clusters investigated and contained)
what_changed: Beginning in January 2025, two clusters of an unidentified illness caused a wave of deaths in the Bolomba and Basankusu health zones of DRC's Equateur province, eventually totaling roughly 2,969 reported cases and 66 deaths across both clusters. Wired reported that the USAID and CDC staff who would normally work directly with DRC's health ministry to identify and contain such an outbreak had been removed from their DRC posts as part of the agency's dismantlement, and that a separate January 2025 executive order required CDC to cease collaboration with the WHO -- reducing U.S. visibility into and support for the response. WHO and CDC investigators ultimately could not definitively confirm a single cause; leading hypotheses included bacterial meningitis and chemical or food-borne poisoning, with one thread of the investigation tracing part of the Bolomba cluster to three children who died after eating a bat carcass. The clusters were brought under control by late March 2025 without ever being conclusively attributed to a single pathogen or cause.

title: Education Department Rescinds Disparate-Impact Standard From Title VI Civil Rights Enforcement
institution: U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights
status: Final rule, effective July 24, 2026
date_of_action: 2026-07-24 (final rule effective)
what_changed: Citing Executive Order 14281, the Department of Education finalized a rule rescinding disparate-impact provisions from its regulations implementing Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, effective July 24, 2026. Disparate-impact provisions had allowed investigators to find a school policy violated federal civil rights law based on its disproportionate effect on students of a particular race or ethnicity -- demographic outcome data alone -- even without a facially discriminatory policy or proof of discriminatory intent. Roughly 60 civil rights and education organizations publicly condemned the change, warning it 'will hurt Black, Latino, Asian American, and Native American students, other students of color, and other marginalized students who face higher rates of discrimination.'

title: SAVE Student-Loan Plan Dismantled Over 18 Months, From Application Freeze to Full Termination for 7.5 Million Borrowers

what_changed: On February 18, 2025, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the Biden-era SAVE (Saving on a Valuable Education) income-driven repayment plan -- which had reduced payments to as little as 5% of a borrower's discretionary income and offered forgiveness after 10 years for borrowers who originally borrowed $12,000 or less -- exceeded the Education Secretary's statutory authority, and directed the lower court to broaden its injunction to block the entire SAVE rule, calling into question the legality of related income-contingent plans (PAYE, REPAYE) as well. Late on February 24, 2025, the Education Department responded by pulling down the online application for all income-driven repayment (IDR) plans and Direct loan consolidation entirely -- not just SAVE -- cutting off enrollment access for borrowers who wanted to switch plans regardless of which IDR plan they were pursuing. By mid-March 2025, the Department had closed applications across every IDR plan and restricted eligibility for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, leaving millions of borrowers unable to access repayment calculators or determine their new payment obligations; some reported being unable to determine whether to take a second job or plan for default. Starting July 1, 2026, loan servicers began issuing notices giving borrowers 90 days to select a new repayment plan; the Department's chosen replacement option, a new income-driven plan called the Repayment Assistance Plan, ties payments to income and household size with fixed 10-25-year terms, but results in higher monthly payments for most affected borrowers than SAVE had. Borrowers exiting forbearance without selecting a new plan in time would resume payments automatically under a plan that could be substantially costlier than what they had budgeted for during the intervening period of relief.

title: EEOC Loses Quorum for Nine Months After Trump Fires Two Democratic Commissioners
institution: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
status: Resolved as a quorum matter (quorum restored October 7, 2025 with Senate confirmation of a third commissioner); the underlying legal challenge to the firings was voluntarily dismissed July 6, 2026 after the Supreme Court's Trump v. Slaughter ruling foreclosed it
date_of_action: 2025-01-28 (firings) through 2025-10-07 (quorum restored); related litigation resolved 2026-07-06
what_changed: On January 28, 2025, President Trump fired EEOC Commissioners Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels, both Democratic appointees, along with General Counsel Karla Gilbride -- in the agency's 60-year history, no commissioner had ever before been removed before the end of their term. Burrows's term was not set to expire until 2028, Samuels's not until 2026. Title VII requires three commissioners for the EEOC to have a quorum; without one, the agency could continue routine case processing but could not initiate formal rulemakings or issue, modify, or revoke formal guidance. The agency operated without a quorum for over eight months. In April 2025, Samuels sued Trump, the EEOC, and Chair Andrea Lucas, arguing her termination before the end of her statutory term was unlawful. Quorum was restored October 7, 2025, when the Senate confirmed Brittany Panuccio as a third commissioner, giving the EEOC a 2-Republican (Lucas, Panuccio), 1-Democrat (Kalpana Kotagal) composition, with Lucas subsequently named permanent Chair on November 5, 2025. With quorum restored, the EEOC gained the votes needed to pursue the policy changes documented elsewhere in this dataset, including the EEO-1 data-collection rescission proposal. Samuels's lawsuit remained pending until the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter on June 29, 2026, substantially expanding presidential removal power over independent-agency officials and overturning the 91-year-old Humphrey's Executor precedent that had previously insulated such agencies from at-will removal. Concluding the ruling foreclosed her claim, Samuels voluntarily dismissed her lawsuit on July 6, 2026.

On May 14, 2026, the EEOC submitted a proposed rule to the White House's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) titled 'Rescission of EEO-1, EEO-2, EEO-3, EEO-4, EEO-5, and Reporting Requirement Under Title VII, the ADA, GINA, and the PWFA.' The proposal would eliminate the mandatory annual and biennial workforce demographic data collections that have applied since 1966 to private employers with 100 or more employees, unions, state and local governments, and public school systems, covering employee race, ethnicity, and sex data across job categories. OIRA concluded its review on June 9, 2026, clearing the way for the proposal to be published in the Federal Register for public comment. As of the last-verified date, the EEOC had not opened its EEO-1 filing portal for 2025 data, leaving employers uncertain whether any further demographic data collection will occur before a final rule is issued. The move follows the EEOC's 2025 decision to rescind the option for employers to report non-binary employees on the form, and a separate, still-pending EEOC proposal to rescind a 1979 regulation permitting voluntary affirmative action plans. Re-verified 2026-07-19: the proposed rule had still not been published in the Federal Register as of this update. The EEOC's own regulatory agenda projects publication in July 2026 with a comment period running into September 2026, and the Commission held a Sunshine Act-noticed meeting on July 17, 2026 that included the draft rescission rule -- both signs publication remains imminent, but no notice-and-comment period had formally opened as of this writing. Update 2026-07-26: On July 21, 2026, the Commission voted 2-1 along party lines to advance the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, authorizing publication in the Federal Register and opening a 30-day public comment period (narrower than the September 2026 window earlier projected in the EEOC's own regulatory agenda); a public hearing on the proposal is scheduled for August 11, 2026. Employers remain subject to EEO-1 filing obligations for the 2026 cycle in the meantime.

title: EPA's Environmental-Justice Screening Tool and NOAA's Billion-Dollar Disaster Database Both Discontinued
institution: Environmental Protection Agency; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
status: Both discontinuations are final as of this entry -- EJScreen taken offline, the NOAA disaster database retired with no updates beyond 2024

what_changed: EPA's EJScreen -- a mapping and screening tool combining environmental and demographic indicators to identify communities facing higher combined environmental and socioeconomic burdens -- was taken offline by the Trump administration between February 3 and February 5, 2025; a nonprofit, the Public Environmental Data Project, has since built a replica to keep the underlying data accessible. title: EPA Eliminated Its Scientific Research Office, Placing the Successor Directly Under the Administrator's Political Control
institution: Office of Research and Development (ORD), Environmental Protection Agency
status: Complete (formally eliminated; Congress notified February 2026 that closure is finalized)
date_of_action: 2025-05 (reorganization first announced) through 2026-02-13 (EPA formally notified Congress of ORD's elimination)
what_changed: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced in May 2025 that the agency's Office of Research and Development -- described by AFGE Council 238 President Justin Chen as 'the heart and brain of the EPA' -- would be eliminated and its scientists redistributed into other EPA program offices. On July 18, 2025, EPA formally announced ORD's elimination and the creation of a replacement, the Office of Applied Science and Environmental Solutions (OASES). Unlike ORD, which operated as its own independent division, OASES was placed directly under the EPA Administrator's office -- a structural change critics say subjects scientific research directly to political oversight rather than insulating it. Notably, 'research' does not appear anywhere in the new office's name, which former ORD senior science adviser Andy Miller said reflects what the reorganization was actually designed to eliminate: 'the kind of work that points out that there are still problems.' More than 300 ORD staff, including senior scientists, had already left via deferred-resignation offers before the formal announcement. As many as 1,155 of ORD's 1,540 positions -- chemists, biologists, toxicologists, and other scientists across 10 facilities nationwide -- were identified as at risk of layoff in documents reviewed by Democratic staff on the House Science Committee. EPA notified Congress on February 13, 2026 that the office's elimination was finalized, roughly nine months after Zeldin first announced the plan; the agency has not disclosed which offices remaining former-ORD employees were transferred to, or when OASES's top leadership positions would be permanently filled.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.role: EPA Administrator
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced and defended the reorganization, framing the mass layoffs using the government euphemism 'reduction in force' and stating it would ensure the agency could 'better fulfill that mission while being responsible stewards of your hard-earned tax dollars.' An EPA spokesperson separately described the restructuring as reflecting 'an unwavering commitment to gold-standard science' through 'integration of scientific expertise directly into EPA's offices' -- the administration's stated rationale is that embedding scientists in program offices improves rather than diminishes the agency's science capacity, a claim directly disputed by the researchers and former officials quoted below. This is the same EPA Administrator whose actions are covered in several deregulation-tracker entries in this project (endangerment finding rescission, MATS mercury standards, etc.) -- this entry covers the elimination of the scientific research infrastructure underlying those separate regulatory actions, not the regulatory actions themselves.

estimated_impact.summary: Independent scientists outside EPA identified specific, concrete functions at risk: ORD maintained toxicology databases used by state and local governments, industry, and nonprofits to assess chemical risks, and its atmospheric/hydrologic models are used by researchers worldwide to study pollutants like particulate matter and ozone. Allen Burton, an environmental scientist at the University of Michigan, specifically warned the closure could delay or prevent new methods for assessing risks from chemical mixtures (which can differ meaningfully from individual-substance risk, a core ORD research function). Rep. Zoe Lofgren, ranking Democrat on the House Science Committee, called it a 'travesty' with 'generational impacts on Americans' health and safety.'

title: FAA Air Traffic Controller Shortage — Chronic Structural Crisis, Acutely Worsened by 2025 Shutdown
institution: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation
status: Ongoing, unresolved (FAA released a new workforce plan in 2026; current administrator says full staffing may never be reached under the existing structure)
date_of_action: Structural decline since 2013; acute crisis point during the Oct-Nov 2025 government shutdown
what_changed: IMPORTANT ATTRIBUTION NOTE: unlike most entries in this tracker, this is predominantly a chronic, multi-administration structural problem, not a single action taken by the current administration. GAO's own December 2025 report traces the roots to the 2013 budget sequester (which froze hiring), the 2018-2019 shutdown (35 days, further hiring/training delays), and COVID-19 (FAA Academy training suspended 4 months in 2020, reduced-rate training through 2022). The controller workforce declined about 6% since 2015 even as flight volume rose ~10%; the FAA employed 13,164 controllers at the end of FY2025, and 19 of the 30 largest facilities are staffed below 85% of FAA's own targets. What IS specific to the current administration: the 43-day Oct-Nov 2025 shutdown further disrupted hiring and training pipelines and forced acute flight reductions (see the related, separate entry on the FAA's 10% traffic cut at 40 airports). Current FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Congress in December 2025 that towers would 'never' reach full staffing under the agency's existing structure, stating plainly: 'The system is designed to be chronically understaffed.' Separately, a 2025 proposal to build a second controller training academy (to relieve the bottleneck at the single Oklahoma City academy) was blocked in Congress amid cost and oversight objections, despite FAA and safety experts' warnings that one campus cannot produce enough certified controllers quickly enough. The FAA's new 2026 workforce plan, released in May 2026, resolved the staffing gap partly by lowering the goal itself: full-staffing target dropped from the 14,633 controllers the agency had forecast needing in 2024 to 12,563, a reduction of more than 2,000 positions from the prior target -- the FAA frames this as a modernization-driven reassessment of actual need, not merely redefining the shortfall away, but the effect is that a large share of the 'gap closing' reflects a lower bar rather than more controllers hired. As of June 2026, the FAA was roughly 3,000 certified controllers below even its original, higher target (about 10,800 actual against a ~13,800 historical goal). The staffing shortfall had concrete summer-2026 consequences: the FAA capped Chicago O'Hare at 2,708 scheduled daily operations from May 17 through October 24, 2026, a nearly 15% cut from airline-planned schedules, with New York and Southern California TRACONs also cited as most strained. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change to the core FAA civilian-controller narrative; a July 21, 2026 DoD Inspector General report on military air-traffic-controller shortages concerns a separate workforce (military, not FAA/DOT) and is not folded into this entry.

primary_proponent.name: Not a single clearly attributable action -- structural, cross-administration problem
primary_proponent.role: N/A
primary_proponent.note: Current FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford is the named official who has publicly acknowledged and described the crisis ('we'll never catch up'), but he is managing an inherited, decades-long shortfall rather than having personally caused it. This entry exists in this tracker because the current administration's 2025 shutdown measurably worsened an already-severe situation, and because the current administration's response (workforce plan, blocked second academy) is itself now part of the ongoing story -- not because the underlying shortage was created by this administration alone.

Congressional briefing materials link the staffing gap to a rise in reported 'near misses' nationally. NATCA (the controllers' union) states the FAA is about 3,800 controllers short of target, with 41% of certified controllers working 10-hour days, six days a week.
