title: FDA vaccine/biologics division leadership purge and COVID vaccine access restriction
institution: FDA — Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER)
status: Ongoing -- leadership churn continued past this entry's prior update: Szarama's tenure as acting director lasted only about three weeks before she was replaced by Karim Mikhail, the current acting director as of this update, while a permanent successor search continues (Houman Hemmati reported as a frontrunner candidate, not yet confirmed)
date_of_action: March 2025 - April 2026
what_changed: CBER, the FDA division that regulates vaccines, gene therapies, and blood products, went through six different directors across it and its sister division (CDER) since January 2025. Longtime CBER director Peter Marks resigned in March 2025 amid reported disagreements with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over vaccine policy. Vinay Prasad was installed as CBER director in May 2025. In July 2025 Prasad was forced out after backlash over his handling of Sarepta Therapeutics' Duchenne muscular dystrophy gene therapy, then reinstated roughly two weeks later after Commissioner Marty Makary intervened. Upon returning, Prasad fired the official in charge of vaccine safety/surveillance and took direct control of that function himself, and went on to push out at least seven other agency leaders during his second tenure. In May 2025, Makary and Prasad co-authored a New England Journal of Medicine framework limiting FDA approval of updated COVID-19 vaccines to adults 65+ and people with qualifying risk factors, reversing the prior policy of a universal annual-vaccine recommendation for everyone 6 months and older; manufacturers must now run new randomized trials to get approval for healthy people outside that group. Prasad also repeatedly overruled career staff on individual drug and vaccine decisions (initially refusing to review Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine, reversed only after White House pressure; rejecting or discouraging gene-therapy applications from uniQure, Ultragenyx, Capricor, and Replimune). Prasad departed CBER for a second and final time on April 30, 2026; deputy director Katherine Szarama was elevated to acting director, but departed that role herself after only about three weeks. Karim Mikhail was named acting director in mid-May 2026 and remained in that role as of this update, telling STAT News in July 2026 his goal was simply to 'return' the biologics center 'to normal' after the turmoil of the prior year. Dr. Houman Hemmati, an ophthalmologist and COVID-response critic, was reported in April 2026 as the frontrunner candidate for the permanent CBER director role; no permanent appointment had been confirmed as of this update. Re-verified 2026-07-26: Karim Mikhail remains acting director; no permanent appointment confirmed. Trade-press reporting (Zamann Pharma Support, July 24, 2026) indicates the FDA is expected to name permanent CDER and CBER directors together, with Hemmati still described as a frontrunner candidate for CBER -- a signal of movement, not yet a confirmed change.

title: FDA Refused to Even Review Moderna's mRNA Flu Vaccine Despite a 40,000-Person Trial Showing Stronger Protection for Older Adults

title: Trump's Attempt to Fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook Blocked by Supreme Court, Fed Independence Preserved
institution: Federal Reserve Board of Governors
status: Blocked (Supreme Court allowed Cook to remain in office pending further litigation; underlying 'for cause' merits not yet decided)
date_of_action: 2025-08-25 (attempted firing) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling)
what_changed: In August 2025, President Trump attempted to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook -- the first attempted removal of a sitting Fed governor in the central bank's 111-year history -- citing mortgage-fraud allegations against her from before she joined the Fed, raised by FHFA Director (and later Director of National Intelligence) William Pulte. Cook, who denied the allegations and was never charged, sued, arguing her removal was not 'for cause' as the Federal Reserve Act requires and that she was denied due process. A federal district court blocked the firing with a preliminary injunction; the D.C. Circuit declined to lift it; and on June 29, 2026 -- the same day it ruled against FTC Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter in the companion case Trump v. Slaughter -- the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in Trump v. Cook that Cook could remain in her position while her lawsuit proceeds. Chief Justice Roberts, writing for a majority that included conservative Justice Kavanaugh alongside the Court's three liberals, held that accepting the administration's position 'would in effect transform the Federal Reserve's for-cause protection into at-will employment' and stressed that 'not only the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve's design.' The Court explicitly carved the Federal Reserve out of the broader independence-narrowing logic it applied to the FTC, CPSC, NCUA, and other agencies the same day. Cook remained in her seat throughout, participating in the Fed's September 2025 rate-setting meeting. Trump responded on Truth Social that the ruling was 'strictly procedural' and vowed further action; Pulte stood by his fraud allegations. Re-verified 2026-07-19: no further procedural movement identified since the June 29, 2026 Supreme Court ruling; the case remains before the lower courts on the underlying 'for cause' merits question, unchanged from the prior update. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no further procedural movement identified; the case remains before the lower courts on the underlying 'for cause' merits question, unchanged from the July 19, 2026 update.

estimated_impact.summary: An attempted removal of a sitting Federal Reserve governor -- widely described by Fed Chair Jerome Powell as 'perhaps the most important legal case in the Fed's 113-year history' -- was blocked, preserving the central bank's independence from at-will presidential removal even as the Court simultaneously stripped similar protections from most other independent agencies the same day.

title: Survey of 300+ Fired Federal Workers Finds 95% Report Ongoing Mental Health Harm, Nearly a Year After Court Found Firings Unlawful
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and government-wide probationary workforce
status: Harm ongoing/documented as of survey publication; underlying OPM firing directive was ruled unlawful in September 2025, but reporting reviewed does not indicate systemic reinstatement or compensation for affected workers
date_of_action: 2025-02 (OPM directive to mass-fire probationary employees) through 2026-05 (survey results published)
what_changed: In February 2025, the Office of Personnel Management directed federal agencies to mass-terminate probationary employees -- workers typically in their first one to two years in a position or newly promoted role, who have fewer job protections than tenured federal staff. More than 25,000 probationary employees were fired government-wide as a result. In September 2025, U.S. District Judge William Alsup ruled that OPM had unlawfully directed agencies to carry out these terminations. In May 2026 -- more than a year after the initial firings and roughly eight months after the court's unlawfulness finding -- a group of former fired probationary employees conducted and published a survey of more than 300 of their fired colleagues. The survey found that 95% of respondents reported continuing mental health effects, including depression and sleep disruption, and that nearly half described PTSD-like symptoms; about a quarter said they had started new medication to cope. The survey's release pushed back specifically against the narrative that affected workers had 'moved on' in the year-plus since being terminated.

primary_proponent.role: Federal government's central human-resources agency, which directed the probationary firings later found unlawful
primary_proponent.note: OPM's directive is the originating action; this entry documents the human-impact evidence that emerged more than a year later, distinct from the agency-specific staffing entries elsewhere in this tracker (e.g., IRS, CISA, NPS) that document firings' operational effects rather than firsthand psychological impact on the workers themselves.

estimated_impact.summary: The survey's testimonials describe lasting psychological harm well beyond the initial job loss: respondents reported ongoing nightmares, new medication use, and a sense that the firings 'will reverberate through my life for years,' as one respondent put it. The scale (300+ respondents drawn from a pool of 25,000+ terminated workers, with 95% reporting continuing effects) suggests the psychological impact was not a short-term disruption but a durable harm, more than a year after the terminations and roughly eight months after a federal court found the underlying directive unlawful.

title: FedRAMP Approved Microsoft's Government Cloud Despite Reviewers Calling It Unassessable and 'a Pile of Shit,' Citing How Embedded It Already Was Across Government
institution: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP), General Services Administration
status: Finalized -- GCC High was authorized despite unresolved security concerns; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: Review conducted over roughly 3-5 years, concerns documented from late 2024; authorization finalized and reported March 2026
what_changed: A ProPublica investigation found federal cybersecurity reviewers concluded Microsoft's Government Community Cloud High (GCC High) -- cloud infrastructure widely used across federal agencies to store sensitive government data -- lacked proper documentation of how it encrypts data in transit, a basic security requirement that competitors Amazon and Google routinely documented for their own competing federal cloud products. FedRAMP spent 480 hours and conducted 18 technical deep-dive reviews over roughly three years and still concluded it had a 'lack of confidence' in GCC High's overall security posture; one FedRAMP reviewer was quoted describing the product as 'a pile of shit.' Despite these unresolved concerns, FedRAMP authorized GCC High anyway. ProPublica's reporting found the authorization decision was shaped by how deeply embedded Microsoft's cloud products already were across the federal government -- rejecting the authorization would have been highly disruptive -- and by internal deference to Microsoft evident in memos, logs, and interviews, even as Microsoft had separately suffered major prior breaches. ProPublica's reporting also connects the deference and the review's ultimate outcome to FedRAMP's own staffing cuts, which reduced the program's capacity to hold a vendor as large as Microsoft to the same documentation standard applied to smaller competitors.

primary_proponent.name: FedRAMP / General Services Administration
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency responsible for authorizing cloud products for government use
primary_proponent.note: Sourcing reviewed did not identify a single named individual FedRAMP or GSA official who made the final authorization decision; ProPublica's reporting attributes the outcome to institutional dynamics (Microsoft's market embeddedness and FedRAMP's own reduced staffing capacity) rather than one identified decision-maker.

estimated_impact.summary: Sensitive federal government data across numerous agencies now sits on cloud infrastructure that the government's own technical reviewers, after years of dedicated review, said they could not verify meets basic security standards -- a documented instance of federal cybersecurity oversight yielding to a vendor's market entrenchment and the reviewing program's own reduced capacity, rather than resolving the underlying security gap.

title: FEMA Cancelled $3.6B in Disaster-Resilience Grants, Then Was Ordered by a Federal Court to Restore Them a Year Later
institution: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Reversed by court order and subsequent agency action -- FEMA reinstated the program in March 2026 with $1B in new funding, after a federal judge's December 2025 order
date_of_action: 2025-04 (program termination) through 2026-03 (reinstatement)
what_changed: In April 2025, the Trump administration ended FEMA's Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) program, which funded predisaster projects -- floodwalls, elevated infrastructure, fire-resistant building retrofits, and similar hardening work -- for hundreds of communities nationwide. The termination halted $3.6 billion in funding that had already been awarded to specific, in-progress projects but not yet paid out, and separately refused to award another $882 million in grants that had been planned for the following fiscal year. Twenty states, led by New York Attorney General Letitia James among others, sued the administration, arguing FEMA lacked legal authority to cancel a program funded and directed by Congress, that the cancellation undermined already-underway projects, and that it left disaster-prone communities more vulnerable to floods, fires, and storms. In December 2025, a federal judge in Massachusetts sided with the 22 states and D.C. that had joined the suit by that point, ordering FEMA to restore the canceled funding. In March 2026, FEMA announced it would reinstate the program -- rebranded as the 'Building Resilient Communities and Infrastructure' program -- making $1 billion available for states, local governments, territories, and tribes to pursue hardening projects against wildfires, floods, earthquakes, and hurricanes, though at less than a third of the originally canceled $3.6 billion figure.

title: FEMA Capacity Collapse — Staff Exodus and Spending Bottleneck Delayed Texas Flood Response
institution: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing institutional instability (four different acting/nominated administrators within roughly a year; agency's future role still under review; staffing continued to decline into 2026 even as a limited hiring campaign began ahead of hurricane season)
date_of_action: Staff departures throughout 2025; acute failure documented July 4-10, 2025 during Texas floods
what_changed: Throughout 2025, FEMA underwent a wave of staff departures -- about 18% of the agency's permanent full-time employees had left as of June 2025, including 24 senior-level staffers, per GAO. In May 2025 alone, 16 senior officials departed, taking with them a combined 200+ years of disaster-response expertise. Separately, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem implemented a rule requiring her personal sign-off on any FEMA expenditure over $100,000 -- for an agency whose disaster costs routinely run into the billions, officials described this threshold as effectively 'pennies.' This bottleneck had direct, documented consequences during the deadly July 4, 2025 Texas Hill Country floods: FEMA's disaster survivor call-center contract funding lapsed on July 5, and it took Noem five days -- until July 10 -- to approve renewed funding, during which most survivor calls went unanswered (an internal memo documented the call-answer rate collapsing from 99.9% to 20%, with survivors waiting over 90 minutes). NPR reported in August 2025 that this documented 10-20% call-answer rate directly contradicted Acting Administrator Richardson's own claim to Congress that most survivor calls had been handled during the crisis. Noem also did not authorize deployment of FEMA's Urban Search and Rescue teams until more than 72 hours after the flooding began. Ken Pagurek, head of FEMA's Urban Search and Rescue branch, resigned on July 23, 2025, citing the delayed deployment caused by Noem's $100,000 sign-off requirement as a direct factor in his decision. Acting FEMA Administrator David Richardson did not travel to Texas for a full week after the disaster, telling a House committee he had stayed in Washington to 'kick down the doors of bureaucracy' -- and separately acknowledged he had been camping with his sons over the July 4 weekend when the floods hit. The Washington Post separately reported in September 2025 that FEMA staff could not reach Richardson for nearly 24 hours during the acute phase of the disaster, a communications gap that further delayed critical rescue-deployment decisions on top of the sign-off bottleneck itself. Even as FEMA was actively responding to the ongoing Texas disaster, Noem publicly said on July 9, 2025 that FEMA should be 'eliminated as it exists today,' criticizing the agency's response times and bureaucracy and calling instead for a state-led disaster system -- remarks made during a federal disaster-system reform meeting held while FEMA personnel were still deployed to the flood response. The following month, Reuters reported that Trump officials began reassigning FEMA personnel to help ICE hire 10,000 new agents, warning staff they could be terminated if they refused the reassignment -- a redirection of disaster-response staff toward immigration enforcement that came at the height of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season. Richardson resigned in November 2025 after six months in the role, the second of three different acting administrators to lead FEMA within the year. In January 2026, FEMA abruptly stopped renewing contracts for its Cadre of On-Call Response/Recovery (CORE) employees -- term-limited hires who can hold senior disaster-response roles -- then paused the cuts in late January as a major winter storm affecting roughly half the country's population approached; FEMA managers confirmed in early February 2026 that the CORE staff reductions would resume once the storm passed, though no specific restart date was given. Around the same period, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who has overseen FEMA's cuts, received a draft report from the Trump-appointed FEMA Review Council recommending the agency's workforce be cut in half. During the February 2026 DHS funding lapse, DHS halted nearly all employee travel department-wide, including FEMA disaster-response deployments, according to internal emails The Washington Post obtained -- disrupting FEMA's ability to send personnel to respond to active or anticipated disasters during the lapse; a separate internal FEMA email obtained by The Washington Post warned that national continuity operations were 'significantly constrained' during the same shutdown, limiting the agency's ability to maintain critical continuity-of-government functions. A second documented instance of the same DHS approval bottleneck emerged around the same time: CNN reported FEMA failed to renew a $200,000 contract for a tornado-tracking mapping tool used by rescue teams to identify storm damage paths. The contract expired in February 2026 and remained stuck in the DHS approval process even as deadly tornadoes struck the Midwest and Plains, forcing rescue teams to rely on news reports and manual searches to locate the hardest-hit areas instead of the mapping tool. By March 2026, FEMA's overall staffing had fallen further, from roughly 26,000 employees in January 2025 to about 21,100 -- an approximately 19% decline -- with 18 of the agency's 38 senior leadership positions vacant, including deputy administrator and chief of staff. A CNN KFile investigation published March 20, 2026 found Gregg Phillips -- installed to lead FEMA's Office of Response and Recovery, a key role directing federal disaster-response operations, despite limited emergency-management experience -- has a documented history of promoting conspiracy theories and using violent rhetoric, including saying in January 2025 he would 'like to punch' then-outgoing President Biden 'in the mouth,' and repeatedly claiming on podcasts to have been involuntarily 'teleported,' including once to a Georgia Waffle House 50 miles away. Rep. Tim Kennedy cited Phillips's 'violent statements' and 'deeply troubling bigoted comments about immigrants' as evidence he was 'wildly unfit for his role'; Phillips defended the teleportation claims in a follow-up CNN report the following month, saying 'haters gonna hate.' Robert Fenton (FEMA's Region 9 administrator) took over as senior official performing the duties of administrator; Trump nominated Cameron Hamilton as permanent administrator. Facing the 2026 hurricane season, FEMA began a limited hiring campaign: it rehired 14 staff Secretary Noem had fired for signing the 'Katrina Declaration,' and DHS approved roughly 300 near-term new hires with hopes of filling up to 700 vacancies. Fenton told reporters FEMA has about 30-40% of its disaster workforce available at any given time, which he characterized as normal availability rather than a crisis-level shortfall; NOAA's 2026 Atlantic hurricane season outlook predicts a below-normal season (8-14 named storms, 3-6 hurricanes). Hamilton previously served as acting FEMA administrator from January-May 2025 before being fired for telling Congress he did not believe eliminating FEMA was in the public interest. At his June 17, 2026 confirmation hearing, Hamilton pledged to be 'fair and reasonable' in assessing disaster-aid requests -- a notable pledge given the separate, related pattern this tracker documents in the FEMA disaster-aid partisan-approval-gap entry. Update 2026-07-26: Hamilton's nomination for permanent FEMA Administrator advanced out of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on an 8-4 vote, roughly a month after his confirmation hearing, and now awaits a full Senate floor vote whose timing before the August recess is not yet clear.

primary_proponent.note: Noem personally implemented and enforced the $100,000 spending-approval rule that created the call-center funding bottleneck. A DHS spokesperson publicly defended the change as shifting FEMA from 'bloated, DC-centric dead weight to a lean, deployable disaster force,' attributing the framing directly to Noem's leadership. title: FEMA Disaster Aid Approvals Skewed Toward Republican-Led States
institution: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing pattern -- most recent documented denial episode July 2026, no reversal or independent (GAO/IG) audit announced as of this writing
date_of_action: 2025-2026 (pattern); most recent documented episode 2026-07 (four-state blizzard aid denial)
what_changed: An E&E News/POLITICO analysis of roughly 2,500 major disaster declaration decisions dating back to the Reagan administration found that under Trump, Democratic-led states have had disaster aid requests approved at a 23% rate, compared to 89% for Republican-led states -- the lowest approval rate for Democratic-led states of any president since Reagan (every prior president approved at least 67% of their requests). The same analysis found Democratic-led states waited an average of 80 days for a decision versus 39 days for Republican-led states, and documented at least $250 million in specific state disaster requests blocked or left pending, including $34 million to Washington, $41 million to Colorado, and $46 million and $83 million in separate Illinois storm-damage requests. The pattern produced a concrete, dated episode in July 2026: Trump denied Major Disaster Declaration requests from New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island -- a combined $227 million sought after a February 2026 blizzard that buried New York City, Long Island, and the Mid-Hudson region, with Rhode Island separately citing record snowfall and cold -- after all four states' damage assessments exceeded FEMA's own threshold for triggering aid. The denials came two days after Trump approved disaster declarations for six Republican-led states; Trump has publicly touted having granted over $846 million in disaster relief to Republican-led states. White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson defended the pattern, saying Trump "provides a more thorough review of disaster declaration requests than any Administration has before him." This is a distinct mechanism from a separate, later legal fight over FEMA's Homeland Security Grant Program: on July 24, 2026, a coalition of 23 Democratic-led states, two Democratic governors, and DC sued DHS in Rhode Island federal court alleging it illegally conditioned that separate grant program on states adopting specific election policies (hand-marked paper ballots, manual audits, the SAVE program) -- a related pattern of FEMA/DHS funding being used as leverage, but a different funding stream and a different specific demand than the major-disaster-declaration approvals this entry tracks. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no new denial episode identified since the four-state February 2026 blizzard denial already documented. The July 24, 2026 lawsuit over FEMA grant conditions (noted in this entry as related context) is now more precisely quantified: DHS/FEMA plan to withhold 20% of the plaintiff states' federal disaster grant funding, at least $148 million, if they don't adopt the demanded election-system changes -- filed by the attorneys general of California, Illinois, New Jersey, and Rhode Island, joined by 19 other states, the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania, and DC.

title: Forest Service Chief's Own Internal Memo Contradicted Agriculture Secretary's Public 'Fully Staffed' Claims — 5,000 Firefighting Positions Vacant
institution: U.S. Forest Service, Department of Agriculture
status: Ongoing, with a genuine mixed 2026 update -- the Forest Service met its 2026 seasonal wildland-firefighter hiring goal (crediting recent pay raises), even as permanent-staff attrition (~6,000 lost since January 2025) and consolidation continue, and the 2026 fire season itself has been severe
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial layoffs) through 2025-08 (peak fire-season staffing crisis and reorganization announcement)
what_changed: In February 2025, the Trump administration laid off approximately 700 Forest Service employees who support wildland fire operations -- human resource managers, ecologists, and trail-crew workers who hold 'red card' fire-response certifications even though their primary jobs are not firefighting. Many were subsequently rehired, but the administration then pushed remaining staff toward deferred-resignation and early-retirement offers; ultimately at least 1,800 fire-qualified ('red-carded') employees left the agency, out of 4,800 total Forest Service departures in 2025 (more than 13% of the agency's total workforce). Internal Forest Service data reviewed by ProPublica, High Country News, and Capital & Main found at least 5,000 firefighting positions vacant as of mid-July 2025 -- directly contradicting the agency's own public claim of having exceeded its 2025 hiring goal (11,364 firefighters on board by end of July). USDA spokesperson Cat McRae disputed the vacancy data as reflecting 'outdated org charts and unfunded positions'; ProPublica confirmed its analysis had already excluded unfunded positions. Days after that public dispute, a memo Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz sent to agency leadership -- obtained by High Country News -- stated plainly: 'As expected, the 2025 Fire Year is proving to be extremely challenging... we know the demand for resources outpaces their availability,' and directed that all red-carded employees, including IT and HR staff, be made available for fire assignments. At an internal spring planning meeting, one employee was told directly, 'Help is not on the way' -- a phrase the employee said they had 'never been told before' in their career. The agency subsequently took the unusual step of waiving a statutory 1,039-hour cap on seasonal-employee work hours (raising it to 1,560 hours) and asked 1,400 firefighting-qualified former employees to return; as of August 12, only 100 had accepted. Separately, USDA announced a reorganization eliminating the Forest Service's nine regional offices and consolidating them into five 'hub' locations, with Secretary Brooke Rollins acknowledging up to half of affected staff may not relocate. For the 2026 fire season, the Forest Service set a goal of 11,300 wildland firefighters onboard by mid-July and reported 11,816 onboard as of July 6, 2026 -- 104% of goal, which Chief Tom Schultz attributed to recent pay raises improving seasonal recruitment. This is a genuine, verifiable improvement on that specific metric, distinct from the broader permanent-workforce attrition: the agency has still lost close to 6,000 permanent staff (rangers, timber technicians, and others who also held fire-response 'red card' certifications) to layoffs, buyouts, and early retirement since January 2025, and outside observers (including Washington's public lands commissioner) warn this erodes surge capacity in a severe fire year even with seasonal hiring goals met. As of mid-July 2026, more than 17,000 personnel were assigned to 46 large, uncontained fires nationwide, with over 3.6 million acres burned for the year. Update 2026-07-26: the 2026 fire season's severity escalated further -- on July 18, 2026, the country reached 'Preparedness Level 5,' the highest level on the scale measuring how taxed wildfire resources are nationally, only the third time since 2010 that threshold has been reached this early in the season (after 2021 and 2024). This reinforces, rather than changes, the entry's existing point: seasonal hiring goals being met doesn't resolve the separate concern about permanent-staff attrition eroding surge capacity in a severe fire year. Update 2026-07-28: NPR reported that fire-prevention work itself, not just firefighter staffing, declined sharply in 2025 -- prescribed burning fell to about 900,000 acres, roughly half of the 1.6 million-plus acres burned in each of 2023 and 2024, and total vegetation-management work (which reduces the dense underbrush that fuels catastrophic fires) fell to 2.6 million acres in 2025 from more than 4 million acres in 2024, a decline of almost 1.5 million acres. This directly connects the staffing losses already documented in this entry to a concrete reduction in the preventive work meant to reduce wildfire severity, distinct from firefighting-response capacity alone.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Agriculture
primary_proponent.note: Publicly maintained the Forest Service was 'fully equipped and operationally ready to protect people and communities from wildfire' even as her own agency's Chief, Tom Schultz, was privately telling leadership the opposite in writing. A USDA spokesperson later attempted to reconcile the two statements by saying Schultz's memo referred to a broader pool of red-carded employees who could be 'called on to bolster' response as fire activity increases, while Rollins's statement referred only to full-time firefighters -- a real distinction, though one that doesn't fully resolve why the agency disputed the underlying vacancy data as inaccurate while its own Chief was independently describing a resource shortfall in nearly identical terms.

estimated_impact.summary: This is one of the more directly self-contradicting cases in this tracker: the dispute isn't primarily outside advocates versus the administration, but the Agriculture Secretary's public statements versus her own Forest Service Chief's internal, contemporaneous memo -- both documented, both on the record. Frontline accounts corroborate the operational strain described in Schultz's memo: a California Forest Service survey found 26% of engine captain positions and 42% of engineer positions vacant, and wildland firefighters described being assigned non-firefighting duties like trail-building and lawn-mowing due to short-staffing elsewhere in the agency.

title: FTC Cuts Workforce 10%, Loses Bipartisan Independence After Supreme Court Upholds Commissioner Firings

status: Complete (workforce reduction implemented in 2025; commissioner-firing litigation permanently resolved by the Supreme Court on June 29, 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-03-18 (commissioner firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling); staff reduction implemented through 2025
what_changed: On March 18, 2025, President Trump fired the FTC's two Democratic commissioners, Rebecca Slaughter and Alvaro Bedoya, without citing any statutory cause, instead stating their continued service was 'inconsistent with my Administration's priorities.' This left the five-seat Commission with only its two sitting Republican members. Slaughter and Bedoya sued; Bedoya later resigned and dropped his claim, but Slaughter's case proceeded, with a district court initially ordering her reinstated. Separately, on May 15, 2025, Chairman Andrew Ferguson testified to Congress that the FTC was implementing a 10% workforce reduction, bringing headcount to approximately 1,100 employees (down from 1,221), the agency's lowest staffing level in a decade. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter that the FTC's for-cause removal protections for commissioners are unconstitutional, permanently allowing the president to remove commissioners at will and explicitly overruling the 1935 precedent Humphrey's Executor v. United States, which had protected the independence of the FTC and similar agencies for 90 years. Re-verified 2026-07-19: the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Chair Andrew Ferguson and Mark Meador) as of this update, with legal commentary noting little short-term incentive to restore a five-member bipartisan structure -- no material change to the entry's core claims. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Ferguson and Meador); no new nominations or structural changes identified since the prior update.

title: Fish and Wildlife Service Loses Over 1,500 Staff; Zero New Species Listed as Endangered
institution: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
status: Ongoing (staffing and budget cuts continue; the zero-new-listings streak this entry was built around ended July 21, 2026, when FWS finalized endangered status for three Florida Keys reptiles -- the term's first new listings after roughly 18 months at zero; 400+ species remain in the backlog)
date_of_action: 2025-01 to 2026-02 (staffing reductions); ongoing effects on listing backlog through the last-verified date
what_changed: Between January 2025 and February 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service saw a net reduction of 1,538 employees, according to Office of Personnel Management data compiled by the Congressional Research Service, with independent analyses from the Center for Biological Diversity estimating the cuts included more than 500 biologists specifically. The Interior Department separately proposed a FY2026 budget cutting the agency's Endangered Species Act listing-activity funding by 36% year-over-year, part of an overall reduction in FWS's average annual appropriations from roughly $1.94 billion (2017-2025 average) to approximately $1.6 billion for FY2026; the same budget proposed eliminating funding for the State and Tribal Wildlife Grant program entirely. The Service also discontinued its Refuge System Strategic Growth Policy and, according to conservation groups, has effectively stopped conducting the annual Florida panther population count last performed in 2015. As of reporting in April 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service had added zero new species to the federal endangered or threatened species list during Trump's second term, compared to 22 species added during the entirety of his first term, a gap the Center for Biological Diversity described as the longest period without a new listing decision since the Endangered Species Act was implemented. A backlog of more than 400 species remains pending final agency listing decisions. Recent Federal Register activity through mid-July 2026 continues the zero-new-listings pattern with specific examples: on June 16, 2026, FWS found listing 'not warranted' for two petitioned species (Sangre de Cristo peaclam, black-backed tanager); on July 14, 2026, FWS issued 90-day findings (a preliminary step, not a listing decision) for 10 more petitioned species including the Cascade red fox and plains spotted skunk; and on the same day, FWS rejected -- for the second time -- a petition to list long-tailed macaque monkeys. None of this recent activity constitutes an actual new listing, consistent with the entry's core finding. Separately, in June 2026 FWS announced a partnership with Colossal Biosciences to collect and cryopreserve cell/tissue samples from every species on the endangered list -- a genomic-preservation initiative distinct from, and not a substitute for, the listing process itself. CORRECTION 2026-07-26: on July 21, 2026, FWS finalized endangered-species status for three Florida Keys reptiles -- the Florida Keys mole skink, Key ring-necked snake, and rim rock crowned snake -- effective August 20, 2026. These are the first new species listings of Trump's second term, ending the zero-listings streak that was this entry's central, headline finding; the listing process itself took 14 years from initial proposal to finalization, so this reflects the conclusion of a long-pending case rather than a change in the administration's overall listing pace. Separately, FWS finalized an Endangered Species Act regulatory change in July 2026 removing the 'blanket rule' option that had automatically extended full endangered-level protections to newly listed threatened species by default, a change conservation groups argue weakens protection for future threatened listings even as it doesn't affect already-endangered species like these three. The 400+ species backlog and FY2026 budget/staffing cuts already documented in this entry are unaffected by this correction and remain current.

The administration moved quickly: by March 31, all but 12 of the agency's roughly 70-75 employees were placed on administrative leave, with a reduction-in-force notice set for May 4; nearly all IMLS board members were dismissed; and beginning April 1, the agency's Acting Director (Keith Sonderling, who stated he would act 'in lockstep' with the administration) began terminating previously-awarded, congressionally-appropriated grants nationwide, including Grants to States, National Leadership Grants, and Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian grants. Unlike most entries in this tracker, this story does not end in unreversed loss: the American Library Association and AFSCME sued (ALA v. Sonderling), and 21 state attorneys general separately sued in Rhode Island v. Trump. On May 1, 2025, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking further staff terminations. In November 2025, the U.S. District Court for Rhode Island ruled the dismantlement actions 'arbitrary and capricious and contrary to federal law,' and IMLS reinstated all previously terminated grants that December. On April 6, 2026, the administration withdrew its appeal of that ruling, and on April 9, 2026, ALA, AFSCME, and the Department of Justice signed a binding settlement agreement ensuring IMLS remains intact and continues its congressionally mandated work going forward -- closing the litigation with the agency fully restored, not merely paused.

During the roughly 8-month period before reinstatement, real, documented harm occurred at the institutional level: the Dubuque Museum of Art in Iowa had already begun hiring and training staff against a $74,979 grant that was frozen: the Science Center of Iowa's planned internship program, backed by a $196,046 grant, was jeopardized. title: IRS Lost 27% of Its Workforce and a Third of Its Auditors — Independent Watchdogs Project $600B in Lost Revenue
institution: Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
status: Ongoing (2026 filing season completed under reduced staff; FY2027 budget request proposes a further ~4,800-employee cut, concentrated almost entirely in enforcement)
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial probationary firings) through 2026-04 (most recent GAO/TIGTA reporting)
what_changed: Beginning February 2025, the IRS workforce was cut by approximately 27%, falling from roughly 102,000 employees in January 2025 to about 74,000 by December 2025 -- a reduction of nearly 28,000 people, primarily via probationary-employee terminations (~7,300), deferred-resignation buyouts (~4,700), and further attrition. The cuts were not evenly distributed: Taxpayer Services (which processes returns, answers phones, and handles correspondence) lost about 21-22% of its staff; the agency's IT function lost 27%; and revenue agents -- the specialists who conduct complex audits of high-income individuals, partnerships, and large corporations -- lost roughly 3,600 people, about 31% of the entire auditing workforce. The cuts extended to physical infrastructure as well as headcount: in late February 2025, the General Services Administration sent the IRS a letter proposing to terminate or not renew leases on more than 110 (some reporting says up to 120) Taxpayer Assistance Centers -- the walk-in offices where taxpayers get in-person help with identity theft, audits, and other complex issues -- right at the height of tax-filing season. After pushback from taxpayers, tax professionals, and lawmakers, the IRS agreed to keep TAC offices open through the 2025 filing season, but the closures resumed afterward: by September 2025 the IRS confirmed it would close nine specific centers across six states (Pennsylvania, Iowa, New York, Kentucky, California, and West Virginia), effective November 30, 2025. Congress separately cut the IRS enforcement budget by 8% for FY2026 (the lowest inflation-adjusted level since 1988) and cut $1.1 billion (12%) from the IRS's base budget overall, rescinding most of the remaining Inflation Reduction Act funding that had been allocated to rebuild the agency; the base budget is now about 40% below its 2010 level after inflation. The IRS responded by lowering its own phone-service target from 85% to 70% of calls answered, and an independent analysis by the Center for Taxpayer Rights found call wait times on the main line increased more than 70% between February 2025 and February 2026. A March 2026 GAO audit found the IRS's staffing reductions 'were not targeted or strategic' and that the agency still lacks an updated strategic workforce plan. Notably, IRS Commissioner Frank Bisignano simultaneously serves as the Senate-confirmed Commissioner of the Social Security Administration -- see the related SSA entry in this tracker -- splitting his attention across both agencies during this period. The IRS's FY2027 budget request, released in 2026, seeks $9.8 billion in discretionary funding, down $1.4 billion from the $11.2 billion Congress enacted for FY2026, and proposes eliminating roughly 4,800 more positions (about 17% of remaining staff) on top of the 27% already lost in 2025. Nearly all of the proposed staffing reduction falls on enforcement -- examinations and collections -- which would see an 18% budget cut, while taxpayer-service funding would see a small 3% increase. The IRS's own budget documents describe the enforcement-side cuts as yielding roughly $778 million in savings once implemented. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- the FY2027 budget request remains a proposal, not enacted; no new congressional action identified since the prior update. Re-verified 2026-08-05: despite Bisignano's 'less people and better results' framing, internal documents reported by NOTUS show the IRS has been rushing to backfill critical staffing gaps, hiring roughly 2,000 employees as of January 2026 -- a partial rehire that still leaves the agency at a net ~28% workforce reduction from its January 2025 level, and that reporting characterizes as evidence of operational strain the agency's public statements had downplayed.

primary_proponent.role: IRS Chief Executive Officer / Commissioner (concurrently SSA Commissioner)
primary_proponent.note: Publicly defended the cuts before the Senate Finance Committee, stating the agency can achieve 'less people and better results,' and that the IRS cut phone-center 'idle time' by nearly 50%. Committee Democrats, led by Ranking Member Ron Wyden, disputed this characterization directly in the same hearing. Bisignano told senators he treats running both SSA and IRS as managing 'two large organizations,' sometimes working 14-hour days across both.

estimated_impact.summary: The Yale Budget Lab modeled the specific 2025 staffing reductions (broken down by IRS operating function, using the agency's own budget-activity categories) and projected the cuts will reduce federal revenue collection by almost $600 billion over the 2026-2035 window -- a striking figure since the IRS collects 96% of all federal revenue, meaning even modest enforcement-capacity losses compound into large fiscal effects. The National Taxpayer Advocate (an independent office within the IRS that reports directly to Congress) has been notably even-handed in its assessments -- praising the 2025 filing season as one of the most successful in recent memory, while explicitly warning that the more severe 2026 season risks are now 'markedly different' given the compounding effect of workforce loss, budget cuts, and simultaneous major tax-law changes from the 2025 reconciliation bill.

title: LIHEAP Heating Assistance Program Staff Eliminated, Funding Delayed for Millions
institution: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), Administration for Children and Families, HHS
status: Funding eventually released (Nov. 28, 2025); underlying staff elimination not reversed
date_of_action: 2025-04-04 (entire program staff terminated); 2025-10-01 through 2025-11-28 (funding delayed during shutdown)
what_changed: In April 2025, the Trump administration fired the entire federal staff team responsible for administering LIHEAP -- the ~$4.1 billion program that helps roughly 6 million low-income households pay heating and cooling bills, serving all 50 states, D.C., U.S. territories, and federally recognized tribes. This is the same program Trump's budget proposed zero-funding entirely. Six months later, when the October-November 2025 government shutdown (the longest in U.S. history at 43 days) hit, LIHEAP's annual funding allocation -- normally distributed to states by early November -- was delayed with no dedicated federal staff left to expedite the process once Congress acted. States including Pennsylvania, New York, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Connecticut, and Kansas had to delay or suspend their heating-assistance seasons entirely during the onset of winter. The $3.6 billion in delayed funding was finally released to states on November 28, 2025, over two weeks after the shutdown ended (Nov. 12) and roughly a month later than the program's normal early-November distribution. Trump's FY2027 budget, released April 3, 2026 and documented in more detail elsewhere in this tracker (trump-fy2027-budget-defense-tradeoff-2026.json), again proposed eliminating LIHEAP entirely, even as utility costs continued to rise and the program retained bipartisan congressional support.

primary_proponent.note: HHS did not name a specific individual responsible for the staff terminations in available reporting -- flag as agency-level, not individually attributable, though HHS Secretary Robert F. An HHS spokesperson publicly blamed the delay entirely on 'congressional Democrats' without directly answering PBS's question about whether the earlier staff firings affected the agency's ability to process the funding quickly once released.

estimated_impact.summary: Roughly 6 million households nationally depend on LIHEAP, and about 68% of LIHEAP households also receive SNAP -- meaning the same families were simultaneously hit by both the LIHEAP delay and the SNAP funding freeze during the same shutdown window, compounding hardship. An estimated 21 million U.S. households were already behind on energy payments heading into the delay, with nearly 4 million disconnections possible for the season per the Center for Law and Social Policy.

title: FDA Commissioner Marty Makary Resigned After Being Pressured to Approve Flavored Vapes and Restrict the Abortion Pill
institution: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
status: Resignation effective as of May 12, 2026; Deputy Commissioner for Food Kyle Diamantas serving as acting commissioner
date_of_action: 2026-05-06 (FDA approves flavored e-cigarettes under reported White House pressure) through 2026-05-12 (Makary's resignation)
what_changed: FDA Commissioner Marty Makary resigned on May 12, 2026, amid internal conflicts over two major policy disputes. On flavored vaping products: the FDA approved flavored e-cigarettes from vaping company Glas Inc. on May 6, 2026, a move the Wall Street Journal reported came only after President Trump personally pressured Makary to approve the fruit-flavored vapes, which Makary had been refusing to authorize; a source told CBS News Makary is leaving specifically over this dispute, having been forced by other administration officials to approve products he did not want to approve. title: CMS Narrows Medical Frailty Exemption Beyond Statute in Medicaid Work-Requirement Rule -- Cancer and HIV Patients Left Unexempted
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services
status: In effect -- interim final rule published June 1, 2026; national enforcement deadline January 1, 2027; several states (Nebraska, Montana, Arkansas) already implementing ahead of that deadline; public comment period on the rule remains open
date_of_action: 2026-06-01 (CMS interim final rule published)
what_changed: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law July 4, 2025, required Medicaid expansion-population adults aged 19-64 to complete at least 80 hours per month of qualifying work, education, job training, or volunteer service to keep coverage, with a statutory exemption for individuals who are 'medically frail.' On June 1, 2026, CMS -- under Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz -- published an interim final rule implementing the requirement nationwide. Rather than applying the statute's medical-frailty categories as written, CMS added an additional functional-capacity requirement: individuals must affirmatively demonstrate that their condition 'significantly impairs' their ability to perform the 80 hours of required activity, a threshold not present in the underlying statute. In practice, advocates and reporting say this leaves out people with early-stage cancer who are undergoing radiation treatment but are still nominally capable of some work, and people with HIV who are stable on treatment but technically employable -- both groups are not automatically exempted under CMS's narrower reading, and must instead navigate state reporting/paperwork processes to prove exemption eligibility or ongoing compliance. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the work-requirement provisions would cause roughly 5 million people to lose Medicaid coverage, out of a program covering about 68 million low-income Americans, and that the requirements account for roughly a third of the $900 billion in Medicaid savings scored under OBBBA overall (i.e., roughly $300 billion of that total tied to work-requirement-driven disenrollment). Nebraska became the first state to implement the requirement on May 1, 2026; Montana and Arkansas followed by July 1, 2026 (Arkansas delayed enforcement to January 2027), with additional states phasing in through the January 2027 national deadline. Update 2026-08-02 (detail): Per CNN's June 6, 2026 reporting on the same rule, the medical-frailty exemption requires more than a diagnosis -- enrollees must submit documentation, such as a signed statement from a medical professional, affirmatively showing their condition 'significantly impairs' their ability to meet the 80-hour work standard. A cancer patient in active chemotherapy who remains physically able to sit at a desk part-time may not qualify for the exemption on that documentation standard alone, regardless of diagnosis.

primary_proponent.name: Dr. Mehmet Oz
primary_proponent.role: CMS Administrator
primary_proponent.note: Oz publicly framed the rule as reducing loneliness and building 'skills and independence through work,' stating: 'This rule helps Americans build skills and independence through work, education, job training, or community service, creating new opportunities for themselves and their families.' CMS's specific choice to add a functional-capacity threshold beyond the statute's medical-frailty categories -- the discretionary regulatory action this entry documents -- was made under his administration of the agency.

estimated_impact.summary: Health-policy advocates and reporting describe the rule's core mechanism as bureaucratic rather than substantive: eligible, low-income people who are already working, studying, or too sick to reliably navigate monthly reporting requirements lose coverage not because they fail to meet the underlying policy goal, but because they fail the paperwork. People undergoing active cancer treatment or living with HIV -- conditions advocates argue should self-evidently qualify as medically frail -- are not automatically exempted under CMS's narrower functional-capacity standard.

The specific accountability question this entry documents is narrower: whether CMS's discretionary choice to layer an additional functional-capacity threshold onto the statute's medical-frailty exemption -- rather than applying Congress's own listed categories -- was a reasonable implementation choice or an administrative narrowing of an exemption Congress wrote more broadly. That legal/administrative question was not resolved as of this entry's sourcing.

title: MSPB Loses Quorum for 8 Months After Trump Fires Whistleblower Board Chair Cathy Harris
institution: Merit Systems Protection Board
status: Resolved against Harris (the Supreme Court denied her petition for certiorari on June 30, 2026 -- one day after Trump v. Slaughter -- leaving the D.C. Circuit's December 2025 ruling upholding her firing as the final word in her individual case; the Board's quorum was separately restored in October 2025 via an unrelated confirmation, so the practical quorum crisis had already ended, but the removal-power precedent from the D.C. date_of_action: 2025-02-10 (firing) through present; the Board's quorum was separately restored in October 2025 via a new member's confirmation, independent of Harris's litigation
what_changed: On February 10, 2025, President Trump fired MSPB Chair Cathy Harris via a one-sentence email without citing any cause, three years before her Senate-confirmed term was set to expire in 2028. Harris sued; a district court granted a temporary restraining order reinstating her on February 18, and on March 4, Judge Rudolph Contreras granted summary judgment finding the firing unlawful. The government appealed, and a three-judge D.C. Circuit panel stayed her reinstatement on March 28. The full en banc D.C. Circuit voted 7-4 to vacate that stay and reinstate Harris on April 7, but two days later, on April 9, Chief Justice Roberts granted the government's emergency application for a stay, again removing Harris and leaving the Board without the quorum needed to issue decisions. In December 2025, a 2-1 D.C. Circuit panel (Judges Katsas and Walker, both Trump appointees) ruled on the merits that Congress cannot restrict the president's authority to remove NLRB or MSPB members who 'wield substantial executive power,' with a dissenting judge warning the majority's reasoning implies 'no independent agencies may lawfully exist in this country.' The Board separately regained a functional quorum in October 2025 through the unrelated Senate confirmation of a new member, James Woodruff. On March 17, 2026, Harris petitioned the Supreme Court for review, arguing her case is legally distinct from the FTC's Slaughter case because MSPB is purely adjudicatory, does not set policy, and structurally resembles multimember bodies with roughly 150 years of established constitutional standing. A group of Senate Democrats filed an amicus brief in April 2026 urging the Court to hear her case. The June 29, 2026 Trump v. Slaughter ruling did not directly resolve Harris's petition but substantially weakens her argument by holding broadly that agencies exercising 'executive power' must have removable leadership. Correction 2026-07-19: the Supreme Court denied Harris's petition for certiorari on June 30, 2026, one day after deciding Trump v. Slaughter -- this entry's prior 'remains formally unresolved' status is now out of date. The denial leaves the D.C. Circuit's December 2025 2-1 panel ruling (Katsas and Walker) as the final word on Harris's individual removal; the Supreme Court's order gave no reasoning beyond the standard denial, consistent with how it typically treats cert denials, so the underlying legal question (whether purely adjudicatory bodies like MSPB warrant different treatment than the FTC) was not resolved on the merits, only left undisturbed as decided below.

title: National Archives Loses Its Archivist and Digital Access Office Amid Deep Budget Cuts
institution: National Archives and Records Administration
status: Ongoing (leadership remains unsettled -- GSA Administrator Edward Forst dually serves as acting archivist since April 2026; Trump's nominee for permanent archivist, Bradford P. Wilson, awaits Senate confirmation; FY2026 budget cuts partially implemented)
date_of_action: 2025-02 (Archivist Colleen Shogan fired) through 2026 (ongoing reorganization, office eliminations, and records-center closures)
what_changed: In February 2025, President Trump fired Archivist of the United States Colleen Shogan without citing cause, an unprecedented removal of the position's confirmed leader. Deputy Archivist William Bosanko briefly became acting archivist before announcing his resignation along with several other senior staff. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was then named acting archivist while continuing his separate Cabinet role, a dual appointment a U.S. senator later suggested may have violated federal law given how long Rubio held both positions simultaneously; Jim Byron subsequently served as senior adviser performing archivist functions before departing in April 2026, when GSA head Edward Forst was named acting archivist. Separately, NARA's FY2026 budget request set the agency's funding at $414.7 million, nearly $60 million less than projected FY2025 spending, eliminating 136 full-time positions agency-wide. The proposal included full elimination of NARA's 50-person Office of Innovation, which runs the agency's online records catalog, digital access initiatives, and the public 'citizen archivist' transcription project, with NARA stating those functions would be 'transferred elsewhere' rather than continued directly. In June 2025, NARA issued reduction-in-force notices affecting roughly 100 employees (about 3% of staff), which two NARA employees said effectively 'wiped out' the Office of Innovation and the division supporting field offices and presidential libraries; the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library was briefly forced to close in February 2025 after probationary employees were terminated. The FY2026 proposal also cut funding for NARA's Electronic Records Initiative by roughly 33%, even as the agency faces a growing volume of incoming digital records, with only about 3% of its roughly 12 billion textual paper pages digitized as of the most recent count. In 2026, NARA also announced it would vacate three federal records centers (Chicago, San Francisco/San Bruno, and Seattle) and sunset its free public History Hub reference forum to save an estimated $370,000 annually. On March 2, 2026, Trump nominated Bradford P. Wilson to be the permanent Archivist of the United States; as of this update, Wilson's confirmation was still pending in the Senate. In the interim, GSA Administrator Edward Forst was named acting archivist under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act in April 2026, telling GSA staff he would 'dually serve' in both roles -- meaning NARA's day-to-day acting leadership is held by an official whose primary job is running a different agency. title: National Park Service Lost 24% of Its Permanent Staff — Internal Report Contradicts Interior's Public 'False Narrative' Denial
institution: National Park Service (NPS), Department of the Interior
status: Ongoing -- the 2025 pattern repeated into the 2026 summer season: permanent staffing losses (~24%, ~4,000 people) remain unreversed, and 2026 seasonal hiring again fell short of its own target heading into peak season
date_of_action: 2025-02-14 (initial mass layoff, dubbed the 'Valentine's Day Massacre' by affected staff) through 2025-08-27 (internal operational-status report surfaces)
what_changed: On February 14, 2025, NPS laid off approximately 1,000-1,700 probationary employees just weeks before peak visitor season began across the system's 63 national parks and 370 other managed sites. By July 2025, independent analysis of Interior Department workforce data by the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA) found NPS had lost 24% of its permanent staff overall (about 4,000 people) since January, while only roughly 4,500 of a promised ~8,000 seasonal positions had been filled. In April 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum issued Secretarial Order 3426, mandating that every park remain 'open and accessible' regardless of staffing levels -- meaning parks could not close facilities or reduce services in response to the shortages, only quietly absorb the strain. Per Order 3426's own reporting requirement, every park unit had to submit an updated operational status by July 25, 2025; an internal NPS report compiled from those submissions, first reported by the New York Times, documented widespread, specific impacts: nearly 70 parks reduced visitor center hours, 22 postponed maintenance, and 11 closed or delayed opening facilities. Specific documented examples include all 13 lifeguard positions vacant at Assateague Island National Seashore (leaving the beach unguarded), the fire management team reduced to one person at Cumberland Island National Seashore, and Indiana Dunes National Park's ranger-led tours cut from 575 to approximately 100 for the year after 4 of 6 interpretive-division supervisors took early retirement. When this internal report became public, Interior deputy press secretary Aubrie Spady called the reporting a 'false narrative,' stating 'staffing levels and operations at our National Parks this summer are on par with previous years. Full Stop' -- a direct denial of findings drawn from the agency's own internal, Order-3426-mandated data collection. For the 2026 season, NPS again fell short of its own seasonal-hiring target: roughly 4,500 of a planned 5,000+ seasonal positions were filled heading into peak summer season, with reporting citing paperwork delays, background-check backlogs, and housing shortages as contributing causes -- a smaller absolute gap than 2025's (~4,500 of ~8,000 filled), but the same shortfall pattern for a second consecutive year. The ~24% permanent-staff loss and its downstream effects (documented in this entry's 2025 examples) had not been reversed as of this update. Update 2026-07-26: the 2026 peak season brought the staffing crisis to a head -- record crowds collided with reduced capacity at parks including Yosemite, where seasonal employees reportedly went weeks without pay, scientists and hydrologists were reassigned to cleaning restrooms and staffing entrance gates, and some campgrounds closed for lack of staff to run them. NPS also removed timed-entry reservation systems at some of the busiest parks and introduced a new $100-per-person fee for international visitors, both of which affected entrance-line flow during the July 4th weekend's record crowds. On a partial-relief note, NPS was approved to refill roughly 600 staff positions -- a real but small fraction of the several thousand permanent positions lost since January 2025, not a reversal of the underlying staffing loss this entry documents.

primary_proponent.note: Burgum's Secretarial Order 3426 is the specific policy mechanism that turned a staffing shortage into a documented service-quality crisis -- by prohibiting parks from closing or scaling back in response to short-staffing, the order effectively required remaining staff to absorb the gap rather than allowing an official acknowledgment of reduced capacity. Interior's own deputy press secretary's 'false narrative' denial is difficult to reconcile with the fact that the cited findings came from data Interior itself required parks to report under Burgum's own order.

estimated_impact.summary: NPCA President and CEO Theresa Pierno characterized the situation as predictable: 'This crisis was both predictable and preventable. Gutting staff, freezing seasonal hiring, and pushing out experienced rangers was a recipe for disaster.' Beyond visitor-experience impacts, several documented examples touch public safety and resource protection directly -- the loss of fire response capacity at Cumberland Island, halted pest/disease monitoring (including zoonotic disease surveillance for plague, rabies, and hantavirus) at Grand Canyon, and unstaffed entrance stations at Glacier National Park during normal operating hours.

title: Trump Administration Moves to Remove Supercomputers From NCAR, Disrupting Weather and Climate Research for 1,500+ Scientists
institution: National Science Foundation / National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR)
status: Blocked as of June 1, 2026 -- a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction halting further dismantling steps, following UCAR's March 2026 lawsuit alleging the plan was retaliation against Colorado; the underlying litigation over the plan's ultimate fate remains ongoing
date_of_action: 2025-12-16 (first reporting of White House plan to 'break up' NCAR) through 2026-02-13 (NSF letter confirming supercomputer removal plan)
what_changed: Reporting first surfaced in mid-December 2025 that the administration was moving to dismantle the National Science Foundation's National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado -- a 60-plus-year cornerstone of U.S. weather and climate science -- with officials characterizing it as a source of "climate alarmism." That earliest reporting specifically named NCAR's Mesa Laboratory campus as a target for shutdown, described plans to eliminate research programs internally labeled "woke," and indicated only select functions such as weather modeling would be transferred elsewhere rather than preserved intact. Following a January 2026 White House announcement of intent to 'break up' NCAR, an NSF letter released February 13, 2026 confirmed plans to remove NCAR's supercomputing facility and transfer it to an unspecified third party. The facility supports weather forecasting models, climate simulations, and extreme-weather prediction research used by approximately 1,500 researchers across more than 500 universities; NOAA itself relies on the facility to run some of its current forecasting models. Former NCAR director James Hurrell and other prominent colleagues in the weather and climate research community warned NSF that 'any path that leads to the fragmentation or dismantling of NSF NCAR is fundamentally not in the nation's interest,' and that the move could further set back NOAA's own weather-modeling capabilities, which the researchers noted have already lagged behind international competitors. On March 16, 2026, the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR) -- the nonprofit consortium of 129 universities that manages NCAR -- sued the federal agencies and officials behind the breakup plan, alleging the effort was retaliation against Colorado: specifically, that the administration was using NCAR's dismantling to pressure the state over Gov. Jared Polis's refusal to grant clemency to Tina Peters, a former county clerk convicted of tampering with voting machines in pursuit of Trump's 2020 election-fraud claims, and over the state's broader resistance to ceding authority over its own elections. OMB Director Russell Vought had publicly framed the plan as 'breaking up' NCAR because it was 'one of the largest sources of climate alarmism in the country,' and a White House spokesperson told CNN that Colorado's treatment depended on having 'a governor who actually wanted to work with President Trump.' On June 1, 2026, U.S. District Judge R. Brooke Jackson issued a preliminary injunction blocking the administration from taking further steps to dismantle NCAR, a win for the researchers and UCAR that halted the removal plan pending further litigation.

estimated_impact.summary: Removing the supercomputing facility disrupts a shared national research resource relied on by 1,500+ scientists at 500+ universities and by NOAA's own forecasting operations, at a time when U.S. weather-modeling capability already trails international competitors according to the researchers who objected.

title: NCUA Board Reduced to a Single Member After Trump Fires Both Democratic Board Members
institution: National Credit Union Administration
status: Ongoing (Harper and Otsuka filed their D.C. Circuit brief in mid-July 2026 formally arguing NCUA deserves Fed-like removal protection, following the district court's finding that Congress modeled NCUA's structure on the Federal Reserve; no ruling yet, and the two remain off the single-member board as of this update)
date_of_action: 2025-04-15 (firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling narrowed path to reinstatement)
what_changed: In April 2025, President Trump fired both Democratic members of the National Credit Union Administration's three-person board -- former Chairman Todd Harper and Tanya Otsuka -- by email, without citing cause, leaving Republican Chair Kyle Hauptman as the sole remaining board member. Harper's term was not set to expire until April 2027 and Otsuka's not until August 2029. The Federal Credit Union Act defines the NCUA board as a three-member body with staggered six-year terms, structured (according to a subsequent district court finding) to mirror the Federal Reserve's governance model and insulate credit union regulation from political turnover. With only one board member, the NCUA could continue routine supervision and enforcement but could not vote on new rulemakings or policy changes; a scheduled board meeting was canceled. Harper and Otsuka sued; in July 2025 U.S. District Judge Amir Ali ruled the firings unlawful and ordered reinstatement, finding Congress had deliberately restricted the president's removal power when it added fixed terms to the statute in 1978. The two briefly returned to a board meeting before an appeals court granted the administration an emergency stay, sidelining them again. The case was held in abeyance pending Trump v. Slaughter; when the Supreme Court ruled for the administration on June 29, 2026, credit-union trade groups and legal analysts concluded the ruling 'effectively ends' the Harper/Otsuka challenge, since the Federal Credit Union Act -- unlike the Federal Reserve Act -- contains no explicit 'for cause' removal language for the NCUA to lean on. Harper and Otsuka's attorneys have since asked the D.C. Circuit to let them argue the NCUA deserves Fed-like treatment given its similar market-regulatory structure, but as of this writing they remain off the board, which continues to operate with a single member. Update 2026-07-19: in a filing with the D.C. Circuit in mid-July 2026, Harper and Otsuka's attorneys formally argued NCUA deserves Federal Reserve-like removal protection, leaning on the district court's earlier finding that Congress deliberately modeled NCUA's governance structure on the Fed's -- the same distinction that succeeded for Cook but was rejected for MSPB's Harris. No ruling on this argument had issued as of this update; the appeal remains pending. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no ruling identified yet on Harper and Otsuka's mid-July D.C. Circuit filing arguing for Fed-like removal protection; the appeal remains pending and the board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member.

estimated_impact.summary: A statutorily three-member, bipartisan financial regulator serving over 140 million credit union members has operated with a single board member for over a year, unable to vote on new rulemakings during that period, with a Supreme Court ruling now narrowing the fired members' path back to the board.

Harper and Otsuka counter that Congress deliberately modeled the NCUA's structure on the Federal Reserve -- which the same June 29, 2026 ruling explicitly protected -- and that the district court already found this historical intent persuasive. Industry groups (America's Credit Unions, Defense Credit Union Council) have taken a notably neutral, process-focused position, calling mainly for a restored three-person board regardless of who fills the seats, rather than defending either side's substantive position. The litigation over the underlying legal question remains technically open at the D.C. Circuit even though most analysts consider the practical outcome settled.

title: NEA Terminates Over Half of Its Open Grants in a Single Weekend
institution: National Endowment for the Arts
status: Complete for terminated grants (effective May 31, 2025); the agency's proposed full elimination was not enacted as of the last-verified date, though grantmaking priorities remain altered under new leadership
date_of_action: 2025-05-02 to 2025-05-12 (termination notices); leadership confirmed December 19, 2025
what_changed: On the evening of May 2, 2025, hours after the administration released a preliminary FY2026 budget proposing to eliminate the NEA entirely, the agency emailed termination or withdrawal notices to hundreds of grantees nationwide, affecting more than half of its open awards, in amounts ranging from $10,000 to $100,000, effective May 31, 2025. A second round of termination notices followed on May 12, 2025. Affected organizations spanned all 50 states, Puerto Rico, and Washington, D.C., including theaters, orchestras, literary magazines, and community arts programs. Some grantees whose projects appeared to match the NEA's own newly stated priorities were terminated anyway; California Symphony, for example, lost funding for a commission specifically written to celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, one of the NEA's own listed new priorities. On May 5, 2025, ten NEA discipline directors and two members of senior leadership announced they would take deferred resignation, departing by the end of May. Mary Anne Carter, who had led the NEA during Trump's first term, was serving as senior adviser overseeing the agency at the time the terminations were issued (the previous Biden-appointed chair, Maria Rosario Jackson, had resigned on Inauguration Day); Carter was confirmed by the Senate as permanent NEA Chair on December 19, 2025. Separately, a federal judge in Rhode Island struck down a related NEA policy disfavoring grant applications the agency deemed to 'promote gender ideology' on September 19, 2025.

title: National Endowment for Democracy Funding Withheld, Partially Restored Only After Court Order
institution: National Endowment for Democracy (funded via State Department appropriation)
status: Ongoing (FY2025 funds released under court order; FY2026 funding and DOJ appeal still contested)
date_of_action: 2025-01-22 (funding access first denied) through ongoing litigation as of 2026
what_changed: Since January 22, 2025, the executive branch withheld the National Endowment for Democracy's (NED) access to congressionally appropriated funding, according to NED's federal lawsuit. NED, a nonprofit created by the 1983 National Endowment for Democracy Act, is statutorily directed to receive annual grants through the State Department; it distributes roughly 83% of its funds directly to democracy, free-press, and anti-corruption groups in more than 90 countries. NED sued in March 2025, alleging the withholding of nearly $240 million violated the Administrative Procedure Act, the NED Act, and constitutional separation-of-powers and appropriations provisions. The funding halt forced NED to furlough 75% of its staff and, per the lawsuit, created a 'devastating' cash flow crisis affecting 226 approved grants, 124 board-recommended grants, and 53 'core institute' projects. On August 11, 2025, U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich -- a Trump appointee -- granted a preliminary injunction, finding the administration had likely violated the NED Act by conditioning fund disbursement on alignment with 'Administration priorities,' calling that rationale 'not plausible' given repeated delays and shifting justifications. Following the ruling, DOJ released the roughly $95 million that remained withheld from NED's FY2025 appropriation. The administration appealed to the D.C. Circuit on October 9, 2025 (case ongoing as of this writing), and separately proposed eliminating NED's funding entirely in its FY2026 budget request, citing (among other claims) an allegation -- which NED's own fact sheet disputes as false -- that NED funded a Ukrainian group accused of doxing U.S. journalists. As of early 2026 court filings, the parties remained in disputes over whether and when NED's FY2026 appropriation would be obligated and disbursed. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no ruling change -- the D.C. Circuit appeal (docket 25-5361) remains held in abeyance. A concrete counter-signal to OMB's proposed elimination of NED funding: the House Appropriations Committee has recommended $315 million for NED in FY2026, well above both the administration's zero-funding request and NED's FY2025 baseline -- meaning the FY2026 funding fight, like several others in this tracker, pits congressional appropriators against the administration's budget request rather than reflecting a settled outcome.

primary_proponent.role: Director, Office of Management and Budget
primary_proponent.note: Named as a defendant in NED's lawsuit; OMB was identified in court filings as the office directing that NED's funding be held for 'review for alignment' with administration priorities, the practice the district court found unlawful.
