title: NIH Grant Freeze Found to Violate the Impoundment Control Act (GAO)
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Department of Health and Human Services
status: GAO Legal Finding Issued (nonbinding; underlying funding dispute partially reversed, full compliance unconfirmed)
date_of_action: 2025-08-05 (GAO report issued); underlying actions Feb 2025 - Dec 2025
what_changed: Following Trump executive orders in early 2025 targeting DEI and 'gender ideology' funding, NIH terminated more than 1,800 previously-awarded research grants and, separately, obligated roughly $8 billion less in new/continuing grant funding between February and June 2025 than in the same period the prior year -- a drop of more than a third. NIH also paused grant review meetings entirely from late January to early March 2025, delaying funds to hospitals and universities -- NPR reported on February 22, 2025 that this freeze alone had stalled roughly 16,000 pending grant applications worth about $1.5 billion, as the administration blocked the Federal Register notices required to schedule the review meetings. Separately, on February 24, 2025, NPR reported the administration's plan to cap NIH's reimbursement rate for research institutions' indirect costs (overhead such as facilities and administrative support) at 15%, down from a historical rate as high as 56% at some institutions -- a change research universities warned would force layoffs and halt projects even where direct grant funding remained intact, since indirect-cost reimbursement funds much of the physical and administrative infrastructure research depends on. NIH's funding contraction had a direct staffing dimension too: CBS News reported NIH issued surprise layoff notices to nearly 250 employees on May 6, 2025, including about 50 from the National Cancer Institute specifically. The pattern continued into the funding-mechanism itself later in the year: the New York Times reported that in December 2025, Trump ordered NIH and NSF to issue multi-year grants as upfront lump sums rather than the traditional annual-installment structure, a change that depleted available budgets faster and resulted in roughly 40% fewer new projects funded, alongside mass delays and grant cancellations reported as politically motivated by affected researchers. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan congressional watchdog, concluded on August 5, 2025 that the original 2025 funding actions violated the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which requires the executive branch to spend congressionally appropriated funds unless it follows a specific legal process to formally request a rescission -- a process NIH/HHS did not use. GAO noted HHS had taken down a public spending-tracking website, which itself hampered GAO's ability to investigate.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: Director, Office of Management and Budget
primary_proponent.note: Named directly by House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro as responsible alongside Trump: 'GAO has determined that President Trump and OMB Director Vought illegally withheld billions in funding.' This is the same official and legal mechanism (Impoundment Control Act) already tracked in the Cabinet-Level Legal Exposure database's Vought entry -- that entry covers a parallel GAO finding regarding OMB more broadly; this entry is specific to the NIH funding impoundment.

estimated_impact.summary: GAO's own finding is that $8 billion in already-appropriated NIH research funding was illegally withheld over a 5-month period -- money intended for research into cancer, Alzheimer's, ALS, diabetes, mental health, and maternal mortality, per Senate Appropriations Vice Chair Patty Murray's public statement. This was the fifth GAO impoundment finding against the administration in recent weeks as of August 2025, alongside similar findings on EV charging infrastructure funding, museum/library funding, Head Start funding, and K-12 energy efficiency funding -- suggesting a pattern rather than an isolated incident.

title: NIOSH Loses 85-90% of Staff, Gutting Firefighter Cancer Research, the 9/11 World Trade Center Health Program, and Fatality Investigations
institution: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), Department of Health and Human Services (part of CDC)
status: Ongoing as of mid-2025 reporting -- a partial reinstatement followed public backlash, but the entry's own sources describe only 'a fraction' restored, with downstream program disruptions (WTC Health Program, firefighter cancer/fatality research, dangerous-occupation safety training) continuing
date_of_action: 2025-02-21 (initial WTC Health Program staffing cut reported) through 2025-06-03 (training-program funding shortfalls reported)
what_changed: On February 21, 2025, the New York Times reported layoffs and buyouts had already cut about 20% of staffing at the World Trade Center Health Program specifically, jeopardizing research grants and delaying certifications critical to treating 9/11 responders and survivors -- a cut initially reinstated after pushback from lawmakers and veterans' groups, though the program's staffing crisis recurred and deepened in the following months as described below. Beginning February 20, 2025, Trump administration cuts began hitting NIOSH more broadly, the CDC institute responsible for occupational safety and health research. Early casualties included Patrick Montague, an investigator for the National Firefighter Registry for Cancer, fired along with colleagues in his program citing probationary status. By April 3, 2025, hundreds of NIOSH staff had been fired, including key personnel from the World Trade Center Health Program -- which provides medical care to 9/11 first responders and survivors -- and the program's longtime director, Dr. John Howard, was also removed. By April 13, the Guardian reported the WTC Health Program had been plunged into disarray, with cancer treatment, PTSD care, and other services for 9/11 survivors and first responders disrupted with no public transparency about what coverage remained available. By April 22, ProPublica reported the purge had eliminated 7 of the 8 members of NIOSH's firefighter fatality investigation team, halting major studies into firefighter cancer risk alongside the WTC-program disruption. On May 12, more than 100 current and former NIOSH employees sent a joint letter to Congress warning that mass purges were putting American workers at risk, stating more than 90% of NIOSH staff had received layoff notices and that critical programs -- the 9/11 Health Program and black lung screening among them -- had already been disrupted. By May 27, the Guardian confirmed an 85% NIOSH staff purge, with only a fraction of positions reinstated after public backlash. By early June, Reuters reported the cuts -- nearly 900 staff purged in April alone -- were forcing shutdowns of occupational-safety training programs specifically serving fishermen, farmers, and loggers, among America's most dangerous occupations, with key training centers warning they would run out of funding by summer or fall 2025.

title: NIST workforce reduction and standards/research budget cuts
institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology (Department of Commerce)
status: Ongoing, with a partial reversal on MEP specifically -- after issuing RIF notices to the entire program's staff despite full congressional funding, NIST released a Notice of Funding Opportunity in July 2026 for 14 MEP centers (applications due Aug. 21, 2026), while the Coons-led congressional inquiry into the earlier RIF action remains unanswered
date_of_action: 2025-02 to 2026-01 (workforce cuts); FY2026 budget proposal released June 2025
what_changed: NIST, the 125-year-old nonregulatory agency that sets the country's measurement, cybersecurity, and technology standards (including the widely used Cybersecurity Framework, the AI Risk Management Framework, and post-quantum encryption standards), lost more than 700 positions between the start of the Trump administration and January 2026 through resignations, retirements, and voluntary deferments, including roughly 500 recent hires who were let go early in 2025 while still in probationary status. A lab responsible for testing and validating the federal government's encryption implementations lost 89 staff. On March 26, 2025, the administration moved to eliminate NIST's Atomic Spectroscopy Group, which maintains atomic measurement data used as a foundational reference across nuclear fusion, astrophysics, and semiconductor-manufacturing research nationwide -- a specific, named-program elimination distinct from and in addition to the broader probationary and encryption-lab losses already documented in this entry. The administration's FY2026 budget request proposed cutting NIST's $1.2 billion budget by $325 million, eliminating the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership Program entirely (97 positions, $175 million, serving small and mid-size manufacturers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico) and cutting $125 million and 556 positions from NIST's core Scientific and Technical Research and Services program, citing cybersecurity/privacy, health and biological measurements, and physical-infrastructure research as target areas. House appropriators later rejected the steepest of these cuts and restored funding above the administration's request, but the agency has already absorbed the workforce losses and, as of early 2026, is still awaiting a formal Reduction-in-Force and reorganization plan. Congress's final FY2026 appropriation funded NIST's Scientific and Technical Research and Services program at $1.25 billion -- more than $542 million above the administration's request, and higher than even the $980 million House figure already cited in this entry -- and fully funded the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership at $175 million, rejecting the administration's proposal to eliminate it. Despite that enacted funding, NIST issued Reduction-in-Force and possible-separation notices to every MEP employee, prompting Sen. Chris Coons and colleagues to send a formal letter demanding an explanation for what they characterized as an 'unauthorized dismantling' of a program Congress had just funded. NIST's Computer Security Division also lost its division head and roughly a dozen subordinates to retirement offers, a specific loss to the cybersecurity-standards function this entry already documents as strained. Update 2026-07-26: NIST released a Notice of Funding Opportunity for 14 Manufacturing Extension Partnership centers (Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, California, Georgia, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Missouri, Montana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Utah, and Vermont), with an informational webinar scheduled July 28, 2026 and applications due August 21, 2026. Trade press (Advanced Manufacturing) frames this as a real reversal after NIST's earlier funding notice for the program's next tranche of centers was delayed until December 4, 2025 -- itself more than six months behind schedule and a gap that, combined with the RIF notices, had already pushed roughly 90% of MEP centers into layoffs or hiring freezes, with some at risk of closing entirely. This doesn't resolve Sen. Coons's still-unanswered oversight letter about the RIF notices themselves, but is a concrete sign the program is continuing rather than being wound down.

title: NLRB Loses Statutory Quorum for Nearly a Year After Trump Fires Board Member Wilcox
institution: National Labor Relations Board
status: Complete (Wilcox's removal is now considered constitutionally settled following Trump v. Slaughter, June 29, 2026, though the Supreme Court has not yet formally disposed of her specific case)
date_of_action: 2025-01-27 (firing) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court's Slaughter ruling resolves the underlying legal question); board lacked a working quorum for roughly 11 of the intervening months
what_changed: On January 27, 2025, President Trump fired NLRB Board Member Gwynne Wilcox without citing any of the statutory grounds (neglect of duty or malfeasance) required by the National Labor Relations Act, leaving the five-seat Board with only two active members, below the three-member quorum required to issue decisions. Wilcox sued on February 5, 2025. U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell ruled the firing unlawful on March 6, 2025, calling it a 'blatant violation of the law' and a 'power grab,' and ordered Wilcox reinstated, which briefly restored the Board's quorum. A three-judge D.C. Circuit panel stayed that ruling on March 28; the full en banc D.C. Circuit reversed course and reinstated Wilcox again on April 7; Chief Justice Roberts then issued an emergency stay removing her again on April 9. On May 22, 2025, the Supreme Court declined to reinstate Wilcox in a 6-3 emergency-docket order, explicitly not a ruling on the merits. The Board remained below quorum until regaining one in December 2025 through new Trump nominations. On January 28, 2026, the D.C. Circuit declined en banc review of the panel decision upholding Wilcox's termination. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court's decision in the related case Trump v. Slaughter overruled the 90-year-old Humphrey's Executor precedent underlying Wilcox's legal theory; legal analysts across firms now consider her removal constitutionally settled even though the Court has not yet formally disposed of her specific still-pending case.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Fired Wilcox directly via a short email citing loss of confidence in her leadership, then pursued the legal theory that his Article II authority permitted the removal all the way to the Supreme Court, a position the Court substantially validated in the related Slaughter case.

estimated_impact.summary: The National Labor Relations Board, the sole federal agency responsible for enforcing private-sector labor law and adjudicating unfair-labor-practice and union-election disputes, was left without a functioning quorum for nearly all of 2025, halting its ability to issue binding decisions during that period.

estimated_impact.caveat: The administration's position, ultimately validated in substance by the Supreme Court's Slaughter ruling, is that the President's Article II authority requires the ability to remove officials exercising executive power at will, regardless of statutory for-cause protections. Labor advocates and a 20-state coalition of attorneys general (led by California AG Bonta, in an amicus brief) argued the firing created a 'dangerous regulatory vacuum' that left workers without a functioning forum to resolve unfair-labor-practice complaints or conduct union elections for most of a year. Notably, the legal question was genuinely unsettled for over a year: a federal district court and an initial D.C. Circuit panel sided with Wilcox, before the en banc D.C. Circuit, a Supreme Court emergency stay, and ultimately the Slaughter precedent sided with the administration, reflecting real legal uncertainty rather than a one-sided dispute.

title: NNSA Nuclear-Weapons-Complex Staffing Crisis -- From Accidental Firings to a Shutdown Furlough That Halted Weapons Work for the First Time in History
institution: National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), a semi-autonomous Department of Energy agency responsible for the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile; related developments at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
status: Ongoing, with escalating severity through the year -- initial erroneous firings (Feb 2025) gave way to a documented brain-drain (Mar-May 2025), then a historic shutdown-driven near-total work stoppage (Oct 2025), followed by a policy shift that reduces regulatory oversight of new reactor construction (Dec 2025)
date_of_action: 2025-02-17 (initial erroneous firings) through 2025-12-30 (Reactor Pilot Program launch)
what_changed: In February 2025, DOGE-driven federal workforce cuts mistakenly fired NNSA employees -- some working on the nuclear stockpile and on tracking nuclear threats, including in Ukraine -- and the administration then could not contact them about reinstatement because their government email accounts had already been deactivated. ABC News reported on February 21, 2025 that this confusion was not limited to NNSA: hundreds of federal employees initially terminated from agencies including NNSA, the VA, and USDA had their dismissals rescinded, but many remained unclear on their actual employment status even after the reversal, reflecting a broader pattern of chaotic, poorly-tracked terminations across the initial wave of DOGE-directed cuts. By March 2025, the New York Times reported more than 130 senior scientists, engineers, and security experts had been forced out of NNSA, jeopardizing nuclear modernization programs and safety protocols. By May 2025, USA Today reported the cuts had derailed years of hiring progress and raised new safety concerns at weapons facilities including Los Alamos, the Y-12 National Security Complex, and Pantex. The staffing erosion reached the Nuclear Regulatory Commission as well: at a September 4, 2025 Senate hearing, two of the NRC's three remaining commissioners said they feared Trump could purge them too if they resisted his push to fast-track new reactor approvals, part of a stated goal to quadruple U.S. nuclear generating capacity by 2050. The crisis peaked during the October 2025 government shutdown: NNSA warned it would furlough 80% of its workforce as shutdown funding ran out, leaving only 375 'essential' employees and placing facility contractors in 'minimum-safe' status; by October 21, more than 1,400 employees -- over 75% of staff -- had actually been furloughed, leaving fewer than 400 on duty and suspending nearly all work on the U.S. nuclear weapons program, the first time in the program's history that weapons assembly and modernization work came to a complete stop. Funding for the Office of Secure Transportation, which physically moves nuclear warheads and materials, was confirmed only through October 27 as the shutdown continued. Then, on December 30, 2025, Trump officials launched a Reactor Pilot Program fast-tracking construction of new, largely untested nuclear reactor designs, with oversight shifted from the traditionally independent Nuclear Regulatory Commission to the Department of Energy itself -- aiming to bring at least three experimental reactors online by July 4, 2026 under an aggressive political deadline and with limited public transparency.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
primary_proponent.role: Directed the initial 2025 workforce cuts across NNSA and related agencies
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing the NNSA-specific cuts; the erroneous-firing episode in particular was reported as a process failure (deactivated emails preventing reinstatement contact) rather than a deliberate targeting decision, though it occurred within DOGE's broader, deliberately aggressive workforce-reduction push. The later Reactor Pilot Program and its shift of oversight from NRC to DOE reflects a distinct, deliberate administration policy choice.

estimated_impact.summary: Substantial, escalating loss of specialized nuclear-weapons-complex staffing capacity, culminating in the first complete halt to U.S. nuclear weapons assembly and modernization work in the program's history, alongside a shift of new-reactor oversight away from the traditionally independent nuclear safety regulator

title: NOAA Climate Research Zeroed Out in FY2026 Budget Proposal, Princeton Partnership Defunded
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
status: Partially implemented, and repeating -- the Princeton funding cut took effect and the administration proposed eliminating NOAA's climate research office again in its FY2027 budget, for the second year running; Congress rejected the same elimination in FY2026 and House appropriators' initial FY2027 markup signals they are likely to do so again
date_of_action: 2025-04-08 (Princeton funding cut announced) through the FY2026 budget cycle (proposal released July 2025; Congress had not enacted it as of the last-verified date)
what_changed: On April 8, 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced the termination of nearly $4 million in NOAA cooperative research funding to Princeton University, effective June 30, 2025, covering three programs including the Cooperative Institute for Modeling the Earth System, which supports Princeton's partnership with NOAA's Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL), widely regarded as producing some of the world's most advanced climate modeling. The Commerce Department's official announcement stated the program 'promotes exaggerated and implausible climate threats, contributing to a phenomenon known as climate anxiety.' In July 2025, NOAA's proposed FY2026 budget was reported to contain a literal line reading 'Total, Climate Research: $0,' along with the proposed elimination of the entire Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR), NOAA's research arm, and defunding of all of OAR's climate and weather cooperative institutes nationwide, including CIRES at the University of Colorado Boulder, which houses the National Snow and Ice Data Center. The overall proposal called for cutting NOAA's budget by more than 25% and its ~13,000-person workforce by roughly 17%, along with a 44% reduction in planned investment in next-generation geostationary weather satellites. Congressional spending panels rejected the FY2026 budget request as proposed, but the administration proceeded with some of the changes administratively regardless, including terminating contracts for planned satellite instruments in August 2025 as what agency officials described to staff as a 'down payment' on the broader proposed cuts. The administration's FY2027 budget request, released in 2026, again proposes eliminating the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR) -- the same office Congress rejected eliminating in the FY2026 cycle -- along with more than $1 billion in additional NOAA program cuts, including defunding the network of global monitoring laboratories and 14 other climate laboratories nationwide. At an April 2026 budget hearing, NOAA officials defended the cuts while members of both parties on the relevant committee pushed back. The House Commerce-Justice-Science Appropriations subcommittee's initial FY2027 markup was reported as favorable to NOAA's weather enterprise, suggesting Congress may again decline to enact the full elimination, consistent with the FY2026 outcome. The administration's separate FY2026 budget request also proposed eliminating all $43.5 million in federal support for NOAA's Integrated Ocean Observing System, a real-time data source used by harbor pilots, weather forecasters, and military operations, according to AP reporting in May 2025. By September 2025, the Washington Post reported the cuts had moved beyond budget proposals into concrete instrument shutdowns: the administration was closing down climate-monitoring satellites, shutting off carbon-tracking instruments, and scrapping sensors used to monitor water contamination and greenhouse gases, with internal budget documents directing NOAA to focus solely on 'weather-only' tools -- consistent with Project 2025's earlier call to dismantle federal climate research capacity. One consequence of NOAA's shrinking disaster-tracking function became visible that fall: NBC News reported in October 2025 that after the administration effectively shut down NOAA's billion-dollar disaster-cost-tracking database, a group of former NOAA scientists rebuilt an equivalent tracker independently through the nonprofit Climate Central -- their reconstruction found the costliest six-month stretch of U.S. weather disasters on record, with 14 separate events each exceeding $1 billion in damage, led by the Los Angeles wildfires at more than $61 billion.

estimated_impact.summary: A federal agency responsible for the data and modeling underlying weather forecasting, hurricane prediction, and climate research had its dedicated climate research funding line proposed at zero and lost a 57-year research partnership with one of the world's leading climate modeling laboratories.

estimated_impact.caveat: The administration's stated rationale, per the Commerce Department's own announcement, is that the affected Princeton research 'fosters fear rather than rational, balanced discussion' and that eliminating it will 'streamline and reduce the cost and size of the Federal Government.' Critics, including former NOAA research director Craig McLean, argue the cuts amount to dismantling the scientific basis for hurricane and severe-weather forecasting, and ProPublica reporting noted that Secretary Lutnick's former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, had itself described climate change in prior public materials as 'the defining issue of our time' and warned it would be 'disastrous and life threatening' if unchecked, a contrast critics cite as evidence the funding decision reflects political priorities rather than a reassessment of the science. It is also important to note the FY2026 budget eliminating NOAA's climate research entirely is a proposal, not enacted law: congressional appropriators in both parties have been reported as skeptical of the scale of the cuts and have not approved the request as written, even though the administration has moved ahead with some individual actions, such as satellite contract terminations, independent of congressional approval.

Strong for the FY2026 budget proposal and OAR elimination plan, independently corroborated across NPR, Colorado Public Radio, Eos, Science/AAAS, PBS NewsHour, and ProPublica, with the important caveat clearly noted that this remains a budget proposal Congress has not enacted as of the last-verified date. Re-verified 2026-07-20: this is now a repeating pattern rather than a one-time proposal -- the administration has proposed eliminating OAR in back-to-back budget cycles (FY2026 and FY2027) and Congress rejected it the first time; whether that holds again for FY2027 was not yet resolved as of this update (House subcommittee markup only, not enacted). Frame as an annual recurring fight, not a settled outcome either direction.

title: DOGE Cuts Gutted NOAA's Space Traffic Coordination Office, Then FY2026 Budget Sought to Eliminate Its Core System Entirely
institution: NOAA Office of Space Commerce (Commerce Department)
status: Ongoing (some senior staff reinstated; FY2026 budget proposal would eliminate the office's core system entirely, not yet enacted as of the sourcing reviewed)
date_of_action: 2025-02-27 (initial firings) through 2026 budget cycle (proposed elimination of TraCSS funding)
what_changed: On February 27, 2025, DOGE-driven cuts hit NOAA's Office of Space Commerce (OSC), a roughly 25-person office, on a few hours' notice -- about a third of the office's staff, including the chief of the Traffic Coordination System for Space (TraCSS), Dmitry Poisik. TraCSS is the civilian satellite traffic coordination system OSC has been building since 2018 (under Space Policy Directive 3, signed in Trump's first term) to warn commercial and government satellite operators of potential collisions as low Earth orbit becomes increasingly crowded. The cuts also hit OSC's Commercial Remote Sensing Regulatory Affairs Division, which licenses commercial imaging satellite companies; affected licensees received an email stating 'no senior personnel remain in the office' and warning of 'significant delays' processing licensing actions. Since the initial layoffs, three staffers in leadership roles were brought back, but congressional Democrats (Reps. Valerie Foushee and Zoe Lofgren among others) continued to warn about the office's reduced capacity. In 2026, the administration's budget request went further, proposing to cut OSC's budget by 85% and eliminate 18 positions, while eliminating federal funding for TraCSS entirely -- a group of space-industry organizations wrote to House and Senate leaders warning the cuts would put both commercial and government satellite operators at risk of collision.

title: NRC Commissioner Fired Without Cause, Agency Independence and Staffing Cut Under DOGE Reorganization
institution: Nuclear Regulatory Commission
status: Ongoing (Hanson's firing remains final and unlitigated; the resulting vacancy was filled and the commission restored to its full five members by December 2025, with Ho Nieh designated the new NRC chairman on January 8, 2026, succeeding David Wright, who remains a commissioner; DOGE-directed reorganization and regulatory rewrite continuing on EO 14300's original schedule)
date_of_action: 2025-05-23 (executive order) and 2025-06-13 (Hanson firing)
what_changed: On June 13, 2025, President Trump fired NRC Commissioner Christopher T. Hanson, effective immediately, via a two-line email from the White House Presidential Personnel Office. It was the first removal of an NRC commissioner since the agency's creation in 1974; Hanson's term was not set to expire until 2029, and no cause was cited beyond a White House spokesperson's comment that 'all organizations are more effective when leaders are rowing in the same direction.' Hanson, originally appointed by Trump in his first term and later chaired the commission under Biden, said he was terminated 'without cause, contrary to existing law and longstanding precedent regarding removal of independent agency appointees.' The firing left the five-member commission at a 2-2 partisan split with one vacancy, and came three weeks after Trump signed Executive Order 14300, 'Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission' (May 23, 2025), which directs the NRC to reorganize and undertake reductions in force in consultation with its DOGE Team, shrink the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards to the statutory minimum, and complete a 'wholesale revision' of its safety regulations and guidance documents within 18 months, with rulemaking routed through OMB Director Russell Vought's office -- a process not previously applied to this traditionally arms-length safety regulator. Career staff departures followed; NRC's No. 2 career operations official, a 32-year veteran and self-described two-time Trump voter, retired in May 2025 partly in protest of political operatives being embedded in senior leadership positions with what he called potential to 'significantly influence decision-making.' The DOGE-directed reorganization required by EO 14300 has proceeded on the order's own timeline: the NRC issued its notices of proposed rulemaking for the 'wholesale revision' of safety regulations by the February 2026 deadline, and in mid-2026 launched a major organizational restructuring -- consolidating around new-reactor, operating-reactor, and materials/waste business lines, and creating two new offices (Office of Advanced Reactors; Office of the Chief Nuclear Reactor Inspector) -- targeted for completion by September 2026, with final rules due under the EO's 18-month deadline (November 2026). No update on Hanson's own removal was found; it remains final and unlitigated as of this recheck. CORRECTION 2026-07-26: this entry's prior recheck (2026-07-20) still described the commission as sitting at a 2-2 partisan split with one vacancy from Hanson's June 2025 removal -- that vacancy was actually filled months earlier, when Doug Weaver was sworn in December 22, 2025, restoring the commission to its full five-member statutory complement. Separately, on January 8, 2026, Trump designated Commissioner Ho Nieh -- a Republican who previously ran NRC's Office of Nuclear Reactor Regulation from 2018-2021 -- as the NRC's 20th chairman, succeeding David Wright, who continues serving as a commissioner. The commission's current composition includes Republicans Nieh and Wright alongside Democratic commissioners Matthew Marzano and Bradley Crowell. Hanson's own removal remains final and unlitigated as of this update; the leadership-composition correction here is about the vacancy his firing created, not about the firing's legality. Extending the deregulatory push, the NRC voted in April 2026 to phase out its own agency-led 'force-on-force' security drills at nuclear power plants -- mock attack exercises historically run and evaluated by NRC inspectors to test each plant's defenses -- shifting to a model where plant operators run their own exercises and NRC staff only observe. title: NSF Fires 168 Staff Including Antarctic Program Managers, Disrupting U.S. Polar Research Logistics
institution: National Science Foundation
status: Implemented -- February 18, 2025 firings took effect; downstream disruption to Antarctic program management reported as ongoing as of the sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-02-18 (NSF firings) through at least 2025-03-10 (reported downstream Antarctic Program disruption)
what_changed: On February 18, 2025, DOGE-driven cuts eliminated 168 NSF positions -- roughly 10% of the agency's staff -- including probationary employees and expert appointments. Several of those fired were program managers for the U.S. Antarctic Program, the office responsible for maintaining communication with the Antarctic infrastructure and logistics contractor, planning scientist deployments to the continent, and tracking budgets and funding for operations and maintenance work at the three permanent U.S. Antarctic stations (McMurdo, Palmer, and the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station), which host research including the South Pole and BICEP telescopes, the IceCube neutrino detector, and long-running atmospheric climate monitoring. One scientist whose NSF project manager was fired told WIRED, 'Without them, everything stops.' By early March 2025, researchers reported losing clarity on reporting structures and proposal-submission processes, and warned that a shutdown of the South Pole station in particular would be 'basically nearly impossible to bring... back up' given the logistical difficulty of restarting polar operations. Around the same time, NSF also removed gender-inclusive housing-preference language from Antarctic staffer forms for McMurdo Station. Scientists and members of Congress warned the disruption risked ceding ground at the South Pole: reporting identified Germany, Canada, Spain, and China as already recruiting displaced or frustrated American Antarctic researchers, and raised concern that Russia and China could expand their own polar presence into any resulting U.S. capability gap. House Science Committee leaders Zoe Lofgren and Valerie Foushee separately criticized the broader wave of NSF firings publicly and pressed the National Science Board to intervene.

title: DOGE Terminated 1,752 NSF Research Grants Using a Senator's Keyword List, Then NSF Formally Weakened Its Own Peer Review Standards
institution: National Science Foundation (NSF)
status: Largely complete (terminations executed; peer-review rule changes formally in effect since Dec. 15, 2025)
date_of_action: 2025-04-14 (DOGE arrives at NSF) through 2025-12-15 (formal peer-review process change takes effect)
what_changed: On April 14, 2025, three DOGE personnel arrived at NSF headquarters and were given direct access to the agency's internal grant management systems -- an unusual level of access for political appointees into a agency's live award-processing systems, which one NSF program officer told Nature 'raises the hairs on the back of our neck.' DOGE ordered NSF's grants division to pull back all proposals that had already cleared full peer review and internal approval but were awaiting final signoff, instructing career program officers to perform undefined 'mitigation work' to bring the proposals into compliance with Trump executive orders restricting research related to diversity, equity, and inclusion or climate change. NSF ultimately terminated 1,752 active grants worth $1.4 billion. The screening process relied substantially on a list of roughly 3,400 grants compiled by Sen. Ted Cruz's office, which Cruz characterized as funding 'neo-Marxist class warfare propaganda'; independent analysis by the Grant Watch project found the terminated grants' titles and abstracts most frequently contained the words 'Black,' 'climate,' 'student,' 'justice,' 'identity,' and 'teacher' -- and that NSF's STEM Education directorate alone lost 839 grants worth $888 million, nearly half of all dollars terminated agency-wide despite being a small fraction of NSF's total budget. NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan resigned during this period. Separately, effective December 15, 2025, NSF formally revised its own peer review standards (PAPPG 24-1 Supplement 1): the minimum number of required external reviews per proposal dropped from three to two, one of which may now be an NSF staff member rather than an outside expert; panel discussions became optional rather than required; and panel summary write-ups were capped at three to five sentences, down from what had often run several paragraphs. NSF attributed the peer-review changes to a proposal backlog and workforce reductions, not to the DOGE-driven terminations directly. Update 2026-07-28: On April 24, 2026, all 22 members of the National Science Board (NSF's presidentially-appointed governing/oversight body) received an email notifying them, without explanation, that their positions were 'terminated, effective immediately.' On May 12, 2026, roughly 1,500 members and supporters of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine -- including 37 Nobel Prize winners -- denounced the dismissal in an open letter calling it 'an alarming attack on the ability of the US to engage in basic and applied research.' Separately, nearly 150 NSF employees sent their own letter of dissent to Congress, warning that the administration's actions -- including steep budget cuts, mass firings, grant terminations, and withholding of billions in appropriated funds -- threaten to dismantle the agency, and calling for congressional intervention.

primary_proponent.name: DOGE personnel Luke Farritor and Zachary Terrell
primary_proponent.role: DOGE staff embedded at NSF with direct grant-system access
primary_proponent.note: Then-NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan wrote in an internal priorities update that efforts to broaden research participation 'should not preference some groups at the expense of others' -- the stated policy rationale for the review -- before resigning shortly afterward. Sen. Ted Cruz is the named source of the keyword-flagged grant list that substantially shaped which proposals were targeted, though NSF and the White House have not published an official list or criteria of their own, leaving outside researchers (Grant Watch) to reconstruct the pattern independently from grant titles and abstracts.

estimated_impact.summary: Congress separately and explicitly rejected a much larger cut: the FY2026 appropriations bill (signed January 23, 2026) funded NSF at $8.75 billion, refusing the White House's request to cut the agency to $3.9 billion (roughly 55%), which NSF's own internal projections said would have dropped grant funding rates to approximately 7%. The Senate Commerce Committee described the enacted funding level as preventing 'an existential threat to U.S. science funding.' This creates a notable split: Congress protected NSF's overall budget, while DOGE's targeted, keyword-driven terminations and the subsequent peer-review rule changes altered the agency's internal operations and standards in ways that did not require, and were not subject to, the same congressional appropriations fight.

title: NSF Announced Dismantling 80% of $368M Ocean Monitoring Network, Then Reversed Course After Bipartisan Congressional Revolt
institution: National Science Foundation (NSF)
status: Reversed -- NSF announced in mid-June 2026 it would terminate the dismantlement plan and reinstall already-removed Pacific Northwest instruments, following bipartisan Senate and House letters demanding the array's preservation
date_of_action: 2026-05 (dismantlement announced) through 2026-06-18 (reversal announced)
what_changed: In May 2026, NSF announced plans to remove roughly 900 deep-sea instruments from the Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI), a $368 million network operating continuously since 2016 that monitors ocean currents, marine heat waves, carbon absorption, coastal flooding risk, fisheries conditions, and broader climate indicators across sites off Oregon, Washington, Alaska, North Carolina, and the Irminger Sea between Greenland and Iceland. NSF said it would begin removing instruments in June 2026, projecting roughly $48 million in annual operational savings, and had in fact begun removing equipment from Pacific Northwest waters before Congress intervened. On June 16, 2026, a bipartisan group of senators -- led by Democrat Jeff Merkley and Republican Lisa Murkowski, joined by Sens. Markey, Warren, Baldwin, Murray, Cantwell, Whitehouse, Van Hollen, and Wyden -- sent a letter to NSF directing it to terminate the dismantlement plan and maintain the array; House lawmakers sent a parallel letter the same day. On June 18, 2026, NSF issued an unsigned statement reversing course: it would terminate the plan to disband 80% of OOI and reinstall the equipment already removed from Pacific Northwest waters.

primary_proponent.name: National Science Foundation leadership (unsigned June 18, 2026 reversal statement; original dismantlement announcement made under NSF's Trump-appointed leadership)
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency responsible for basic-science funding and infrastructure, including OOI
primary_proponent.note: NSF's original decision to dismantle 80% of a $368 million active climate-monitoring network -- and its reversal only after direct, bipartisan congressional intervention -- is the accountability record this entry documents; no single named official's public statement defending the original dismantlement decision was identified in reporting reviewed.

estimated_impact.summary: Scientists and lawmakers characterized the initial plan as eliminating one of the only continuous, real-time ocean-climate monitoring systems along U.S. coasts at a moment of accelerating climate risk, warning it would create a lasting data gap for tracking phenomena like Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) slowdown, marine heat waves, and coastal flooding risk. The bipartisan, cross-chamber reversal within roughly five weeks of the announcement is itself notable: an unusually fast congressional check on an agency-level dismantlement decision, in contrast to many other entries in this tracker where similar actions proceeded without reversal.

title: National Weather Service Lost ~600 Staff, Including a Vacant Position Tied to the Texas Flood Warnings
institution: National Weather Service (NWS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Department of Commerce
status: Partially reversed (active rehiring underway, but experience/institutional-knowledge loss is not recoverable by rehiring alone)
date_of_action: Early-mid 2025 (initial cuts); ongoing reorganization through at least April 2026
what_changed: Early in 2025, DOGE-driven early retirement incentives and probationary-employee firings cut roughly 600 employees (about 15% of staff) from the National Weather Service nationwide, part of broader cuts to its parent agency NOAA. NOAA workers described the process to NBC News as chaotic and intentionally disorienting: employees reported being fired, then reinstated, then fired again within the same stretch of weeks, in some cases losing pay, health insurance, and unemployment-benefit eligibility during the gaps. By May 2025, 52 of the NWS's 122 weather forecast offices had staffing vacancy rates above 20%, and at least 8 offices could no longer maintain 24/7 operations, including Sacramento, Goodland (KS), and Jackson (KY). Former NWS directors wrote publicly that 'our worst nightmare is that weather forecast offices will be so understaffed that there will be needless loss of life.' Specifically at the Austin/San Antonio forecast office -- which covers the Texas Hill Country -- the warning coordination meteorologist position (responsible for working directly with emergency managers and the public on what to do when a disaster strikes) had been vacant since the person who held it for decades accepted an early-retirement offer at the end of April 2025, roughly two months before the deadly July 4, 2025 Guadalupe River flash flood that killed more than 100 people. Two days after that flood, the administration issued a memo stating no federal vacancies could be filled until October, after the extreme weather season ended. In 2026, NOAA began actively rehiring (recruiting ~150 entry-level meteorologists, filling 200+ positions since late 2025), but experienced meteorologists warn the resulting workforce skews inexperienced -- 'because there are no old-timers left,' as one Alaska-based former NWS meteorologist put it -- and 'upper air' atmospheric data collection has noticeably degraded since January 2025, a data source considered fundamental to forecast accuracy.

primary_proponent.name: DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) / NOAA leadership
primary_proponent.role: Executed the early-2025 workforce reductions
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in available reporting as personally directing the NWS-specific cuts -- this was part of the broader, DOGE-driven federal workforce reduction effort. NOAA Administrator Neil Jacobs stated during his confirmation hearing that he would 'ensure that staffing the Weather Service offices is a top priority,' an on-the-record commitment worth checking against subsequent NWS staffing trends.

estimated_impact.summary: The Center for American Progress's analysis of the Texas floods specifically is careful to note the Austin/San Antonio office still issued timely, accurate, impacts-based forecasts despite the vacancy -- crediting 'the extraordinary dedication of the current staff' -- while also stating plainly that the vacant warning coordination meteorologist role is 'responsible for working with emergency managers and the public to ensure people know what to do when a disaster strikes,' the exact communication function that came under scrutiny after the floods. This is a case where the forecasting itself held up, but a specific staffing gap affected the human coordination layer between forecast and public action.

title: NWS Suspends or Cuts Weather Balloon Launches at Multiple Sites Following Staffing Cuts, Coinciding With Missed Tornado Warnings
institution: National Weather Service (NOAA, Department of Commerce)
status: Ongoing -- suspensions/reductions announced March 2025 remained in effect through mid-2026, with some restored launches shifted to midday rather than the original schedule
date_of_action: 2025-03-20 (initial suspension/reduction announcement) through 2026 (ongoing effect)
what_changed: On February 26, 2025, OMB Director Russell Vought and then-Acting OPM Director Charles Ezell issued a memo directing federal agencies to prepare for mass layoffs. The next day, February 27, 2025, the Office of Personnel Management fired approximately 880 NOAA employees; NOAA followed roughly two months later by approving over 1,000 additional deferred resignations or buyouts. Citing the resulting staffing shortages, the National Weather Service announced on March 20, 2025 that it would suspend or reduce twice-daily weather balloon (radiosonde) launches at 11 upper-air observation sites: full suspension at Kotzebue, Alaska; Omaha, Nebraska; and Rapid City, South Dakota; reduction to once daily at Aberdeen, South Dakota; Grand Junction, Colorado; Green Bay, Wisconsin; Gaylord, Michigan; North Platte, Nebraska; and Riverton, Wyoming; and intermittent suspension at Albany, New York, and Gray, Maine, with NWS stating twice-daily launches would resume 'when staffing permits.' At sites that kept launching, many shifted the traditional early-morning flight to midday to align with when day-shift staff are on duty, rather than the pre-dawn atmospheric-sampling window the schedule was originally designed around. The disruption continued into the 2026 severe-weather season: NPR and NBC News reported that meteorologists in Kansas and Missouri linked reduced balloon data to tornado outbreaks catching forecasters by surprise, including a specific April 13, 2026 episode in which NWS forecast almost no chance of tornadoes in East Central Kansas and a balloon was launched only after storms had already begun forming. The Boston Globe reported that March 2026 saw 202 tornadoes nationally -- more than double the 30-year average for that month -- and April 2026 saw 250 versus a 180 average, with forecasters attributing part of the shortfall in advance warning to staffing and resource gaps at NWS offices, of which 122 exist nationwide.

title: HR1 ("One Big Beautiful Bill") Federal Funding Cuts Strip Essential Plan Coverage From ~450,000 New Yorkers

status: Ongoing -- eligibility changes took effect July 1, 2026; New York State has taken some mitigating action but has not restored coverage to all affected enrollees

what_changed: HR1, the reconciliation law Trump signed in 2026 and that the administration has branded the 'One Big Beautiful Bill,' cut federal funding underlying New York's Essential Plan -- a Basic Health Program that had provided low-cost coverage to low- and middle-income residents who earn too much for Medicaid but still qualify for ACA marketplace subsidy support. title: Acting DNI Bill Pulte purges Office of the Director of National Intelligence staff
institution: Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI)
status: Ongoing -- 4th round of cuts completed as of 2026-07-27; Washington Post reports ~200 total employees purged since June 1, workforce reduced to ~1,300 (roughly half of ODNI's size when Trump returned to office)
what_changed: Before he had officially taken office, Bill Pulte showed up at ODNI headquarters a day early, catching staff -- including outgoing DNI Tulsi Gabbard, who was given only a brief heads-up -- off guard. CNN reported Pulte requested a list of every ODNI employee so he could assess whom to fire, repeatedly asked whether he would have access to a government plane, requested a security detail, asked about the status and classification level of his newly issued security clearance, and asked ODNI staff in a briefing whether he could bring the President's Daily Brief to his house. Pulte was the first person to lead ODNI since its creation after September 11, 2001 without any prior intelligence or national-security experience and without having previously held a security clearance. Beginning about a week after Tulsi Gabbard resigned as DNI, Acting Director Bill Pulte began firing and reassigning ODNI staff in successive rounds of cuts. An initial round removed 6 career and political intelligence staff and sent 45 others back to their home agencies -- just over 50 people removed from ODNI roles in total. A source told NBC News that Pulte had ordered staff to identify roughly 400 employees for termination at the National Counterterrorism Center, though other sources said the Center itself was ultimately not hit by that specific round; the National Counterintelligence and Security Center was separately reported as expected to face significant cuts. Pulte has said publicly that his goal is to reduce the size of ODNI and refocus it on national security. Separately, Pulte's authority to hold the role at all has been disputed: the DNI has no supervisor other than the president, making it a 'principal officer' under the Constitution's Appointments Clause that legal analysts (Cato Institute, Lawfare) say should require Senate confirmation even in an acting capacity, and federal law arguably required the Senate-confirmed principal deputy DNI to assume the role automatically once it became vacant rather than a new outside appointee. A Project on Government Oversight legal expert said the appointment meets the Vacancies Reform Act's technical requirements but flagged that the Act's eligibility rules are so broad (allowing the president to choose from 350+ federal officials regardless of relevant qualifications) that they may not satisfy the Constitution's stricter requirement for principal officers. Senate Intelligence Vice Chairman Mark Warner publicly objected to the appointment, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin introduced the MERIT Act on July 16, 2026 to require any acting DNI to have national security experience -- legislative responses that read as a direct rebuke of the Pulte pick. If a court ultimately found the appointment invalid, Pulte's purge decisions and other agency actions taken under his tenure could themselves be legally exposed to challenge. As of July 27, 2026, Pulte's office confirmed a 4th round of what it called 'measured layoffs' had just been completed, indicating the reductions are continuing rather than a single one-time action. Update 2026-07-27: The Washington Post separately reported ODNI has purged approximately 200 employees through firings and reassignments since June 1, 2026, reducing the office's workforce to roughly 1,300 -- just over half its size when Trump returned to office -- describing the cuts as part of a broader campaign to replace experienced civil servants with political loyalists.

title: OMB Proposes Political-Appointee Pre-Issuance Review of Federal Grants, Ending Post-WWII Norm of Apolitical Peer Review
institution: Office of Management and Budget (OMB)
status: Proposed rule, not yet finalized -- published in the Federal Register May 29, 2026; public comment period closed July 13, 2026 after drawing roughly 90,000 comments; implementation targeted for October 2026
date_of_action: 2026-05-29 (proposed rule published)
what_changed: On May 29, 2026, OMB -- led by Director Russell Vought -- published a more than 400-page proposed rule in the Federal Register that would overhaul the federal government's Uniform Grants Guidance, the regulatory framework governing how agencies award more than $1 trillion annually in federal grants to research institutions, state and local governments, nonprofits, and small businesses. The proposal requires senior political appointees to conduct 'pre-issuance reviews' of grant awards, including assessing whether funded projects 'demonstrably advance the President's policy priorities.' It also states that 'peer review remains advisory and does not replace agency discretion' -- a direct departure from the practice, standard since the post-World War II establishment of federal science funding, of grant approval being determined primarily by apolitical technical experts assessing scientific and programmatic merit. The proposal additionally grants agencies broad new authority to terminate already-awarded grants at any time and imposes new restrictions on international research collaborations. Public comment closed July 13, 2026, drawing more than 90,000 submissions, with implementation targeted for October 2026.

title: OPM/MSPB Propose Scrapping the Douglas Factors, the 44-Year-Old Framework Protecting Federal Employees From Arbitrary Discipline
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB)
status: Proposed rule -- published in the Federal Register July 7, 2026, not yet finalized as of this entry
date_of_action: 2026-07-07 (proposed rule published)
what_changed: OPM and the Merit Systems Protection Board jointly proposed eliminating the 'Douglas factors' -- a 12-part framework established by a 1981 MSPB case that agencies have used for over four decades to ensure federal employee discipline is proportionate and considers factors like offense severity, past performance, and rehabilitation potential. title: HHS/ORR Ends Confidentiality Wall Protecting Unaccompanied Migrant Children and Their Sponsors, Sharing Data With ICE and Cutting Legal Aid
institution: Department of Health and Human Services -- Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), affecting unaccompanied migrant children in federal custody
status: Ongoing -- the ICE data-sharing arrangement remained active as of mid-2026 reporting; the legal-aid contract termination was blocked by a court order and funding was later restored
date_of_action: 2025-02-15 (fingerprinting reimposed) through 2026-07-28 (cumulative-impact figures reported)
what_changed: Beginning in February 2025, ORR reimposed strict fingerprint-based background-check requirements for every adult in a household sponsoring an unaccompanied migrant child -- a policy first introduced in 2018 and later rolled back after it was found to cause mass detention overcrowding and discourage otherwise-qualified sponsors, many of whom are themselves undocumented, from coming forward for fear of their own deportation. In March 2025, the administration went further, rolling back a roughly 2008-era wall that had kept sponsors' immigration status information from being shared with immigration enforcement specifically so status alone would not deter family reunification; ORR began providing ICE with sponsor and household immigration-status data on request, and no longer barred denying a child's release based on a sponsor's immigration status. Separately, DOJ moved on March 21, 2025 to terminate a roughly $200 million contract with the Acacia Center for Justice, which funds legal representation for unaccompanied children in immigration court -- a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking the termination, and funding was later restored, though not before significant disruption to the legal-aid network. By mid-2026, cumulative reporting found ORR had shared more than 460,000 'investigative leads' involving unaccompanied children, sponsors, and other household members with ICE since January 2025, resulting in more than 12,000 arrests, and that the additional vetting requirements had driven the average time a child spends in ORR custody from about 30 days in fiscal year 2024 to 194 days by June 2026.

title: FBI Director Kash Patel Runs Successive Purges of Field-Office Leaders and Agents Tied to Trump-Related Investigations
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation
status: Ongoing -- multiple rounds since 2025, most recently the July 2026 Chicago field office departure
date_of_action: 2025 (initial rounds of forced exits) through 2026-07 (Chicago field office head departure)
what_changed: FBI Director Kash Patel has conducted multiple successive rounds of forced removals, reassignments, and administrative-leave actions against senior FBI leaders and agents, concentrated among personnel connected to investigations touching Trump, the January 6 Capitol attack, or the Mar-a-Lago classified-documents case. In a January 2026 round described as 'renewed,' at least a dozen personnel were removed in a single week, including: Vanessa Tibbits, a 20-year veteran and former senior adviser to ex-FBI Director Christopher Wray, placed on administrative leave from her role as acting assistant director in charge of the New York field office; Lyonel Myrthil, removed from the New Orleans field office after previously overseeing part of the January 6 investigation response in Washington; the Atlanta field office's special agent in charge, forced out; a former Washington office leader who had overseen January 6 investigations, terminated; and multiple Miami agents who had worked the Mar-a-Lago classified-documents case. In several of these cases, the FBI's own Office of Professional Responsibility had recommended lesser discipline (short suspensions), but Patel personally overrode those determinations and removed the employees instead. The Washington Post's February 26, 2026 report on this same January 2026 purge round detailed that the roughly dozen agents and staff removed included personnel who specialized in Iran and its regional proxies, not only Jan. 6/Mar-a-Lago-linked staff -- and that the firings began just three days before the United States launched a major military strike on Iran. CNN's follow-up reporting found the purge gutted the FBI's national-security division counterintelligence team specifically tasked with tracking Iranian threats, and that veteran bureau leader Brian Driscoll -- who had previously helped prevent a mass firing of thousands of FBI employees connected to Jan. 6 casework -- was also removed. The Post's related reporting characterized this as leaving national-security offices across the FBI and DOJ measurably weakened heading into an active Mideast military conflict, extending this round from a personnel-retaliation concern to one with a direct national-security-capacity dimension. In response to the scale of the firings and reassignments, former FBI officials launched the FBI Support Network in June 2026 to provide legal, mental health, and career assistance to current and former employees affected by Patel's purges and by firings the group says were tied to Trump-related investigations and allegations of political bias -- itself evidence of the purges' documented scale and impact on agency personnel. Also in June 2026, Patel's FBI fired several analysts -- four intelligence analysts and a supervisory analyst -- tied to a 2023 internal memo (the 'Richmond memo') that examined a potential link between 'Radical Traditionalist Catholic' ideology and racially/ethnically motivated violent extremism. FBI leadership had previously condemned the memo's findings once it became public, and prior internal reviews had found no intentional misconduct by the analysts who produced it. The analysts' attorney, David Laufman, called the firings 'manifestly unjust, completely unsupported by the facts, and subverts standard FBI policy and procedure.' Unlike the Jan. 6/Mar-a-Lago-linked personnel actions detailed above, this round targeted analysts over a substantive intelligence-assessment topic (domestic religious-extremism research) rather than direct involvement in a Trump-related investigation -- but follows the same documented pattern of Patel personally overriding prior internal findings (here, a prior review clearing the analysts of misconduct) to remove personnel whose work became politically inconvenient. The purge continued into mid-2026: on July 12, 2026, Douglas DePodesta, head of the FBI's Chicago field office, left after colleagues said he had been pushed to retire, in what reporting described as a continuation of Patel's pattern of forcing out agents and supervisors viewed as insufficiently supportive of Trump. Patel has denied the removals constitute political retaliation, saying the personnel involved failed to meet bureau standards; the FBI declined further comment on individual personnel actions when asked by reporters.

title: Peace Corps Headquarters Staff Cut by Roughly 40%
institution: Peace Corps
status: Largely complete -- Peace Corps' own FY2027 budget justification confirms realized cuts by end of calendar year 2025 (not just a target), while the 21-member congressional request for a force-analysis justification, sent Feb. 19, 2026, remained unanswered in public reporting as of this update
date_of_action: 2025-03 to present
what_changed: Beginning in March 2025, DOGE staff directed Peace Corps supervisors to compile lists of personnel and programs to cut, following the earlier governmentwide 'Fork in the Road' deferred resignation offer. By May 2025, roughly 250 employees took a second deferred-resignation push after being told they faced termination if they declined. In September 2025, the Peace Corps Union received formal notice of intent to involuntarily separate 26 bargaining-unit and 11 non-bargaining-unit employees, part of a plan to bring headquarters down to 575 full-time-equivalent staff. That RIF notice period was tolled during the Oct. 1-Nov. 12, 2025 government shutdown and then again by a continuing-resolution moratorium on RIFs through Jan. 30, 2026. The governmentwide RIF moratorium expired Feb. 13, 2026, clearing the way for the cuts to proceed. Recruitment and placement staff have been hit especially hard, with reporting describing a roughly two-thirds reduction in the office responsible for outreach, application review, and volunteer placement across more than 60 countries. The cuts are paired with an agency goal to more than double the number of active volunteers, from about 3,000 to 8,000 by 2030. Peace Corps' own FY2027 Congressional Budget Justification, submitted in 2026, confirms the cuts as realized rather than merely planned: the agency reports operating with at least 375 fewer U.S. Direct Hire and expert staff (approximately a 40% reduction) and at least 275 fewer Host Country National Personal Services Contractors (approximately a 16% reduction) by the end of calendar year 2025 -- the agency's own subsequent budget filing, not just the September 2025 RIF notice or the lawmakers' letter, now confirms the reduction actually took effect. No public response to the 21-member congressional letter's request for a force-analysis justification was identified as of this update, roughly five months after it was sent.

title: Pentagon dismantles civilian harm reduction program despite congressional mandate, watchdog finds
institution: Department of Defense (Department of War) -- Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Action Plan / Civilian Protection Center of Excellence
status: Ongoing -- Inspector General found continued noncompliance as of May 2026; Congress has not acted on Pentagon's 2025 proposal to repeal the underlying statutes

title: PEPFAR Funding Disruptions Close 1,714 HIV Treatment Sites Worldwide, Cut Treatment for 77,000+ Children
institution: PEPFAR (President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief) / USAID / State Department
status: Ongoing -- surveyed impacts cover November 2025-April 2026; disruption effects continuing as of mid-2026
date_of_action: 2025 (funding disruptions begin) through 2026-07 (amfAR study findings presented at AIDS 2026/IAS 2026)
what_changed: amfAR and partner organizations surveyed country-level PEPFAR implementing partner organizations worldwide from November 2025 to April 2026, receiving responses from 166 of 708 organizations contacted (23% response rate), and presented findings at the AIDS 2026 conference. The survey found that Trump-administration funding disruptions to PEPFAR -- the two-decade-old U.S. global HIV/AIDS program -- led to 1,714 HIV service delivery sites closing worldwide, including 1,010 public health facilities, 325 community access points, and 126 drop-in centers. In the 21 countries surveyed, 77,163 fewer children living with HIV received PEPFAR-supported treatment in 2025 (when disruptions began) compared with 2024. More than 16,000 healthcare workers lost their jobs after PEPFAR awards were delayed or canceled. Among partner organizations, 21% had permanently stopped at least one HIV clinical care activity, and roughly three-quarters had stopped serving populations at highest risk of HIV -- including sex workers, transgender people, gay men, and people who inject drugs -- the populations survey respondents said were most likely to have services permanently discontinued. A separate UNAIDS/UNICEF/WHO report published June 2026 found the number of people receiving pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) medication fell 38% between 2024 and 2025 across initial data from 62 countries -- more than a million fewer people -- with the report attributing most of the overall decline to U.S. HIV disbursement cuts, since the U.S. had provided roughly 75% of global donated HIV funding. The same report found condom-distribution funding cut by more than 90% in some countries, and a related 2026 survey of 79 organizations across 47 countries found PrEP delivery by community-led organizations down 50%, HIV testing down 22% in resource-limited countries (especially sub-Saharan Africa), and support services for people living with HIV down 50%.

title: RFK Jr. Diverted CDC Staff to Compile Measles Data, Blocked Briefings, Spread Vaccine Disinformation -- CDC Chief Medical Officer Resigned in Protest
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
status: Reported as a completed episode during the 2025 outbreak; Houry's resignation was final as of summer 2025. Update 2026-07-27: the Washington Post reports the U.S. recorded 2,295 measles cases in 2026 as of late July -- the highest annual total since 1991 -- with more than five months remaining in the year, which public health experts attribute to declining vaccination rates and sustained outbreaks across multiple states. Update 2026-08-05: Utah's outbreak, part of the sustained 2026 transmission WSJ and CIDRAP report has continued since early 2025, has reached 679 cumulative cases (197 in 2025, 482 in 2026) with measles detected in every health jurisdiction in the state; the CDC has said the U.S. is at risk of losing its measles elimination status -- unbroken since 2000 -- if any transmission chain remains continuous for a full year, a threshold Utah's outbreak is approaching. Utah's kindergarten MMR vaccination rate (78.5% in 2023-2024) is well below the ~95% threshold public health officials say is needed to prevent sustained spread.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Corry's resignation) through Houry's resignation in summer 2025, with the broader outbreak-related pattern continuing into 2026
what_changed: Communications turmoil under Kennedy surfaced early: Thomas Corry, HHS's top communications official, resigned without explanation on LinkedIn in early March 2025, just two weeks after taking office and shortly after Kennedy downplayed the severity of the West Texas measles outbreak and misstated the number of deaths -- a resignation The Hill and CBS News both linked to internal frustration over canceled vaccine-advisory meetings, stalled research funding, and Kennedy's mishandling of the unfolding public health crisis, months before the more widely reported resignation of CDC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Debra Houry described below. Former CDC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Debra Houry said that while CDC staff were actively responding to the largest U.S. measles outbreak in decades -- more than 2,000 cases nationwide in 2025, including two child deaths linked to a West Texas outbreak cluster, with 93% of cases involving people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status -- HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his aides requested 15 years of historical data on every individual measles case, including comorbidities among the deceased. Houry said the requests diverted CDC staff time and attention away from active outbreak management, stating publicly that 'the active measles response has to take priority,' and characterized the data requests as 'not based on science or reality, but trying to answer an agenda that was already in place.' Houry said Kennedy separately declined briefings from CDC's top medical officials on the measles epidemic despite CDC's offers to provide 'correct statistics, correct information,' spread false claims about vaccines (including the MMR vaccine) that CDC experts were prevented from countering, and relied on advisers she said lacked medical, scientific, or government background. Houry resigned in protest in summer 2025, saying she could no longer protect the agency's scientific integrity and citing measles, whooping cough, and flu deaths she witnessed: 'I couldn't stand behind that.' Her resignation followed Kennedy's June 9, 2025 removal of all 17 members of CDC's vaccine advisory committee (ACIP, tracked separately in this database), whose replacements included members with ties to lawsuits against vaccine makers -- notable given that Kennedy himself had collected referral fees from such lawsuits before becoming HHS Secretary. By the eighth week of 2026, CNN reported measles cases had already surpassed 1,100 nationally -- roughly six times the total typically seen in a full year -- with 96% of infections among unvaccinated people and health officials warning deaths would likely rise, putting the U.S. at risk of losing its measles elimination status -- a designation held since 2000 -- for the first time. A Reuters analysis of Michigan state data found the state's childhood vaccination series-completion rate fell nearly 3 percentage points, to 66.5%, between January 2025 and January 2026 -- about 13 times the average annual change over the prior 18 years. Reuters found the decline had different drivers across communities: Kennedy's vaccine-skeptic messaging was the primary influence among white families, while the administration's ramped-up immigration enforcement led Latino families to avoid public clinics and other activities outside the home for fear of deportation, after their vaccination rates had partially recovered post-COVID. A related disease is also reappearing: NBC News reported in late March 2026 that doctors were warning that Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) -- a bacterial disease once nearly eradicated in the U.S. through vaccination -- is resurging as childhood vaccination rates decline, with cases still low in absolute terms (8 cases reported nationally as of March 21, 2026) but rising, including severe recent infections and at least one reported death in an unvaccinated infant. A parallel state-level story, reported the following month, shows the same dynamic playing out through exemption law rather than data or messaging: Informed Consent Action Network (ICAN) -- a private anti-vaccine advocacy group whose founder Del Bigtree is a longtime Kennedy ally -- sued and won a court ruling restoring broad religious exemptions from Mississippi's previously strict school vaccine mandate, celebrating it as 'the right to medical choice for the citizens of Mississippi.' Mississippi Today/The Guardian reported that in the following year, the state's whooping cough (pertussis) cases reached their highest level in at least a decade, and in September an infant died of the disease -- Mississippi's first pertussis death in 13 years. More than one in five kindergarten religious exemptions issued that year came from newly-eligible families, and Kennedy allies were reported to be using the Mississippi outcome to push similar exemption rollbacks in other states. This entry documents ICAN's lawsuit and its allied framing, not a direct HHS or federal action -- distinct from the federally-driven measles-data-diversion and ACIP-panel actions above, though part of the same broader vaccine-skepticism ecosystem this entry tracks.

title: SAMHSA Banned Federal Grant Funding for Fentanyl and Xylazine Test Strips, Reversing Harm-Reduction Policy

status: Final guidance in effect as of April 24, 2026; no reversal identified as of this entry

what_changed: On April 24, 2026, SAMHSA issued guidance prohibiting federal grant funds from being used to purchase 'substance test kits, including fentanyl test strips and xylazine test strips,' as well as test strips for medetomidine, a veterinary sedative increasingly found contaminating the illicit drug supply -- reversing the prior (Biden-era) policy that had funded harm-reduction organizations' distribution of these low-cost testing supplies. title: White House-directed content review and exhibit alterations at the Smithsonian
institution: Smithsonian Institution (Washington, DC museums, via White House Domestic Policy Council/OMB)
status: Ongoing (review targeting first-phase museums largely complete; White House published findings report July 2026; second-phase museums and further 'content corrections' still pending)

what_changed: President Trump's March 27, 2025 executive order 'Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History' directed Vice President JD Vance, who sits on the Smithsonian's Board of Regents, to work to 'remove improper ideology' from Smithsonian museums, and instructed OMB and the Vice President to condition future appropriations on exhibits not 'degrading shared American values' or 'dividing Americans based on race.' In August 2025, White House aide Lindsey Halligan, Domestic Policy Council Director Vince Haley, and OMB Director Russell Vought sent a letter to Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch launching a formal review of eight flagship DC museums (including the National Museum of American History, the National Museum of African American History and Culture, and the National Portrait Gallery), demanding exhibition texts, future exhibition plans, internal curatorial guidelines, staff manuals, and organizational charts, with a 120-day deadline for museums to begin 'content corrections' replacing 'divisive or ideologically driven language.' The National Museum of American History removed references to Trump's two first-term impeachments from a display in July 2025 as part of an internal content review the Smithsonian undertook under White House pressure; the references were restored about a week later after public criticism. The Smithsonian's Office of Diversity was closed. National Portrait Gallery director Kim Sajet resigned in mid-2025 after Trump publicly said he was firing her, calling her 'a highly partisan person, and a strong supporter of DEI' (the Smithsonian said only Secretary Bunch could make that personnel decision). Artist Amy Sherald canceled a planned exhibition of her work at the National Portrait Gallery in late July 2025 following a dispute over a painting depicting a transgender Statue-of-Liberty figure. title: 770,000+ Children Lost SNAP Benefits in the Year After Trump's Domestic Policy Law, Despite Promises Children Would Be Protected
institution: USDA / Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
status: Ongoing -- ProPublica's analysis covers the 12 months following the law's July 2025 enactment, published June 2026
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed) through 2026-06 (ProPublica analysis published)
what_changed: A ProPublica analysis published June 17, 2026 found at least 776,134 children stopped receiving SNAP benefits in the 12 states that report participation by age, in the year following Trump's signing of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, 2025 -- legislation that cut roughly $186 billion from SNAP over a decade, the largest cut in the program's history, imposed new work requirements on older adults and parents of teenagers, and shifted billions in administrative and benefit costs onto states. Republicans had promised during the law's passage that children and other vulnerable groups would be shielded from its effects.
