title: SNAP Benefits Withheld During 2025 Government Shutdown
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Nutrition Service
status: Resolved (shutdown ended, full funding restored through Sept. 2026) but litigation exposed underlying legal violations
date_of_action: 2025-10-31 through 2025-11-13 (peak crisis); shutdown began Oct. 2025, was the longest in U.S. history
what_changed: During the government shutdown, the Trump administration initially announced SNAP benefits (food stamps for ~42 million Americans, about 1 in 8 people in the U.S.) would not be paid in November 2025 at all, breaking from the precedent of prior administrations tapping a contingency fund to keep benefits flowing during shutdowns. After lawsuits, a federal judge in Rhode Island (John McConnell) first ordered partial funding (~65% of normal benefits) from the contingency fund, then found the administration's partial-payment approach itself 'arbitrary and capricious' and ordered full funding by a set deadline. Some Democratic-led states issued full benefits before the Supreme Court intervened with a temporary stay blocking the order, creating a chaotic situation where some recipients got full benefits and others got partial or none, based on which state they lived in and how quickly that state's officials acted. USDA then ordered states to 'immediately undo' full benefit issuances already made. The dispute was ultimately mooted when Congress passed a bill ending the shutdown with SNAP funded through September 2026. Re-verified 2026-07-26: one additional litigation detail worth noting -- the administration itself moved to drop its own First Circuit appeal of the Rhode Island judge's order, rather than the appeal being denied on the merits, consistent with this entry's existing framing that the dispute was ultimately mooted by the funding CR rather than resolved by any appellate ruling.

primary_proponent.note: Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly defended the administration's position, calling Judge McConnell's order 'judicial activism at its worst' and arguing a 'single district court in Rhode Island should not be able to seize center stage.' USDA official Patrick Penn signed the memo directing states to reverse full benefit payments already issued. Judge McConnell's own order found the administration's justification for partial-only payment was 'arbitrary and capricious' and suggested the delay may have been for 'political reasons.'

estimated_impact.summary: Nearly 42 million Americans -- disproportionately children, seniors, and people with disabilities -- had food assistance disrupted or fully withheld for a period during the shutdown, forcing food banks nationwide into 'unprecedented demand' per multiple contemporaneous reports, and leaving benefit amounts dependent on which state a recipient lived in rather than a uniform national standard.

title: Social Security Administration Lost 8,000+ Staff — Lowest Headcount Since 1967 — Then Stopped Publishing Its Own Service Metrics
institution: Social Security Administration (SSA)
status: Ongoing (staffing losses not reversed; some but not all withheld metrics later restored)
date_of_action: 2025-02-24 (earliest documented office closures under Leland Dudek) through 2026-04 (ongoing, per Center on Budget and Policy Priorities' most recent tracking); see also the March 2025 O'Malley warning and April 2025 reclassification push noted below
what_changed: Since January 2025, the Trump administration drove out more than 8,000 SSA employees -- the agency's largest one-year staffing reduction on record, leaving SSA with fewer employees than at any point since 1967, even as it now serves roughly 52 million more beneficiaries than it did then (nearly 75 million total). More than 40 states and D.C. saw staffing cuts greater than 10% between January 2025 and April 2026. This pattern was already visible within DOGE's first weeks at SSA: ProPublica reported that by February 24, 2025, DOGE operatives working inside the agency under appointee Leland Dudek had already closed at least 10 local field offices and eliminated 41 positions, drawing early alarm from beneficiaries and staff. The staffing cuts produced concrete technical and administrative failures in the following months: the Washington Post reported the SSA website repeatedly crashed starting around April 8, 2025, disrupting access for millions, with the outages tied directly to Musk-led cuts that slashed IT staff and rushed out undertested software; the next day, CBS News reported SSA mistakenly told some Supplemental Security Income recipients -- including disabled individuals and low-income seniors -- that their benefits had been terminated, with their benefit histories temporarily disappearing from their accounts before the error was corrected roughly a day later. By May 6, 2025, CBS News reported a further, more consequential error pattern: thousands of Americans, disproportionately immigrants and other vulnerable individuals, were being wrongly declared dead or purged from SSA's systems entirely, cutting off Social Security benefits, disability payments, and in some cases banking access tied to a valid Social Security number. On June 16, 2025, Wired reported Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden formally warned that DOGE's rushed, AI-driven overhaul of SSA's IT systems was jeopardizing the agency's core function, citing the website outages and access failures already documented above as evidence of elevated risk of further benefit disruptions, data loss, or security compromise going forward. In April 2025, SSA briefly eliminated most phone-based benefit applications entirely (reversed after public backlash), while permanently requiring in-person visits or multi-factor online authentication for direct-deposit changes -- a change CBPP notes the agency's own fraud data does not support, since direct-deposit fraud is rare and rarely phone-initiated. As wait times climbed (86 minutes average by April 2025, a 25% increase over the prior year), SSA responded largely by reassigning field-office staff to phone duty rather than hiring -- pulling employees away from processing claims and creating new backlogs elsewhere. In June 2025, amid worsening press coverage, SSA stopped publicly releasing several of its own regular service-performance metrics, including call wait times and appointment-scheduling delays; some measures were later restored, but key ones (hold-time data, appointment-wait data, backlog counts) remain unreported as of CBPP's most recent tracking. By early 2026, disability-appeal backlogs had grown by 73,000+ cases in just over a year, and fewer than 850 of SSA's roughly 50,000 remaining employees had less than two years of federal service -- the agency hired fewer than 100 new employees in all of 2025, the lowest annual hiring total on record. In June 2026, Commissioner Bisignano told the House Ways and Means Committee and stated in an SSA press release (June 29, 2026) that the agency achieved its 'best all-around performance ever': the National 800 Number's average speed of answer reportedly fell from 34 minutes (2024) to 8 minutes, a 75% reduction; field-office wait times reportedly fell 30%; the initial disability-claims backlog reportedly fell from a high of ~1.3 million (2024) to 853,000, and disability hearing wait times reportedly fell to 266 days, a historic low; the agency also reported 385 million online transactions in FY2026 to date, up 37% from 2024. SSA's workforce continued to shrink over this same period -- roughly 7,000 additional employees left via separation incentives, leaving a workforce of about 50,000, still its lowest headcount in decades. As part of that continued shrinkage, in April 2025 the Washington Post reported the administration was preparing to lay off thousands more SSA workers even after the earlier ~7,000-job elimination, with offices in rural areas losing over half their staff and IT systems already crashing under the strain. Two named-official developments from this same window are worth noting on their own. First, on March 3, 2025, former SSA Commissioner Martin O'Malley (Biden-era) publicly warned SSA could suffer a full 'collapse of the entire system' and an interruption of benefit payments within 'the next 30 to 90 days' if the DOGE-driven cuts continued -- a high-profile, widely covered warning that did not literally materialize on that timeline (Social Security continued issuing payments past the 90-day mark), though the underlying staffing and service-quality trend O'Malley was warning about is independently documented throughout this entry. Second, in April 2025 Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek moved to reclassify entire SSA offices -- including mission support, hearings, and communications staff -- under the newly renamed 'Schedule Policy/Career' (formerly Schedule F) excepted-service category, which strips normal civil-service removal protections; roughly 8,000 GS-15-level federal employees government-wide had already been shifted into equivalent categories by that point. This drew bipartisan pushback, and following pressure from Sen. Ron Wyden and colleagues, the administration confirmed by June 27, 2025 that no SSA frontline workers had actually been recategorized under Schedule Policy/Career -- meaning the April reclassification push, as reported, did not fully proceed as originally described, at least for frontline staff, as of that confirmation. Separately, in May 2025, incoming Commissioner Frank Bisignano told reporters AI would 'soon' handle a significant share of SSA's roughly 400,000 daily phone calls -- an early on-the-record statement of the automation strategy that appears consistent with, and may partly explain the mechanism behind, the dramatically faster call-answer times SSA and its Inspector General later reported for FY2025-2026 (see below), even as field-office staffing and hiring remained sharply reduced. Update 2026-07-26: the independent corroboration this entry's prior update said was missing has since emerged. After Sen. Elizabeth Warren raised doubts about SSA's reported phone-service improvements, Commissioner Bisignano agreed to an independent review, and SSA's own Office of Inspector General published an audit in June 2026 confirming the agency's released 800-number performance data was accurate and that service genuinely improved during FY2025: SSA served 68 million callers (a 65% increase over the prior year), with average wait times falling from a January peak of about 30 minutes to roughly 7 minutes by September. This meaningfully corroborates part of Bisignano's disputed 2026 turnaround claim -- specifically the phone-service metrics -- though it does not address or resolve this entry's separate, independently-sourced findings on workforce reduction (8,000+ lost), the disability-appeal backlog, or the 2025 decision to stop publishing certain other service metrics, which remain accurate and unaffected by this audit.

estimated_impact.summary: This entry has an unusually well-documented secondary pattern worth noting on its own: the agency's decision to stop publishing its own service-quality data specifically after that data generated negative press is a distinct, separately citable transparency-reduction action, not just a byproduct of the staffing cuts themselves. An internal SSA employee survey (Dec. 2025/Jan. 2026) found 65% of staff reported declining service quality and 70% reported declining service speed -- an unusual case where internal staff self-reporting corroborates external advocacy-group findings rather than contradicting them.

estimated_impact.caveat: SSA leadership disputes the characterization that more staffing is the answer, and Commissioner Bisignano has publicly staked out a contrary position (efficiency over headcount) -- this is a genuinely disputed policy question, not just a factual one, and should be presented with his stated rationale alongside the outside critique. However, the decision to stop publishing key service metrics specifically after bad press is a separately verifiable action, not itself a matter of policy disagreement -- CBPP's and NPR's sourcing on that point is direct and specific. A direct, unresolved factual tension has emerged as of mid-2026: SSA's own reported metrics (touted by Commissioner Bisignano in congressional testimony and an official SSA press release) claim dramatic service improvements -- faster phone answer times, shorter backlogs -- achieved with a smaller workforce, which is the opposite of this entry's core framing. The phone-service figures specifically (wait times, call volume) have since been independently corroborated by SSA's own Office of Inspector General in a June 2026 audit prompted by Sen. Warren's concerns -- a genuine confirmation of that piece of the turnaround claim. Other claimed improvements (disability-claims backlog, hearing wait times) have not been independently audited as of this update, and CBPP and government-oversight reporting have also noted Bisignano has been evasive when pressed on methodology in congressional testimony. Present both: the agency's claimed 2026 performance turnaround, sourced explicitly to SSA/Bisignano, alongside the independently-sourced staffing-loss and prior metrics-suppression findings -- don't treat either claim as simply resolving the other. O'Malley's March 2025 '30 to 90 days' collapse warning should be presented as a prediction that did not materialize on its literal timeline, not as a confirmed outcome -- use it as evidence of contemporaneous alarm among former officials, not as proof of an actual system collapse. Similarly, the April 2025 Schedule Policy/Career reclassification push at SSA specifically should be presented as an attempted action that, per the administration's own June 2025 confirmation to Sen. Wyden, had not actually been carried out for frontline SSA workers as of that date -- a genuine attempted-but-contested-and-seemingly-stalled action, not a completed one.

confidence_note: Very strong sourcing: CBPP is a well-regarded, frequently-cited nonpartisan policy institute with detailed, footnoted figures drawn substantially from the agency's own data (OPM staffing records, SSA's own performance metrics) rather than estimates. NPR's on-the-ground reporting from field-office employees corroborates the top-line figures with direct testimony. Sen. Baldwin's official congressional investigation adds a formal oversight dimension. The metrics-suppression angle is corroborated by multiple independent sources (CBPP, Nash Disability Law, 401k Specialist) describing the same June 2025 timing and the same specific withheld metrics. Re-verified 2026-07-20: SSA/Bisignano's June 2026 claimed performance turnaround is a genuine, on-the-record complication for this entry's existing negative framing -- it should be presented as a disputed, agency-self-reported claim (see updated caveat), not omitted and not accepted as settling the question. Independent corroboration of the specific 2026 numbers (8-minute wait time, 266-day hearing wait) was not found as of this recheck; CBPP's underlying staffing and metrics-suppression findings are unaffected. Update 2026-07-26: SSA OIG's June 2026 audit of 800-number performance data is corroborated by Fox News and Washington Examiner reporting on the audit itself; this partially resolves, rather than fully settles, the disputed-claim framing in this entry's prior update -- the phone-metrics piece is now independently confirmed, while workforce and backlog figures remain as previously sourced. Update 2026-08-09: added O'Malley's March 2025 collapse warning (corroborated by Democracy Now!, CNN, Snopes, and the Daily Beast, with Snopes and Yahoo Finance retrospectives specifically noting the predicted 30-90-day timeline did not literally materialize) and the April 2025 Schedule Policy/Career reclassification push at SSA (corroborated by Government Executive's reporting on Dudek's directive and the Senate Finance Committee's own June 27, 2025 press release confirming, after Wyden's pressure, that no SSA frontline workers had actually been recategorized) -- both added with explicit outcome caveats rather than presented as confirmed completed harms.

title: SSA Instructed Newly Reassigned, Minimally-Trained Phone Agents to Tell Suicidal Callers That 'Suicide Is Only One Option'
institution: Social Security Administration
status: In effect as of February 2026 reporting -- no reversal or policy correction confirmed in sourcing reviewed

what_changed: As part of SSA's broader staffing collapse (see ssa-staffing-service-collapse-trump2.json), the agency reassigned employees from other roles to newly-created phone duty with as little as three hours of training, according to GovExec's reporting. title: State Department overhauls diplomat performance reviews into a forced-competition, zero-sum ratings system
institution: U.S. Department of State / Foreign Service
status: Ongoing -- new Employee Evaluation Report (EER) system implemented for the 2026 review cycle, with the submission deadline postponed to May 29, 2026 and some already-submitted evaluations ordered revised downward

what_changed: The State Department rolled out a new, data-driven Employee Evaluation Report (EER) system for Foreign Service officers, requiring diplomats to compete for a limited, fixed number of top ratings rather than being evaluated against an independent standard -- with supervisors themselves facing consequences if they award too many top scores. title: State Department Told Americans to 'Depart Now' From 16 Middle East Countries, Then Told Its Own Evacuation Hotline Callers Not to Rely on Government Help
institution: Department of State
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition -- the war's evacuation-assistance strain and the underlying staffing losses were not reported as resolved in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2026 (Iran war escalation period)
what_changed: As the U.S. war with Iran escalated, the State Department issued 'DEPART NOW' alerts urging U.S. citizens to leave 16 countries across the Middle East -- including Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Israel, the West Bank, Gaza, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, the UAE, and Yemen -- citing serious safety risks. Americans who called the department's evacuation-assistance hotline were told: 'Please do not rely on the U.S. government for assisted departure or evacuation.' NOTUS reported stranded Americans described receiving little practical help as regional airports closed and commercial travel options rapidly disappeared. The Intercept reported that foreign service officers fired in earlier DOGE-driven State Department workforce cuts had previously and specifically warned the department would be unable to adequately assist Americans stranded in a Middle East crisis -- a warning this episode is reported to have borne out. NBC News separately reported thousands of Americans were left stranded in the war zone amid the department's response gap. The State Department did publicize a 24/7 emergency hotline and reported assisting over 130 Americans evacuate Israel specifically, indicating the department was not wholly inactive, but the gap between the 16-country 'depart now' directive and the hotline's own explicit disclaimer against relying on government assistance was widely reported as a substantive breakdown in crisis-response capacity. Additional reporting corroborated and extended the scale of the crisis: as many as 1 million Americans were estimated to be in the Middle East when the war escalated (following an Israeli airstrike that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei), and the 'DEPART NOW' advisory for 14-16 countries did not go out until the Monday after the weekend strike -- a delay Trump attributed to the conflict having 'happened all very quickly' when asked why no evacuation plan existed in advance. CBS News reported Americans arriving back in New York described a 'zero plan for evacuation,' and travelers transiting hubs like Dubai, Doha, and Amman were told for four days not to rely on the U.S. government for assisted departure. The State Department did not open a crisis intake form offering free charter flights until March 4, 2026, with its first chartered evacuation flight arriving in the region and returning to Washington that same week. Separately, NOTUS and Truthout reported that DOGE had fired the State Department's entire team of oil and gas experts in July 2025 -- six months before the Iran war began -- as part of a roughly 1,300-person State Department RIF. The cuts eliminated staff responsible for modeling scenarios in which the Strait of Hormuz was closed, maintaining relationships with Middle East energy companies, and liaising with the International Energy Agency on coordinated strategic-reserve releases; after the cuts, the Bureau of Energy Resources retained only staff focused on critical minerals and clean energy, none with Middle East oil-and-gas crisis expertise. Geoffrey Pyatt, a former assistant secretary of state for energy resources, said of the losses once the Strait of Hormuz became effectively closed during the war: 'I'm sure Secretary Rubio wishes he had that expertise available today.'

title: DHS Suspended, Then Partially Reversed, TSA PreCheck and Global Entry During a Funding Lapse
institution: Transportation Security Administration / Customs and Border Protection, DHS
status: Partially reversed -- TSA PreCheck restored within about a day; Global Entry remained suspended as the shutdown continued. Noem subsequently warned PreCheck could be re-suspended as the shutdown continued. By mid-March 2026, officials warned continued TSA absenteeism (above 30% at some hubs) could force some airport shutdowns entirely if the funding standoff persisted. TSA wait times peaked at the worst levels in agency history in late March 2026 (480+ officers departed, some lines over 4.5 hours) before a funding deal was reached.
date_of_action: 2026-02-20 (suspension announced) through 2026-02-21/22 (PreCheck reversal)
what_changed: DHS Secretary Kristi Noem announced the suspension of TSA PreCheck and CBP's Global Entry expedited-traveler programs, citing the funding lapse from the ongoing partial government shutdown. Less than a day later, TSA reversed the PreCheck suspension after significant pushback from airlines and lawmakers; Global Entry, however, remained suspended as the shutdown continued. Airlines for America president Chris Sununu criticized the suspension, saying the traveling public was 'once again... used as a political football amid another government shutdown.' Sen. Mark Warner noted that in 2025 more than 18 million travelers used Global Entry, saving over 300,000 CBP officer-hours across 79 ports of entry, and that both programs had remained operational throughout the 43-day government shutdown the prior fall -- undercutting DHS's funding-lapse rationale for this specific suspension. Days later, Secretary Noem warned TSA PreCheck could again be suspended as the DHS shutdown continued, while Global Entry remained suspended throughout. The underlying staffing strain continued to escalate: by mid-March 2026, Reuters reported TSA officers were working without pay as the funding standoff continued, with absentee rates spiking above 30% at some major hubs. Officials warned some airports could be forced to shut down entirely if the standoff persisted, with smaller airports with limited checkpoints described as especially at risk. The shutdown dragged into a second month, and ABC News reported tens of thousands of TSA workers were going unpaid, with many receiving $0 paychecks while still required to report for duty; employees described taking second jobs, leaving the agency, and struggling to meet basic expenses. The prolonged standoff had an additional, explicit political dimension: the New York Times reported Trump told Republicans to halt negotiations to reopen DHS and instead use the shutdown as leverage to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, a voter-ID bill -- even as TSA workers went unpaid and airport disruptions worsened. Trump and Senate Majority Leader John Thune clashed publicly over the ultimatum. In the days before a deal was reached, the crisis peaked: the NYT reported TSA union leaders blasted Trump's deployment of ICE and other DHS agents to 14 airports to cover screening shortages, saying the officers were not trained for screening work and did little to reduce lines. CBS News reported wait times stretched up to six hours at major airports even with the ICE deployment, with nearly 12% of TSA officers calling out unpaid on a given day. Bloomberg reported TSA said wait times reached the worst levels in the agency's history after more than 480 officers left during the shutdown, with some lines exceeding 4.5 hours and major airports including Atlanta, Houston, and New York seeing checkpoint closures and lane consolidations. By March 31, 2026, CBS News reported TSA was consolidating security lanes and warned it might be forced to close smaller airports entirely if the funding standoff continued without a deal, with hundreds of agents having quit and wait times approaching 4-5 hours even at major hubs. Trump then ultimately endorsed a deal in late March 2026 to fund DHS (with the exception of key ICE provisions), allowing the SAVE Act to wait rather than continuing to hold TSA funding hostage to it. Trump's FY2027 budget, released April 3, 2026 and documented in more detail elsewhere in this tracker (trump-fy2027-budget-defense-tradeoff-2026.json), proposed cutting TSA funding and pushing smaller airports to replace federal screening officers with private security screeners -- a proposal Reuters noted came just weeks after the shutdown-driven staffing crisis and unpaid-worker escalation this entry documents.

title: African Development Foundation Reduced to Near-Nothing Before Courts Fully Reverse Takeover
institution: U.S. African Development Foundation and Inter-American Foundation
status: Reversed (final federal court orders in 2025-2026 fully vacated the takeovers at both agencies)
date_of_action: 2025-02-19 (executive order) through 2026-03 (final court order restoring USADF)
what_changed: On February 19, 2025, President Trump issued an executive order directing USADF, the Inter-American Foundation (IAF), the U.S. Institute of Peace, and the Presidio Trust to be reduced to 'the minimum presence and function required by law.' Peter Marocco, a State Department official who also oversaw the dismantling of USAID, moved to take control of both USADF and IAF within days. At IAF, Marocco held a one-person 'board meeting' outside the agency's locked headquarters on February 28, 2025, after being unable to gain entry, and declared himself acting CEO and president in a notice entered into the Federal Register. At USADF, staff denied DOGE personnel direct access to internal systems, citing privacy and security requirements, while Marocco announced by email that he would chair the agency's board. On March 11, 2025, District Judge Richard Leon initially found that a large reduction in USADF's staff and funding could itself be legal, declining at that stage to block leadership changes, while ordering DOGE staff to explain how they would maintain the agency's minimum required functions. By early April 2025, the government acknowledged in court that IAF had been reduced to a single employee and a single active grant. On April 4, 2025, Judge Loren AliKhan ordered the indefinite reinstatement of ousted IAF president Sara Aviel and blocked Marocco from serving on IAF's board, unwinding his actions including frozen grants. On July 1, 2025, Judge Leon ruled that Trump had violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act by installing Marocco at USADF without Senate confirmation, voiding the staff terminations and grant cancellations Marocco had directed. A final order in Rural Development Innovations Ltd. v. Marocco fully blocked the USADF dismantlement, and by March 2026, USADF staff were allowed back into their offices for the first time in months.

This is a genuine reversal story: both USADF and IAF ultimately had their takeovers fully undone by final court orders, with USADF staff physically returning to their offices in March 2026, though Devex reporting notes the agency's reentry into the foreign-aid sector 'seems to be just beginning' after a year of program cancellations and funding freezes, and separately references newer, unrelated corruption charges connected to the agency as of that report.

title: USAID Dismantled and Absorbed Into the State Department, Despite Being a Congressionally-Independent Agency
institution: U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID)
status: Operationally dissolved (July 1, 2025) but legally unresolved -- USAID was made an independent agency by Congress in 1998 and can only be formally abolished by an act of Congress, which has not occurred
date_of_action: 2025-01-24 (foreign aid freeze ordered) through 2025-07-01 (official dissolution and merger into State Department)
what_changed: On his first days in office, Trump ordered a near-total freeze on foreign aid, and within weeks the administration placed most USAID employees on administrative leave. By March 10, 2025, Secretary of State Rubio announced 83% of USAID's programs (roughly 5,200 contracts) had been terminated following an internal review; on March 28 he formally notified Congress that USAID would be dissolved and its remaining functions absorbed into the State Department. USAID officially ceased independent operations on July 1, 2025, after 63 years. Staffing was reduced from over 10,000 employees to fewer than 300. USAID's own Inspector General issued a report warning the spending pause and staff furloughs limited the agency's ability to ensure funds didn't reach terrorist-linked recipients, and separately warned that $489 million in humanitarian food aid risked spoiling due to the furloughs; the White House Office of Presidential Personnel fired that Inspector General less than 30 minutes after the report's publication -- despite a federal law requiring 30 days' advance notice to Congress before removing an inspector general. A significant, largely unresolved legal question underlies the entire action: USAID was reorganized by Congress as an independent agency in 1998 specifically to give it statutory protection, and per that same statute can only be formally abolished by an act of Congress -- which has not happened. USAID therefore legally still exists even though it has been operationally dissolved. On the litigation front, the D.C. Circuit held oral argument on April 23, 2026 (before Judges Srinivasan, Pillard, and Pan) on the appeal of the core USAID dismantlement case; no ruling had issued as of this update. In a related case, briefing continues on a schedule running into summer 2026, with the government's reply brief due July 31, 2026. Separately, a federal court in Maryland denied efforts to block depositions of Elon Musk and other DOGE-linked officials in a class-action suit over USAID's shutdown; that case is proceeding through discovery. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no ruling identified yet from the D.C. Circuit panel (Srinivasan, Pillard, Pan) that heard oral argument April 23, 2026; the appeal remains undecided and USAID's operational/legal status is unchanged from the prior update. Added 2026-07-27: former USAID Administrator Samantha Power said in a Bloomberg interview that she does not believe the Ebola outbreak spreading across the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda -- which has killed more than 400 people -- would be spiraling as it has if USAID had not been dismantled, citing the loss of the agency's early-warning disease-surveillance systems and cold-chain infrastructure (whose degradation contributed to delayed detection, since transported swab samples were no longer reliably preserved). The administration's separate withdrawal from the World Health Organization compounded the effect by removing another layer of international outbreak-response coordination. This is presented as a concrete, on-the-ground consequence of the dismantlement documented above, not a new or separate action. Added 2026-08-10: Rubio's 'no one has died' claim was not the only official denial contradicted by the record -- Mother Jones reported in June 2025 that internal State Department cables reviewed by the outlet documented lifesaving HIV treatment programs in Lesotho and food-aid programs in Malawi being cut as a direct result of the dismantlement, with diplomats warning of resulting deaths, hunger, and trafficking risk. That reporting directly contradicts Elon Musk's own public claim, made while leading the DOGE effort that drove the cuts, that 'zero people have died' as a result.

primary_proponent.name: Marco Rubio
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of State
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the program terminations, the dissolution notice to Congress, and USAID's final closure, writing on Substack: 'As of July 1st, USAID will officially cease to implement foreign assistance... This era of government-sanctioned inefficiency has officially come to an end.' Rubio told a congressional hearing in May 2025 that 'no one has died because of USAID [cuts]' -- a claim directly contradicted by subsequent peer-reviewed research (see below) and by on-the-ground reporting, including one documented case of a child in Nigeria who died after the USAID-funded clinic he depended on for urgent care was closed. This action is closely related to, but categorically distinct from, the separately-tracked State Department reorganization entry in this database -- USAID's elimination is the dismantling of an entire congressionally-independent agency, not an internal State Department restructuring.

estimated_impact.summary: A peer-reviewed study published in The Lancet (one of the world's most established medical journals) estimated USAID funding prevented more than 91 million deaths globally between 2001 and 2021, including a 65% reduction in HIV/AIDS mortality and 51% reduction in malaria mortality in the countries it funded. The same study projected that, absent a reversal, the 2025 cuts could contribute to more than 14 million additional preventable deaths by 2030, nearly a third of them children under 5 -- a scale the study's authors explicitly compared to 'a global pandemic or a major armed conflict,' while noting this crisis would stem from 'a conscious and avoidable policy choice.' A follow-up Lancet study one year later, incorporating a full year of real data rather than projections, estimated a somewhat lower but still severe 9.4 million-death figure by 2030 if funding trends continue -- researchers who reviewed the modeling told CNN the precise numbers should be treated with some caution but that the overall conclusion (large-scale, avoidable death) is likely correct. Domestically, the closure eliminated tens of thousands of jobs across USAID staff and its contractor/NGO ecosystem -- one contractor, EnCompass, lost over 400 jobs in under a month.

institution: United States Postal Service
status: Ongoing -- suspension began April 10, 2026 as a stated temporary cash-conservation measure; as of a June 2026 update, USPS no longer expects to exhaust cash reserves in early 2027, but warns the suspension only delays, not resolves, its long-term financial position

what_changed: The USPS Board of Governors suspended the agency's biweekly employer contributions to the Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS), covering roughly 99% of career postal workers, beginning April 10, 2026. The move defers roughly $200 million every two weeks (about $400 million/month, an estimated $2.5 billion for the fiscal year) that would otherwise fund employee retirement benefits, redirecting it to preserve operating cash. title: VA Inspector General Found Severe Staffing Shortages at Every One of 139 Medical Centers — VA Disputes the Metric

title: White House Plan Shifts $200 Billion in Annual Federal Research Funding Away From Universities, Peer Review, Toward Political-Appointee Discretion
institution: Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) / Office of Management and Budget (OMB) -- government-wide federal R&D funding
status: Plan unveiled -- directives to shape federal R&D funding for the remainder of Trump's second term, implementation across federal research agencies ongoing as of this entry
date_of_action: 2026-07 (plan unveiled)
what_changed: The White House unveiled a plan, co-signed by OSTP Director Michael Kratsios and OMB Director Russell Vought, to reshape the roughly $200 billion annual federal research and development budget for the remainder of Trump's second term. The plan directs every federal research agency to supplement traditional, consensus-driven peer review with faster funding mechanisms -- described as 'golden tickets,' 'fast grants,' and portable awards that follow individual researchers rather than their host institutions -- shifting emphasis toward individual scientists and away from universities as institutions, which could particularly affect large universities reliant on federal grants. The plan directs research priorities toward artificial intelligence specifically, alongside stated goals of deploying a functioning quantum computer by 2028 and having 10 new large nuclear reactors under construction by 2030. A related proposed OMB rule would give political appointees greater direct influence over individual grant decisions, aligning funded research more closely with administration priorities rather than independent scientific merit review alone.

primary_proponent.name: Michael Kratsios
primary_proponent.role: Director, Office of Science and Technology Policy
primary_proponent.note: Co-signed the plan alongside OMB Director Russell Vought, directing federal research agencies to adopt faster, less peer-review-dependent funding mechanisms and to give political appointees greater influence over grant decisions.

estimated_impact.summary: Nearly the entire federal research and development budget -- roughly $200 billion annually -- is being redirected via new mechanisms that bypass or supplement traditional peer review with faster, appointee-influenced funding pathways, prioritizing AI research and individual researchers over universities as institutions; critics warn this risks narrowing the range of research pursued and substituting political priorities for independent scientific judgment.

title: White House Downplayed and Previously Blocked Release of FBI/NCTC Iran Threat Warnings
institution: White House / FBI / National Counterterrorism Center
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition -- the March 20, 2026 law-enforcement intelligence report was distributed to state and local law enforcement despite the White House's public downplaying, but the earlier, similarly-described report the White House blocked from release was never independently confirmed to have subsequently reached its intended law-enforcement or public audience
date_of_action: 2026-03-20 (report date); reported 2026-04-08
what_changed: The FBI and National Counterterrorism Center issued a law-enforcement intelligence report on March 20, 2026, warning that the Iranian government 'poses a persistent threat' to U.S. military and government personnel and facilities, Jewish and Israeli institutions, and Iranian dissidents inside the United States (the report did not identify a broad threat to the general American public). Reuters reported the report's public release and law-enforcement distribution came even as the White House publicly minimized the likelihood of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil -- consistent with President Trump's public downplaying of other, similar intelligence assessments in preceding months. The March 20 report followed weeks after Reuters and other outlets reported the White House had blocked release of an earlier intelligence product with similar findings. White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson defended the administration's posture, saying it was 'ensuring any information was properly vetted before release' and that media outlets should not 'irresponsibly sow fear' by reporting on individual law-enforcement memoranda that may lack broader context.

primary_proponent.name: The White House (institutional; no single official named in sourcing as personally directing the earlier report's suppression)
primary_proponent.role: Executive Office of the President
primary_proponent.note: White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson is the only named official on record, defending -- not directing -- the administration's posture toward the reports' release; sourcing reviewed does not identify who specifically ordered the earlier report blocked, an attribution gap flagged per this tracker's institutional-accountability standard rather than blocking the entry on that basis.

estimated_impact.summary: State and local law enforcement, and the public, received a narrower, later, and more downplayed account of a documented Iranian threat than the intelligence community itself assessed -- the pattern (blocking one report, then publicly minimizing a second, similarly-worded one) represents the White House exercising political control over dissemination of an intelligence-community threat product rather than deferring to the community's own assessment of what warranted public warning.
estimated_impact.caveat: No dollar figure or headcount applies to this entry; the harm is informational/preparedness-related (delayed or minimized threat awareness for the public and law enforcement) rather than a quantifiable budget or staffing loss.

confidence_note: MODERATE-HIGH confidence: the core facts (report date, contents, and the White House's downplaying) trace to a single Reuters exclusive, though independently republished across many outlets (Japan Times, Arab News, Jerusalem Post, Detroit News among others) and corroborated by an on-record White House spokeswoman quote confirming the administration's posture, not disputing the report's existence. The claim that the White House 'blocked' an earlier, similarly-described report rests on prior Reuters reporting referenced within this same article; that earlier report and its blocking were not independently re-verified in this entry's own research pass.

title: U.S. Withdrawal From WHO Cut CDC Off From Real-Time Outbreak Surveillance and Sequencing Data
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; U.S. withdrawal from the World Health Organization
status: Ongoing structural condition as of May 2026 reporting -- the U.S. formally left WHO in January 2026 and has not rejoined
date_of_action: 2026-01 (U.S. formal withdrawal from WHO takes effect) through 2026-05 (reporting on the resulting surveillance-access gap, illustrated by a hantavirus cluster on the M/V Hondius cruise ship)
what_changed: Following the U.S.'s formal withdrawal from the World Health Organization in January 2026, health officials told NBC News that the U.S. no longer has immediate access to WHO-coordinated surveillance and contact-tracing information the way it did as a member state. CDC experts are no longer part of the international teams sequencing pathogens during multi-country outbreaks, meaning U.S. public health officials now learn sequencing results secondhand rather than in real time. In February 2026, Trump officials proposed spending $2 billion per year to build an alternative, U.S.-run global disease-surveillance and outbreak-response system to replace the WHO-coordinated access lost by withdrawal -- a tacit acknowledgment of the surveillance gap this entry documents, though the proposal's funding and implementation status remained unresolved as of the reporting reviewed. This structural loss of direct access was illustrated during a May 2026 multi-country hantavirus cluster linked to a cruise ship (the M/V Hondius), where experts said the U.S. might not get immediate access to surveillance data or contact-tracing information on passengers, even though -- as the same reporting noted -- no hantavirus cases in the United States were ultimately associated with that specific outbreak. CNN reported in May 2026 that the administration went further than the structural membership loss described above: NIAID officials were formally barred from directly communicating with WHO during active outbreak response, a restriction in place since the hantavirus/M.V. Hondius cluster and only partially relaxed as the DRC Ebola outbreak grew. Per a May 18, 2026 internal NIAID email, officials may now attend virtual WHO meetings only in small groups and only in a 'listening capacity'; any needed follow-up is routed through HHS political leadership rather than handled directly by NIAID's own scientists. Added 2026-08-10: the funding side of the withdrawal produced its own, earlier consequence for WHO's own operating capacity -- The Guardian reported in November 2025 that WHO announced it would eliminate more than 2,000 jobs, about 22% of its global workforce, after the loss of U.S. funding created a $1.06 billion budget shortfall, with the agency cutting its management team in half and scaling back core health operations worldwide. This predates the formal January 2026 withdrawal documented above and reflects WHO's own institutional capacity loss as a direct funding consequence, distinct from the structural surveillance-access loss that followed formal withdrawal.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Directed the U.S. withdrawal from the World Health Organization, effective January 2026, which health officials and outside experts identify as the direct structural cause of the reduced surveillance and sequencing access described in this entry.

estimated_impact.summary: The withdrawal removes the U.S. from the WHO's real-time international disease-surveillance and pathogen-sequencing coordination network, meaning U.S. health authorities now depend on secondhand or delayed access to information they previously received directly as a WHO member -- a structural capacity loss distinct from any single outbreak's outcome.
estimated_impact.caveat: This entry documents a structural loss of direct access and coordination, not a claim that any specific outbreak response was mishandled as a result -- the hantavirus cluster cited here resulted in no confirmed U.S. cases, and this entry should not be read to assert that the surveillance-access gap caused a specific harmful outcome in that instance. Update 2026-08-02: beyond the passive loss of automatic access described above, reporting also documents an active administration directive restricting NIAID scientists to listening-only participation in WHO outbreak-response meetings, with follow-up routed through HHS political leadership -- a deliberate policy choice layered on top of the structural withdrawal, not merely its passive consequence.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the structural fact (U.S. withdrawal from WHO, and the resulting loss of direct surveillance/sequencing access) -- reported by NBC News citing named health officials, and consistent with the well-documented January 2026 WHO withdrawal itself. This entry deliberately avoids the separate, weaker claim (raised elsewhere in press coverage and flagged by Snopes as misleading) that CDC staffing cuts specifically delayed the response to this hantavirus cluster -- that causal claim is not repeated here. Re-verified 2026-08-02: CNN's reporting on the NIAID listening-only restriction, corroborated by US News, HealthDay, and other outlets citing the same internal May 18, 2026 email, documents an active administration policy choice restricting scientist communication, distinct from and in addition to the passive membership-loss effect already documented in this entry. Reordered 2026-08-06 (chronology cleanup, no new facts): the February 2026 alternative-surveillance-system proposal had been placed after May 2026 content; no facts were added, removed, or altered, only reordered to match actual event dates. Added 2026-08-10: the WHO staff-cut figure is well-corroborated (The Guardian, citing WHO's own announcement) and adds a concrete institutional-capacity number to this entry's existing surveillance-access-loss claim.

title: U.S. Wildland Fire Service Created Without Congressional Approval, Reverses to Discredited Full-Suppression Policy -- Three Firefighters Killed
institution: U.S. Wildland Fire Service (Department of the Interior)
status: Ongoing -- agency operational since early 2026, full-suppression order in effect; no congressional ratification of the agency's creation identified as of this entry
date_of_action: 2025-06-16 (Trump executive order directing DOI/USDA to develop a consolidation plan) through 2026-06-27 (Colorado firefighter deaths)
what_changed: On June 16, 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing the Interior and Agriculture Departments to develop, within 90 days, a plan to consolidate their separate wildland firefighting operations into a single new agency -- immediately shifting thousands of firefighters from the Forest Service's existing structure in the middle of that year's peak wildfire season, which critics called costly and disruptive. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced the resulting consolidation plan in September 2025, and on January 12, 2026 formally established the U.S. Wildland Fire Service by consolidating wildland firefighting personnel from four existing Interior Department agencies -- the Bureau of Land Management, Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Indian Affairs, and National Park Service -- without the customary congressional approval such a reorganization would typically receive. The new agency, headed by Brian Fennessy (formerly chief of the Orange County Fire Authority), operates under a Burgum order requiring 'full suppression for every wildfire under its management' -- a reversal of decades of fire-management policy that had accepted controlled and naturally-occurring fire as a land-management tool, and a return to an approach fire scientists compare to the discredited 1935 '10 a.m. rule' (extinguish every fire by the following morning). On June 27, 2026, three federal firefighters were killed and two more hospitalized with burn injuries battling a fast-growing wildfire near the Utah border in Colorado; the crew was overrun by flames and deployed emergency shelters. At least one of the deceased worked for the new Wildland Fire Service. Critics, including retired BLM official Steve Ellis, argue that severing forest management from firefighting operations 'will make firefighting less safe and put communities at greater risk,' and fire scientist David Calkin noted that suppressing every fire allows fuel to accumulate, making future fires harder to contain. Critics also note the four original agencies already extinguished 98% of the fires they handled before the reorganization, raising questions about what problem the full-suppression policy and new agency structure are meant to solve.

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of the Interior
primary_proponent.note: Personally ordered the consolidation of four agencies' wildland firefighting personnel into the new U.S. Wildland Fire Service and issued the directive requiring full suppression of every wildfire under the new agency's management.

estimated_impact.summary: Three federal firefighters died and two were hospitalized in the first major test of the new agency's full-suppression approach, in a policy reversal that fire-management experts warn increases long-term wildfire risk by allowing fuel to accumulate, and that critics say endangers firefighters by severing forest management from fire suppression decisions.

The 98%-success figure is presented by critics of the reorganization to question its stated rationale, not confirmed via an independent audit.
